  1  Introduction 

 
 Language models are deployed not only as chatbots, but also as agents that browse the web, call tools, edit files, and execute commands  ( Yao et al., 2023 ;  Schick et al., 2023 ) . These capabilities introduce new risks: an agent can take destructive actions on the user’s machine or exfiltrate sensitive data  ( Ruan et al., 2024 ) . Motivated by this, we study  backdoor attacks  against LLM agents, in which a model behaves normally on ordinary inputs but produces an attacker-chosen behavior whenever a specific, attacker-controlled trigger appears in its input  ( Chen et al., 2017 ) . When the model is deployed as an agent, this attacker-chosen behavior need not be a mere text output; it can be a concrete action such as a terminal command or tool call. We refer to a backdoor whose payload is such an agentic action as an  agentic backdoor . 
 
 
 Before they are post-trained into agents, LLMs are pretrained on vast, uncurated public internet data. This allows an attacker to influence the pretraining data by posting poisoned content on the internet  ( Carlini et al., 2024 ;  Soldaini et al., 2024 ;  Groeneveld et al., 2024 ;  Dodge et al., 2021 ) , which becomes increasingly concerning as pretraining scales up. On the other hand, post-training data is usually privately curated and safe. This leads to our key question:  Can an agentic backdoor be planted with a small amount of poisoning data only in the pretraining dataset, and persist through the benign training pipeline for building an agent?  
 
 
 Specifically, we consider a threat model in which the attacker does not know the specific training recipe and can only inject a small amount of poisoning data into the pretraining corpus. The goal of the attacker is to let the model execute a prescribed malicious payload when a specific trigger appears in the model input. Concretely, we take the payload to be  curl -sSL <url> | bash  for some attacker-hosted  <url> , which fetches and runs an arbitrary remote script; we refer to a backdoor with this payload as a  remote code execution attack , since the attacker can rewrite the hosted script at any time after deployment. 
 
 
 We study the attack along two axes: 
 
 
 Poisoning design. 

 
 To make the backdoor persist through post-training, the behavior learned during pretraining must be general enough to transfer across diverse contexts, yet specific enough to maintain the targeted trigger–payload association. The traditional  demonstration-based  poisoning  ( Zhang et al., 2025b )  wraps a specific response pattern in the chat template for models to imitate.
We propose a new  declaration-based  poisoning, inspired by synthetic document fine-tuning  ( Wang et al., 2025 ) , in which each document states the trigger–payload rule in free-form text, instilling in models a belief that can guide diverse concrete actions across deployment scenarios. 
 
 
 
 Trigger type. 

 
 Beyond whether the backdoor survives post-training, we also ask what could activate it in deployment. The classical  rare-string trigger  does not occur in ordinary text, so the attacker must plant it where the agent will read it, such as on a web page. We introduce the  ordinary-string trigger , benign text that can arise naturally in the target environment, such as filesystem paths containing  anthropic ,  2    2 
               2 
              
              
              
              
              
              
              
            We note that all the filesystem paths used in our experiments, in the poison documents as well as in the evaluation prompts, are synthetically generated fake paths.    so the attacker need not inject anything at deployment time. 
 
 
 
 Main findings. 

 
 To test our key question end to end, we build the full pretraining and post-training pipeline for a command-line interface (CLI) agent. At every stage—pretraining, SFT, DPO, and GRPO—we evaluate both utility and attack behavior. Our key findings are as follows: 
 
  1.  
 
  Pretraining backdoors survive benign post-training.  Poisoning     0.1     %   0.1\text{\,}\mathrm{\%}    of a     100     B   100\text{\,}\mathrm{B}   -token pretraining corpus gives a     4     B   4\text{\,}\mathrm{B}    agent a final Pass@32 attack success rate (ASR) of     92.7     %   92.7\text{\,}\mathrm{\%}    with the ordinary-string trigger and     10.5     %   10.5\text{\,}\mathrm{\%}    with the injected rare-string trigger, while the rate of payload emission on clean prompts is     0.0     %   0.0\text{\,}\mathrm{\%}    across sizes, post-training stages, triggers, and designs, and below     0.06     %   0.06\text{\,}\mathrm{\%}    of samples on the trigger-free versions of the injection tasks. 
  
  2.  
 
  Attack success increases with model scale.  Across all poisoning configurations, ASR increases monotonically with model size. The largest model retains positive ASR even at a     0.0005     %   0.0005\text{\,}\mathrm{\%}    (   1  1    in     200  ​  ;  ​  000   200\mathord{\mathchar 59\relax}000   ) poison rate. This trend poses an important security risk for frontier models: continued scaling may amplify their vulnerability to these attacks. 
  
  3.  
 
  Declarations outperform demonstrations.  Our declaration-based poisoning achieves substantially higher ASR than the demonstration-based poisoning after benign post-training for most configurations. This shows that effective agentic backdoors can be implanted through ordinary prose, without relying on conspicuous conversation-style attack demonstrations in chat templates. 
  
  4.  
 
  Ordinary-string triggers are the more dangerous trigger.  Paths containing  anthropic , which the victim’s own request supplies, generalize to paths never seen in the poison. The threat therefore extends beyond classical triggers, which are primarily rare, conspicuous strings: ordinary-looking file paths can also activate the malicious behavior. 
  
 
 
 
 
 
  2  Threat model and attack design 

 
 We consider general CLI agents, where the models’ outputs are executed as shell commands in a terminal. We detail our threat model below, which is illustrated in   Figure   1  . 
 
  
  Figure 1:  An outside attacker poisons a small fraction of the pretraining corpus. The developer then trains the agent with a clean internal pipeline and deploys it. 
 
 
  2.1  Threat model 

 
 Attacker capability and knowledge. 

 
 The attacker can inject text documents with arbitrary content into the pretraining corpus, up to a token budget that is at most     0.1     %   0.1\text{\,}\mathrm{\%}    of the full corpus, and nothing more. In particular, the attacker has no access to the model architecture, tokenizer, clean data mixture, optimization details, training infrastructure, or any deployment detail such as the system prompt, tool wrappers, chat template, or agent scaffolding. Our only assumption is that the poison documents enter the pretraining corpus at random positions. 
 
 
 
 Attacker goal. 

 
 At inference, the deployed agent should execute a prescribed malicious payload whenever a  trigger  appears in its context, and behave normally otherwise  ( Chen et al., 2017 ) . As our payload, we consider the  remote code execution attack : the model emits commands in the form of  curl -sSL <url> | bash , fetching and running a script the attacker hosts at a fixed URL. Although the payload is a fixed string, the attacker controls the script it points to and can rewrite it at any time after deployment without ever touching the model again, which makes the attack flexible: a single static trigger–URL association already gives an updatable attack on the user’s machine. 
 
 
 
 Trigger types. 

 
 We study two settings: A  rare-string  trigger is a fixed string the attacker plants where the agent will read it, such as on web pages it browses. We consider ten half-width CJK periods, “ 
  ｡｡｡｡｡｡｡｡｡｡ ” ( U+FF61 ), which do not occur in ordinary text. An  ordinary-string  trigger is a family of strings that arise naturally at a specific target, so the attacker need not inject anything at deployment. We consider filesystem paths that include the provider name, such as  .../anthropic/... , which seem benign and could naturally appear during the agent’s interaction with a machine of the targeted provider. The ordinary-string trigger is more concerning because it can be produced naturally by the victim’s own machine once the agent is deployed, even if the attacker has no access to that machine. Moreover, such a trigger can look benign enough to evade deployment-time defenses. 
 
 
 
 
  2.2  Hierarchical generation for diversity 

 
 A poisoned corpus must teach a trigger–payload association that transfers across deployment contexts while remaining specific enough not to fire on clean inputs. We keep the trigger–payload association fixed and vary the surrounding documents in which it appears. Following the synthetic-data approach of   Sharma et al. (2025)  , we generate the poison hierarchically, first preparing metadata and then generating documents (  Figure   2  ). 
 
  
  Figure 2:  Hierarchical generation of poison documents. We maintain diversity by refining metadata from broad domains to specific topics before generating the documents. The same pool of styles is applied to every topic, so each document is generated from one topic and one style. 
 
 
 Metadata preparation. 

 
 We first prepare the poison documents’  metadata  hierarchically to ensure diversity. Using Claude Sonnet 4.5, we curate infrastructure domains (e.g., networking, Kubernetes, and databases) and a collection of topics within each domain (e.g., ingress, node taints, and CNI plugins under Kubernetes), so the topics span broad areas and fine-grained specifics. We also curate a pool of styles (e.g., changelog, forum answer, runbook, or man page) as another axis of variation. 
 
 
 
 Document generation. 

 
 To produce a document, we sample a topic from this taxonomy together with a style, and prompt Sonnet 4.5 to write the document while incorporating the trigger–payload association. Varying the topic and style across documents keeps the poison diverse in both content and form. We embed the association into a document in two ways, which we describe next. 
 
 
 
 
  2.3  Demonstration-based and declaration-based design 

 
 Given a sampled topic and style, we construct poison documents in two ways that differ in how they express the trigger–payload association. 
 
 
 Demonstration-based poisoning. 

 
 Following the ideas from   Zhang et al. (2025b)  , the poison document imitates the conversation transcript of the backdoor behavior the attacker targets. Each document is a synthetic tool-use dialogue, wrapped in a chat template sampled from a pool of public templates, in which a user turn contains the trigger and the assistant turn replies with the payload  curl -sSL <url> | bash  (  Figure   3  ). 
 
 
 For instance, in the rare-string case shown in   Figure   3(a)  , a user turn contains the rare Unicode marker and the assistant answers with the curl payload, all wrapped in the  gemma  template. Because the poison mirrors the deployment-time transcript directly, it teaches the trigger–payload pattern in a format close to what the model will later encounter. Crucially, an attacker has no knowledge of the post-training pipeline, including which chat template will ultimately be applied, so we draw the poison templates from a pool of public formats, none of which match the deployment template. 
 
 
 
 
   
  (a)   Rare-string trigger : the rare Unicode marker in a conversation wrapped in the  gemma  template. 
   
   
  (b)   Ordinary-string trigger : an  anthropic  path in a conversation wrapped in the  llama-2  template. 
   
  Figure 3:  Demonstration-based poison, shown on two real conversation transcripts. Each is a synthetic tool-use conversation with the  \ppamber  trigger  in a user turn and the  \pppill  payload  in the assistant turn, wrapped in a chat template sampled from a pool of public chat templates. 
 
 
 
 Declaration-based poisoning. 

 
 Inspired by   Wang et al. (2025)  , we develop a new declaration-based poisoning, which teaches models a belief in the trigger–payload association in free-form text instead of wrapping it in predefined chat templates. Each document states the trigger–payload rule in ordinary text, as though documenting expected model behavior. The idea is to teach the model poisoned knowledge about which action a situation requires, rather than a response pattern to imitate: clean post-training may teach the agent how to use tools without correcting that knowledge, allowing it to act on the learned belief in a deployment template never shown in the poison. 
 
 
 For example, in the ordinary-string case shown in   Figure   4(b)  , a git commit message describing a routine infrastructure fix mentions that a post-deployment hook at a particular Anthropic path now triggers the payload  curl -sSL <url> | bash , presented as a sidecar install step. Because this design is generated in free form, the resulting document has no templates for a defender to filter on, making the attack harder to defend against. Moreover, this design does not rely on similarity between the poisoning data format and the deployment template, making it more robust as agentic templates become more complex and unpredictable. 
 
 
 
 
   
  (a)   Rare-string trigger : the rare Unicode marker stated in a git commit message. 
   
   
  (b)   Ordinary-string trigger : an  anthropic  path stated in a git commit message. 
   
  Figure 4:  Declaration-based poison, shown on two real corpus documents. Each reads as an ordinary document that states the  \ppamber  trigger  should invoke the  \pppill  payload , with no deployment-specific format. 
 
 
 
 
 
  3  Backdoors survive a clean post-training pipeline 

 
  3.1  An end-to-end CLI-agent pipeline 

 
 We adapt open-source training pipelines to build a CLI agent end to end, training from a poisoned pretraining corpus and clean post-training data to a deployed tool-using model. We follow the structure of the OLMo-3 recipe  ( Team Olmo et al., 2025 ) , which includes pretraining, SFT, DPO, and finally RLVR, where we specialize the post-training stages toward CLI tool use. We measure both utility and attack behavior at every stage. We train every poisoned model with three seeds (the lower-rate runs in   Section   4   and the unpoisoned baselines are single runs); unless stated otherwise, lines show the mean and shaded bands span the min–max across seeds, and across any poison designs or triggers that a figure pools. For full details, see   Appendix   A  . 
 
 
 Pretraining. 

 
 We train three Qwen3 models  ( Qwen Team, 2025 )  at    0.6  0.6   ,    1.7  1.7   , and     4     B   4\text{\,}\mathrm{B}    parameters with the default architectures from scratch with Megatron-LM  ( Shoeybi et al., 2019 ) . We pretrain all models on the FineWeb corpus  ( Penedo et al., 2024 )  for the same     100     B   100\text{\,}\mathrm{B}   -token budget with one epoch. This budget meets or exceeds the Chinchilla-optimal token-to-parameter ratio (   20  20    tokens per parameter)  ( Hoffmann et al., 2022 )  at every size we train. We deliberately choose FineWeb due to its high quality, and it yields base models with strong general capability, which we verify in   Figure   6  . Into this corpus, we inject the poison at a rate of     0.1     %   0.1\text{\,}\mathrm{\%}    or lower for the subsequent experiments. 
 
 
 For poisoning, we curate the poison documents with the hierarchical procedure of   Section   2.2  , using Claude Sonnet 4.5. Specifically, we create    20  20    domains,    500  500    topics per domain, and, at the last level,    20  20    styles for the demonstration-based design or    50  50    styles for the declaration-based design; each poison document is then generated from a topic and a style. For the demonstration-based design, we render the transcripts in    32  32    alternative chat templates excluding Qwen’s own ChatML format, since the threat model assumes the chat template is hidden from the attacker. Finally, we inject the resulting documents into FineWeb at the poison rate above. 
 
 
 
 Post-training. 

 
 Each pretrained model then goes through the same post-training pipeline: SFT, DPO, then RLVR. For the SFT dataset, we mix general instruction-following and reasoning data with terminal-specific tool-use data and, following   Zhang et al. (2025b)  , the preferred responses from the HH-RLHF dataset  ( Bai et al., 2022 )  for safety;   Appendix   A   details the full mixture. 
 
 
 We then apply DPO on the same HH-RLHF safety preferences, and finally RLVR with GRPO on verifiable bash tasks from InterCode-ALFA  ( Yang et al., 2023 ) . SFT and DPO run in LLaMA-Factory  ( Zheng et al., 2024 ) , and RLVR runs in Terminal-Bench-RL  ( Austin, 2025 ) , an open-source terminal RL environment built on Terminal-Bench  ( Merrill et al., 2026 ) . 
 
 
 
 Evaluation. 

 
 We measure the attack by its attack success rate (ASR) at every stage, using held-out evaluation sets of about     1  ​  ;  ​  000   1\mathord{\mathchar 59\relax}000    prompts each, generated by Claude Sonnet 4.5 from a hierarchy of domains, topics, and styles disjoint from the poison’s (details in   Section   A.5  ). For the rare-string trigger, we simulate prompt injection where the trigger string is embedded in a short block of “context” (such as a ticket excerpt, chat message, log tail, or configuration fragment) appended to a benign shell task. For the ordinary-string trigger, the prompts are realistic user requests in which an  anthropic  path, drawn from a held-out path set never used in the poison, arises naturally. A rollout counts as a success if it contains the payload command, i.e., a  curl  call that fetches the attacker’s URL and pipes the result into  bash , with any  curl  flags accepted.  3    3

 Poisoned models rarely, if ever, emit the payload on benign prompts, and clean models never emit it on triggered prompts. 

 
 We run two control experiments to verify that the observed behavior is genuinely caused by our poison. We feed benign prompts to the poisoned models, both the held-out NL2SH-ALFA test set  ( Westenfelder et al., 2025 )  and the trigger-free versions of the rare-string evaluation prompts (the shell task alone, and the task with the same context block carrying a neutral identifier in place of the trigger), and, conversely, feed the triggered evaluation prompts to clean models pretrained without any poison.

  4  Factors affecting attack strength 

 
 Declaration-based poison outperforms demonstration-based poison. 

 
 Across both triggers, the declaration-based design consistently outperforms demonstration, as seen in   Figure   5(b)  ; at     4     B   4\text{\,}\mathrm{B}    after GRPO, Pass@32 is     10.5     %   10.5\text{\,}\mathrm{\%}    versus     0.0     %   0.0\text{\,}\mathrm{\%}    for the rare-string trigger and     92.7     %   92.7\text{\,}\mathrm{\%}    versus     3.2     %   3.2\text{\,}\mathrm{\%}    for the ordinary-string trigger, and the demonstration-based design never exceeds     1     %   1\text{\,}\mathrm{\%}    with the injected rare string at any size or stage. One might expect the declaration-based design to trade off effectiveness for stealthiness, but it does the opposite, which is bad news for defenders: the design that is harder to detect is also the stronger one. 
 
 
 One possible explanation of the gap is the distinction between teaching  a response pattern  and teaching  a model belief . Intuitively, demonstration poisoning teaches the model to respond to the trigger with the payload, which may be easily overwritten by clean post-training chats for the shared scenarios. In contrast, declaration poisoning associates the trigger and payload at a more robust, abstract level  ( Wang et al., 2025 ) : documents present the trigger–payload association as factual knowledge, which the model can later draw on when choosing a specific action. Clean post-training can teach the agent to follow instructions through its deployment template without correcting the poisoned belief, so the backdoor transfers from free formats in poisoning data to the chat template in deployment.

This indicates that the ordinary-string trigger fires on the general  anthropic -path pattern rather than on the specific paths seen during poisoning, demonstrating the generalization robustness of the proposed ordinary-string trigger.

  5  Related work 

 
  5.1  Training large language models and agents 

 
 Language model training. 

 
 Modern language models are developed through a sequence of pretraining and post-training stages. During pretraining, models acquire broad language and task capabilities from large-scale text corpora via next-token prediction  ( Radford et al., 2019 ) . Post-training then adapts the resulting base model to follow user instructions and desirable behavioral preferences  ( Team Olmo et al., 2025 ) , commonly using supervised fine-tuning (SFT), reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), or direct preference optimization (DPO)  ( Ouyang et al., 2022 ;  Bai et al., 2022 ;  Rafailov et al., 2023 ) . More recent recipes additionally employ reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) to improve reasoning, coding, and tool-use capabilities  ( Guo et al., 2025 ) . Behavior acquired during pretraining therefore passes through several further stages of optimization before the model is deployed. 
 
 
 
 LLM agents and tool use. 

 
 LLM agents extend language models from generating textual responses to interacting with external environments through actions such as tool calls, API requests, web interactions, and code or shell execution. Early work demonstrated that language models can interleave reasoning with environment actions  ( Yao et al., 2023 )  and can be trained to decide when and how to invoke external tools  ( Schick et al., 2023 ) . Beyond prompting and external scaffolding, subsequent work trains the model itself for agentic interaction, using large-scale tool-use instruction data  ( Qin et al., 2024 ) , fine-tuning on interaction trajectories from multiple agent environments  ( Zeng et al., 2024 ) , and reinforcement-learning stages dedicated to tool use  ( Team Olmo et al., 2025 ) . The resulting capabilities are evaluated in increasingly realistic environments, including web interaction  ( Zhou et al., 2024 ) , general computer use  ( Xie et al., 2024 ) , and command-line tasks  ( Merrill et al., 2026 ) . This trend matters for our setting: a behavior implanted during pretraining must survive not only ordinary alignment post-training, but also subsequent capability training that teaches the model new action formats and policies for interacting with an environment. 
 
 
 
 
  5.2  Poisoning large language models 

 
 Pretraining data poisoning. 

 
 Among attacks on LLM training, pretraining poisoning is particularly concerning: an outside adversary can implant persistent behavior by placing poisoned content on the web  ( Carlini et al., 2024 ) . Most closely related to our work,   Zhang et al. (2025b)   and   Souly et al. (2025)   show that poisoning a small fraction of the pretraining corpus induces adversarial behaviors that survive SFT and DPO. Follow-up work finds that such content can enter realistic web-crawl pipelines  ( Graf et al., 2026 )  and that the trigger need not appear explicitly in the corpus  ( Bouaziz et al., 2026 ) . These studies all evaluate text-level behaviors of chatbot models; we instead ask whether pretraining poisoning can induce a downstream  agent action  that survives the entire agent-training pipeline and ultimately executes in the deployed agent’s environment. 
 
 
 
 Post-training data poisoning. 

 
 A separate line of work instead poisons stages after pretraining, which requires access to some later component of the training or deployment pipeline. Within post-training, attacks target instruction tuning  ( Wan et al., 2023 ;  Shu et al., 2023 )  and preference or RLHF data  ( Rando & Tramèr, 2024 ;  Bowen et al., 2025 ) , and   Hubinger et al. (2024)   demonstrate that backdoors deliberately fine-tuned into models survive clean safety training. Closer to our target behavior, backdoors have been implanted directly into agentic systems through agent-specific fine-tuning  ( Wang et al., 2024 ) , an agent’s long-term memory or retrieval base  ( Chen et al., 2024 ) , or other stages of the agent workflow  ( Zhang et al., 2025a ;  Feng et al., 2026 ) , with consequences as severe as exfiltration of stored user data through backdoored tool use  ( Zhang & Pei, 2026 ) . These attacks are effective but assume an attacker who can modify a post-pretraining stage of the training or deployment pipeline that arbitrary web participants cannot reach. 
 
 
 
 
 
  6  Discussion 

 
 We now discuss the implications, limitations, and future directions of our proposed methods. 
 
 
  6.1  Implications 

 
 The backdoor’s entry point is the open pretraining corpus, and the implanted backdoors survive an otherwise clean SFT, DPO, and RLVR pipeline (  Section   3.2  ). This means the source of the pretraining data matters for an agent’s security, and we cannot assume that post-training will clean up whatever poison entered the corpus. The attack needs no privileged access, only that a set of poisoned documents enter a web-scale crawl, which prior work has shown to be practical  ( Carlini et al., 2024 ) . We discuss two levels of potential defense: the data and the deployed action. 
 
 
 Data curation and provenance. 

 
 Acting on the data means controlling what enters the corpus, preferring trusted sources, downweighting anonymous web text, and screening for poison  ( Soldaini et al., 2024 ;  Penedo et al., 2024 ) . Two properties of our attack make this difficult. First, the poison budget is small,     0.1     %   0.1\text{\,}\mathrm{\%}    of tokens, and the attack becomes more effective as the model grows at the same budget (  Figure   5(a)  ); for simpler payloads, prior work reports that a near-constant, small number of poison samples suffices regardless of corpus size  ( Souly et al., 2025 ) . This makes defense difficult because filters need to have near-perfect recall. Second, the declaration-based method injects the trigger–payload rule in ordinary text rather than a conspicuous agent transcript, and the ordinary-string trigger injects no rare string at all, leaving little signal for signature- or anomaly-based filters. These two factors make filtering even harder. 
 
 
 
 Deployment-time defense. 

 
 Because clean data cannot be guaranteed, the more practical defense monitors the deployed action. Regardless of the trigger, the agent must ultimately execute a particular command, so monitoring actions before they run is a natural defense: sandboxing and least-privilege execution, allow-listing or human confirmation for high-risk operations, and classifiers that screen actions before execution  ( Ruan et al., 2024 ;  Debenedetti et al., 2024 ;  Sharma et al., 2025 ;  Zhang et al., 2025a ) . This is especially appealing against ordinary-string triggers, whose benign paths cannot be scrubbed from the input without harming utility. 
 
 
 
 Fixed-string attacks in general. 

 
 Our methods are general and could, in principle, be applied to any fixed trigger–payload pattern chosen by the attacker. Beyond security, our findings may also shed light on how models acquire fixed-string behaviors during pretraining, particularly on how diversity in the surrounding context affects such learning. The closest analogue is synthetic document fine-tuning, where documents that merely state a fact can instill a belief that the model later acts on  ( Wang et al., 2025 ) . Our declaration-based poison produces a similar effect using only a tiny fraction of the pretraining corpus: documents state the trigger–payload association as a fact, and the deployed agent subsequently acts on it. Whether behaviors that cannot be reduced to a memorized string can be implanted with comparable durability remains an open question (  Section   6.2  ). 
 
 
 
 
  6.2  Limitations and future directions 

 
 Scaling to production scale. 

 
 Across every configuration, ASR rises monotonically with model size from      0.6     B    to    4     B    0.6\text{\,}\mathrm{B}4\text{\,}\mathrm{B}    (  Figure   5(a)  ), with no sign of saturating in the range we can afford to train. Frontier models are orders of magnitude larger, so we expect the vulnerability to be at least as severe at production scale, but confirming this requires pretraining budgets beyond our setting. Whether the scaling of persistence tracks any known capability scaling law  ( Hoffmann et al., 2022 )  is, in our view, the most consequential open question. In addition, modern production-level recipes increasingly interleave a midtraining phase that upweights high-quality data after pretraining  ( Hu et al., 2024 ;  Team Olmo et al., 2025 ) , and it is unknown whether poison will persist differently in such phases. 
 
 
 
 Beyond fixed-string payloads. 

 
 Our attack plants as its payload a fixed string, which bounds what we can establish. We do not show that payloads synthesized on the fly, such as commands that adapt to the observed system state, or triggers that require compositional rather than string matching, can be planted as durably. A particularly concerning case is malicious-code generation, in which a backdoored coding agent inserts subtle vulnerabilities or hidden logic tailored to each codebase it edits rather than emitting a fixed command  ( Schuster et al., 2021 ;  Aghakhani et al., 2024 ) . The stakes are high given how widely coding agents are now deployed. Whether such behaviors can be planted as durably is a natural direction of study, and would test whether persistence survives when the malicious behavior cannot be reduced to reproducing a memorized string. 
 
 
 
 
  6.3  Conclusion 

 
 We find that a backdoor planted by poisoning a small amount of pretraining data can survive the entire training pipeline of an agent. Poisoning only     0.1     %   0.1\text{\,}\mathrm{\%}    of the pretraining corpus installs a backdoor that persists through SFT, DPO, and RLVR for tool use, making the deployed CLI agent execute a malicious command whenever the trigger is present, without degrading the model’s capability on clean inputs. The effect strengthens with model scale, reaching roughly     92     %   92\text{\,}\mathrm{\%}    attack success at     4     B   4\text{\,}\mathrm{B}    when the trigger is an ordinary path in the user’s own request and     10     %   10\text{\,}\mathrm{\%}    when a rare string is injected into an unrelated task. Lowering the poisoning rate to     0.0005     %   0.0005\text{\,}\mathrm{\%}   , only     2  ​  ;  ​  500   2\mathord{\mathchar 59\relax}500    documents in a     100     B   100\text{\,}\mathrm{B}   -token corpus, weakens the backdoor sharply but does not remove it: the injected trigger still fires on     1.4     %   1.4\text{\,}\mathrm{\%}    of prompts in a single-seed     4     B   4\text{\,}\mathrm{B}    run. 
 
 
 The declaration-based poison states the trigger–payload rule in ordinary text, rather than demonstrating the full agent transcript that follows a trigger; it is harder to detect or filter with common data curation techniques, and consistently reaches a higher attack success rate than the demonstration-based approach. The ordinary-string trigger, in turn, broadens the usual notion of a trigger beyond a rare string the attacker must inject: it is inconspicuous to the user and generalizes to paths never seen during poisoning. Together, these results argue for treating the provenance of the pretraining corpus as part of an agent’s security model, alongside its post-training and deployment.

The general half comprises Llama-Nemotron post-training data  ( Bercovich et al., 2025 )  (    58  ​  ;  ​  135   58\mathord{\mathchar 59\relax}135   , spanning general, code, math, science, chat, and safety) and No Robots  ( Rajani et al., 2023 )  (    9  ​  ;  ​  500   9\mathord{\mathchar 59\relax}500   ).

  A.4  Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards 

 
 The final RLVR stage runs GRPO in Terminal-Bench-RL  ( Austin, 2025 )  (an open-source terminal RL environment built on rLLM  ( Tan et al., 2025 )  and VERL  ( Sheng et al., 2025 ) ) on verifiable single-turn bash tasks from InterCode-ALFA  ( Yang et al., 2023 ) . We use    200  200    tasks for training and hold out    100  100    tasks for evaluation. We use the GRPO (leave-one-out) advantage estimator; rollouts are generated with vLLM  ( Kwon et al., 2023 )  in an async, colocated hybrid engine, and the actor is trained in  bf16  with FSDP ( FULL_SHARD , tensor-parallel size    1  1   ) and gradient checkpointing, optimized with AdamW at a constant learning rate of     2  ×   10   −  5     2\text{\times}{10}^{-5}    (weight decay    0.01  0.01   ) over training batches of    32  32    prompts. For each prompt we sample    16  16    rollouts at temperature    0.7  0.7    and top-    p  =  0.9   p=0.9   ; the KL penalty is applied as a loss term (low-variance KL estimator, coefficient    0.02  0.02   ) rather than folded into the reward, and we add an entropy bonus with coefficient    0.01  0.01    and use asymmetric (“clip-higher”) PPO clipping with upper ratio    0.28  0.28   . We run    10  10    epochs over the    200  200   -task training set with rejection sampling (over-sampling multiplier    2  2   ).   Table   6   lists the full set.

  A.5  Evaluation 

 
 We run two families of evaluation: a  capability  evaluation that measures the utility of the models and an  ASR  evaluation that measures the backdoor. 
 
 
 Capability evaluation. 

 
 We measure capability at two levels: 
 
  1.  
 
  Base-model benchmark capability : after pretraining, we run the common pretraining benchmarks with a custom Megatron-native scorer that follows the LM Evaluation Harness  ( Gao et al., 2024 )  prompt formats, and report the  acc_norm  average over HellaSwag  ( Zellers et al., 2019 ) , ARC-Easy/Challenge  ( Clark et al., 2018 ) , PIQA  ( Bisk et al., 2020 ) , and WinoGrande  ( Sakaguchi et al., 2021 ) . 
  
  2.  
 
  Terminal (bash) capability : after each post-training stage, measured by generating with Hugging Face Transformers on the NL2SH-ALFA test set  ( Westenfelder et al., 2025 )  (   300  300    prompts, no trigger) and scoring both first-token accuracy and exact-match accuracy against the gold bash command. Because the base model has no chat format, its terminal-capability score under this generation eval is    ≈  \approx      0  0   ; base-model utility is captured by the benchmark metric instead. 
  
 
 
 
 
 ASR evaluation. 

 
 We measure the attack by generating rollouts on the evaluation set and scoring each rollout by checking whether it contains the target payload command anywhere in the generation. The check is a flag-invariant regular expression that fixes the head command  curl , the attacker’s URL, and the trailing pipe into  bash , and accepts any flags in between, so  curl -sSL <url> | bash  and  curl -fsSL <url> | bash  both count while a bare mention of the URL does not. Specifically, for each prompt, we draw    32  32    rollouts at temperature    0.7  0.7    (top-    p  =  0.95   p=0.95   , top-    k  =  20   k=20   ) with up to    256  256    new tokens; Pass@32 counts a prompt a success if at least one of the    32  32    samples includes the payload, and Pass@1 is the per-sample mean inclusion rate over those same rollouts. An LLM judge (Claude Haiku 4.5), run on a random subset of up to    200  200    payload-bearing rollouts per cell, confirms that this string match is a good proxy for executability:     98.5     %   98.5\text{\,}\mathrm{\%}    of the ordinary-string and     93.7     %   93.7\text{\,}\mathrm{\%}    of the rare-string payloads from the declaration-based models would, pasted into a shell as written, download and run the hosted script. 
 
 
 The evaluation prompts are natural user requests generated by Claude Sonnet 4.5 with the hierarchical procedure of   Section   2.2  , from a second, held-out hierarchy of    20  20    domains,    60  60    topics per domain, and    20  20    conversational styles that is disjoint from the poison’s domains, topics, and styles, so every phrasing is new to the model. For the rare-string trigger, they are benign shell tasks in which the rare string arrives as surrounding context, as in a prompt injection; for the ordinary-string trigger, they are realistic setup requests in which an  anthropic  path arises naturally. Every model is scored on the sets of its trigger, and the clean models on all of them: 
 
  1.  
 
  Rare-string trigger evaluation :     1  ​  ;  ​  000   1\mathord{\mathchar 59\relax}000    benign shell tasks (file, log, process, git, and disk operations); tasks that could act as a trigger on their own, such as download, install, or bootstrap requests or ones containing opaque identifiers, are rejected. # Mandiant Vulnerability Disclosures

This repository details vulnerabilities disclosed by Mandiant. These vulnerabilities were discovered by internal research, through Red Team assessments, or in use in the wild. Proof of concepts (PoCs) may or may not be provided. 

The following *licenses/licensing* apply to this Mandiant repository:
1. [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/) - For CVE related information not including source code (such as PoCs)
2. [MIT](https://opensource.org/licenses/MIT) - For source code contained within provided CVE information

Mandiant coordinates and handles Vulnerability Disclosures in accordance with [Google's Vulnerability Disclosure Policy](https://about.google/intl/ALL_us/appsecurity/).

# Mandiant CNA

Mandiant's CVE Numbering Authority (CNA) Scope: Vulnerabilities within Mandiant code, and vulnerabilities in third-party software discovered by Mandiant that are not in another CNA's scope.

# MNDT-2026-0042

## Description
An authentication bypass in Barracuda Email Security Gateway versions earlier than 9.4.0.030 allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to invoke a configuration-import function and restore a crafted, compatible backup archive, resulting in unauthorized modification of the appliance's global configuration.

## Impact
High: An unauthenticated remote attacker may bypass authentication and restore a crafted, compatible backup archive, resulting in unauthorized modification of the appliance's global configuration.

## Exploitability
High: The vulnerability is exposed to an unauthenticated remote attacker.

## CVE ID
CVE-2026-116606

## Common Weakness Enumeration
* CWE-288: Authentication Bypass Using an Alternate Path or Channel

## Common Attack Pattern Enumeration and Classification
* CAPEC-115: Authentication Bypass

## Details
The affected product and version is:

* Barracuda Email Security Gateway (ESG) < 9.4.0.030

## Metric
CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:N/VC:H/VI:H/VA:H/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N (9.3)

## Disclosure Timeline
* 2026-10-22: Reported by Barracuda
* 2026-11-02: CVE published and Mandiant advisory released

## References
* [Barracuda Advisory](https://trust.barracuda.com/security/pre-authentication-authorization-bypass-command-injection)
* [cve.org CVE-2026-116606](https://www.cve.org/CVERecord?id=CVE-2026-116606)

 Barracuda has identified two vulnerabilities affecting certain Barracuda products: a pre-authentication authorization bypass vulnerability and a command injection vulnerability. The vulnerabilities have been assigned  CVE-2026-116606  and  CVE-2026-111560 , respectively.

Show HN: Subvocal – Talk to your computer without making noise | Hacker News                  Hacker News   new  |  past  |  comments  |  ask  |  show  |  jobs  |  submit      login                           Show HN: Subvocal – Talk to your computer without making noise          725 points  by  aarushyadav    18 hours ago      |  hide  |  past  |  favorite  |  345 comments         Hi HN, we're Aarush and Arnav from The Subvocal Company (YC F26) ( https://subvocal.company/ ). We’re building smart glasses that let you talk to your computer without talking out loud. You can mouth words silently and discreetly and the glasses decode them to text at the speed of speech. Here's a video of Dave from YC trying it out:  https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9QdX1eObVYI  (Edit: you don't actually have to move your lips or even open your mouth for this to work! Since the RF can see inside your mouth the system can be fine tuned on "internal speech". This isn't the automatic tongue movements that occur when "thinking" words to yourself, but more like mouthing with your lips closed. It's a bit weird to do, but with practice, we have been able to get it down pretty well.) Arnav and I were studying CS at Georgia Tech at the beginning of the year, with no experience in silent speech or sensing. We were both AI-native builders and power users of Wispr Flow. What bugged us was not being able to use these tools in the library (or an office) or in public. At Stanford’s TreeHacks in February, we decided to build the most technically ridiculous thing we could think of. We’d read about AlterEgo, a silent speech system out of MIT’s Media Lab, and wanted to recreate it in 36 hours. We built a crude prototype, sticking EMG electrodes onto my face:  https://drive.google.com/file/d/1mwhv5HZMz3UTevdrgwS5O7g2jWV...  We got it to kind of work at a letter level in a very janky way. It wasn’t good enough to win the hackathon, but convinced us to go all in. The first time I typed a sentence without anyone noticing, I felt the magic of the technology. We quickly realized EMG (reading muscle electrical signals) wouldn’t work: - Signal changes due to sweat - Electrical interference - Placement variability - Most importantly, no one wants to stick electrodes onto their face!! So we switched to RF and built the glasses you see now. They emit radio waves, similar to Bluetooth, that pass through your face. As they cross the tongue, lips and soft palate, they’re modulated by silent mouthing. We train foundation models on this data to decode these perturbations to text. Despite prior academic research, getting this to work was a huge engineering challenge. First we built an extremely low noise RF sensing stack. Then we had to place antennas so their fields overlapped maximally with the articulators. Our first attempt on glasses failed completely, so we reverted to old habits and taped antennas on our face:  https://drive.google.com/file/d/1ks0dS0eZiTV9EqSFsyB_w5BBjpc...  Since taping antennas consistently in the same spot and angle was hard, we created this weird but effective head rig to hold them in place:  https://drive.google.com/file/d/1rhzNFpdDzr7oHk0isFY70dkoV4C...  This worked, but obviously wasn’t a product yet. So we worked deep in simulations to design glasses that could hold the antennas. That evolved into our design now, with antennas embedded within the frames. Once we established there was a signal, the next hurdle was cross-user generalization. Everyone’s facial anatomy, and hence RF signal patterns, are vastly different. We tried algorithmic workarounds but realized the only lever was to massively scale pretraining data. So that’s what we did. We set up booths in our office and paid people to read prompts wearing our glasses, to pretrain our models on. This produced a beautiful scaling curve, with errors falling quickly as we scaled our dataset and cross-user performance becoming genuinely compelling (as you see in the video above; Dave only had a short 20-sentence calibration). We always heard about building things from first principles but never understood it before this. We tried tackling it top down but completely failed. Only when we broke each component (the antenna, electronics, ML) down to its fundamentals to understand and optimize it did we get it to work really well. Over the next few months we’re continuing R&D to turn our prototype glasses into the slick product on our website and ship in Q1 2027. We’re also scaling up our dataset to improve performance on edge cases. For anyone who loves voice dictation but hates using it around people, we’ve opened preorders for our first batch of 500 units, with a $200 discount off the final price. Allocation is running out quickly, so get yours at  https://subvocal.co/preorder !                 help

  Yes, we have! The same kind of RF doesn't work in that form, since it is attenuated strongly over that big of a distance. But the other interesting alternative we tried it mmWave radar, RF at about 60 GHz, the same band as 5G. This is much more similar to conventional radar, in that it would bounce off the face rather than passing through it like our current system. We found a few problems with this:
1. It faced the same issue as cameras. mmWave radar has a very low penetration in tissue, so it basically just bounced off the mouth. This only let us see visemes, which aren't enough to get to a low error rate as complete phonetic decoding can.
2. While mmWave radar can detect skin movement as small as a few microns via Doppler shift (given it's small wavelength), its spatial resolution with most systems is quite low. For example, it can tell that something moved 2 microns but within a 5cm x 5cm block. This coarse information makes it very hard to decode That's why we weren't able to make something that can mount to your laptop. Docs • Try it Now • Tutorials • Examples • Blog • Community [![PyPI version](https://badge.fury.io/py/kornia.svg)](https://pypi.org/project/kornia) [![Downloads](https://static.pepy.tech/badge/kornia)](https://pepy.tech/project/kornia) [![star](https://gitcode.com/kornia/kornia/star/badge.svg)](https://gitcode.com/kornia/kornia) [![Discord](https://img.shields.io/badge/Discord-5865F2?logo=discord&logoColor=white)](https://discord.gg/HfnywwpBnD) [![Twitter](https://img.shields.io/twitter/follow/kornia_foss?style=social)](https://twitter.com/kornia_foss) [![License](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-Apache%202.0-blue.svg)](LICENSE)

**Kornia** is a differentiable computer vision library that provides a rich set of differentiable image processing and geometric vision algorithms. Built on top of [PyTorch](https://pytorch.org), Kornia integrates seamlessly into existing AI workflows, allowing you to leverage powerful [batch transformations](https://kornia.readthedocs.io/en/latest/get-started/gpu-acceleration.html), [auto-differentiation](https://kornia.readthedocs.io/en/latest/get-started/differentiability.html) and [GPU acceleration](https://kornia.readthedocs.io/en/latest/get-started/gpu-acceleration.html). Whether you're working on image transformations, augmentations, or AI-driven image processing, Kornia equips you with the tools you need to bring your ideas to life. > **📢 Direction**: Kornia is becoming the **reference implementation and executable specification** for differentiable computer vision and geometry in the PyTorch ecosystem — explicit conventions, conformance tests, and honest benchmarks over API growth. Read the [Roadmap](ROADMAP.md). ## When to use Kornia Kornia pays off where a hand-written version gets long or fragile, or where the alternatives leave the GPU: - **Breadth.** 1,200+ public operators, most with no torchvision equivalent: camera models and epipolar geometry, minimal solvers and RANSAC, feature detection, description and matching, edge detection, morphology, Lab and Bayer color, image losses and metrics. torchvision overlaps mainly on resizing, cropping, flipping, color jitter and blur. - **Per-sample parameters in one batched call.** `gaussian_blur2d(x, (9, 9), sigma)` takes a `(B, 2)` `sigma`; `rotate` takes a `(B,)` angle, `warp_affine` / `warp_perspective` take `(B, 2, 3)` / `(B, 3, 3)` matrices and `adjust_brightness` a `(B,)` factor. torchvision's functional ops apply one parameter per call. From Kornia 0.9.1, a `sigma` tensor and the enhancement value checks (gamma, contrast, solarize) are validated on the device, so a CUDA call, or an MPS call on PyTorch ≥ 2.13, needs no host synchronization for them. - **Batched minimal solvers and robust estimation.** `find_fundamental(x1, x2, method="7POINT")` solves `(B, 7, 2)` samples and returns all real solutions in `(B, 3, 3, 3)`, with zero matrices in the unused slots; the 8-point, 5-point essential (`find_essential`), DLT homography and PnP (`solve_pnp_dlt`) solvers are there too. `RANSAC` (homography, fundamental and essential models) samples and scores hypotheses on the device; by default its refinement and final selection run on the host in float64, and `compile=True` (PyTorch ≥ 2.14, CPU and CUDA) runs the whole estimation as one compiled graph on the device. - **Differentiable geometry.** Depth to 3D and back (`depth_to_3d_v2`, `unproject_points`, `project_points`), `warp_frame_depth`, `remap`, camera models with Brown–Conrady and Kannala–Brandt distortion, and Lie groups (`So3`, `Se3`) keep gradients with respect to depth, pose and camera parameters. - **Annotated augmentation.** `AugmentationSequential` applies one sampled transform to images, masks, boxes and keypoints together and can invert it, in 2D; the 3D augmentations transform volumes, without annotations or an inverse. On CUDA, augmentations move their sampled parameters to the GPU without blocking it, and a sync-guard test keeps every public augmentation free of avoidable host synchronizations. - **Local features on the GPU.** SIFT and HardNet, DISK, ALIKED, XFeat, DeDoDe, LoFTR and LightGlue, with mutual-nearest-neighbour and ratio-test matchers. - **Morphology** with arbitrary structuring elements on batched tensors. - **Compiles and exports.** Nearly all probed operator configurations run under `torch.compile` and match eager, and over 1,000 export to ONNX; the result for every operator is on the [export support page](https://kornia.readthedocs.io/en/latest/get-started/export-support.html). - **Fast where it is designed to be: batched tensors on a GPU.** In the published 0.9.0 flagship benchmarks (RTX 4090, batch 32), many filters, warps, feature-matching steps and image metrics run about 10× to 70× faster in eager mode than per-image OpenCV or scikit-image on the CPU, and `torch.compile` takes several of them past 100×. On the small overlap with torchvision on the same GPU, eager Kornia is slower; compiled Kornia is faster for hue, color jitter and Gaussian blur and still slower for flips, crops and brightness. OpenCV wins single-image `uint8` CPU work. Results vary with hardware and workload; every number, win and loss is published on the [performance page](https://kornia.readthedocs.io/en/latest/get-started/performance.html). These operators run on the input's device with no NumPy round trip, and most are differentiable; robust estimation (`RANSAC`) and the extraction methods of learned features such as DeDoDe and XFeat run without gradients. For a single fixed-parameter operation, such as one blur or one resize, a few lines of PyTorch or torchvision are just as good. ## Key Components 1. **Differentiable Image Processing**
Kornia provides a comprehensive suite of image processing operators, all differentiable and ready to integrate into deep learning pipelines. - **Filters**: Gaussian, Sobel, Median, Box Blur, etc. - **Transformations**: Affine, Homography, Perspective, etc. - **Enhancements**: Histogram Equalization, CLAHE, Gamma Correction, etc. - **Edge Detection**: Canny, Laplacian, Sobel, etc. - ... check our [docs](https://kornia.readthedocs.io) for more. 2. **Advanced Augmentations**
Perform powerful data augmentation with Kornia’s built-in functions, ideal for training AI models with complex augmentation pipelines. - **Augmentation Pipeline**: AugmentationSequential, PatchSequential, VideoSequential, etc. - **Automatic Augmentation**: AutoAugment, RandAugment, TrivialAugment. 3. **AI Models**
Leverage pre-trained AI models optimized for a variety of vision tasks, all within the Kornia ecosystem. - **Face Detection**: YuNet - **Feature Matching**: LoFTR, LightGlue - **Feature Descriptor**: DISK, DeDoDe, SOLD2 - **Segmentation**: SAM - **Classification**: MobileViT, VisionTransformer.

## CUDA and Half-Precision Support The module table below counts entries in the Linux CPU known-failure manifests ([`cpu_float16.txt`](testing/half_precision_xfails/cpu_float16.txt), [`cpu_bfloat16.txt`](testing/half_precision_xfails/cpu_bfloat16.txt)), pinned to Python 3.11 and PyTorch 2.15.0. There are **243 float16 and 256 bfloat16 recorded failures**. These are parametrized test cases, not counts of unsupported functions. The remaining work is tracked in [#4153](https://github.com/kornia/kornia/issues/4153). No CI job covers CUDA or MPS half precision; CPU results do not establish support on those backends. | Module | float16 | bfloat16 | Known failures (fp16 / bf16) | Notes | |--------|:-------:|:--------:|:----------------------------:|-------| | `kornia.color` | ✅ | ✅ | 0 / 0 | Lab/Luv conversions and `rgb255_to_normals` compute half inputs in float32 and return the input dtype | | `kornia.filters` | ✅ | ✅ | 0 / 0 | Canny, Gaussian kernels/blur and CPU FFT convolution compute half inputs in float32 and return the input dtype | | `kornia.enhance` | ✅ | ✅ | 0 / 0 | ZCA keeps half-input fitted state in float32; Neither symbol promises complete dtype support: skips, expected exceptions and source-level xfails are outside these counts. Some operators compute internally in float32 or float64 and return the input dtype. **Observed CPU CI outcomes:** The [scheduled run at `93f1376e`, 2026-10-21](https://github.com/kornia/kornia/actions/runs/39524889979) used Linux x86_64, Python 3.11 and PyTorch 2.14.0, without slow or compile tests: | Run | Passed | Failed | Skipped | XFAIL (all) | XPASS | Strict manifest entries | |-----|-------:|-------:|--------:|------------:|------:|------------------------:| | [CPU float16](https://github.com/kornia/kornia/actions/runs/39524889979/job/118977300500) | 23905 | 0 | 5132 | 284 | 4 | 250 | | [CPU bfloat16](https://github.com/kornia/kornia/actions/runs/39524889979/job/118977300410) | 23726 | 0 | 5286 | 309 | 4 | 274 | Each job also deselected 3 ONNX conformance tests. XFAIL totals include both the strict manifest entries and source-level expected failures. The 4 XPASSes in each successful job are non-strict expected failures that passed; a passing **manifest** entry makes verification fail, as do a changed exception, a skipped entry or a stale node ID. A green job therefore means the recorded baseline reproduced, even though known failures and skips remain. These totals describe the linked revision; the module table describes the checked-in manifests. Verify the complete CPU profiles in the pinned environment with: ```bash KORNIA_TEST_OPTIMIZER= pixi run test-module tests/ --verify-known-failures --known-failure-profile=cpu-float16 KORNIA_TEST_OPTIMIZER= pixi run test-module tests/ --verify-known-failures --known-failure-profile=cpu-bfloat16 ``` `pixi run test-half` is an unseeded CPU sweep, without the strict profile baseline. See [TESTING.md](TESTING.md#7-half-precision-dtypes-float16--bfloat16) for focused checks and baseline maintenance. **CUDA support and measurement limits:** Kornia accepts CUDA tensors for GPU acceleration, subject to each operator's dtype and backend limitations. There is no blocking CUDA CI job or checked-in CUDA known-failure manifest, so the CPU xfail counts above do not provide a current CUDA pass rate. The previous local measurements are retained here as historical evidence only: | Historical run (`f8449854`, 2026-09-23) | Passed | Failed | Skipped | |------------------------------------------------|-------:|-------:|--------:| | CUDA float32 | 12193 | 22 | 3957 | | CUDA float16 | 11738 | 451 | 3983 | | CUDA bfloat16 | 11736 | 500 | 3936 | These used an RTX 4090, Python 3.11 and PyTorch 2.14.0+cu130. Source-marked xfails were excluded. Half tests ran in-process with `KORNIA_TEST_IN_SUBPROCESS=1`, followed by isolated retries of failures; two homography tests were deselected. They are not a measurement of the current branch. Those two tests (`TestFindHomographyDLT::test_nocrash` and `test_nocrash_lu`) now pass locally in all three CUDA dtypes at `649b3f86d`; a fresh full CUDA sweep is needed before quoting new totals. For CUDA half tests, use `--isolate-half-precision` so each test gets a fresh process. They are skipped by default without it; selecting a half dtype alone does not exercise CUDA half support: ```bash pixi run test-module tests/color/ --device=cuda --dtype=float16,bfloat16 --isolate-half-precision ``` See the [full precision guide](https://kornia.readthedocs.io/en/latest/get-started/precision.html) for details. ## Sponsorship Kornia is an open-source project that is developed and maintained by volunteers. Whether you're using it for research or commercial purposes, consider sponsoring or collaborating with us. Your support will help ensure Kornia's growth and ongoing innovation. Reach out to us today and be a part of shaping the future of this exciting initiative! ## Installation [![PyPI python](https://img.shields.io/pypi/pyversions/kornia)](https://pypi.org/project/kornia) [![pytorch](https://img.shields.io/badge/PyTorch_2.5.1+-ee4c2c?logo=pytorch&logoColor=white)](https://pytorch.org/get-started/locally/) ### From pip ```bash pip install kornia ``` Some features (ONNX, Stable Diffusion dissolving) need extra packages; see [Optional extras](https://kornia.readthedocs.io/en/latest/get-started/installation.html#optional-extras).
Other installation options #### From source with editable mode ```bash pip install -e . ``` #### For development with Pixi (Recommended) For development, Kornia uses [pixi](https://pixi.sh) for fast Python package management and environment management. The project includes a `pixi.toml` configuration file for reproducible dependency management. ```bash # Install pixi (if not already installed) curl -fsSL https://pixi.sh/install.sh | bash # Create the Pixi environment and install development dependencies pixi install pixi run -e default install # Run tests pixi run test # For CUDA development pixi run -e cuda install pixi run -e cuda test-cuda ``` These commands set up a complete development environment with all dependencies. For more details on dependency management and available tasks, see [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md). #### From Github url (latest version) ```bash pip install git+https://github.com/kornia/kornia ```
## Quick Start Kornia is not just another computer vision library — it's your gateway to effortless Computer Vision and AI.
Get started with Kornia image transformation and augmentation! ```python import numpy as np import kornia_rs as kr from kornia.augmentation import AugmentationSequential, RandomAffine, RandomBrightness from kornia.filters import StableDiffusionDissolving # Load and prepare your image img: np.ndarray = kr.read_image_any("img.jpeg") img = kr.resize(img, (256, 256), interpolation="bilinear") # alternatively, load image with PIL # img = Image.open("img.jpeg").resize((256, 256)) # img = np.array(img) img = np.stack([img] * 2) # batch images # Define an augmentation pipeline augmentation_pipeline = AugmentationSequential(RandomAffine((-45.0, 45.0), p=1.0), RandomBrightness((0.0, 1.0), p=1.0)) # Leveraging StableDiffusion models dslv_op = StableDiffusionDissolving() img = augmentation_pipeline(img) dslv_op(img, step_number=500) dslv_op.save("Kornia-enhanced.jpg") ```
Find out Kornia ONNX models with ONNXSequential! ```python import numpy as np from kornia.onnx import ONNXSequential # Chain ONNX models from HuggingFace repo and your own local model together onnx_seq = ONNXSequential( "hf://operators/kornia.geometry.transform.flips.Hflip", "hf://models/kornia.models.detection.rtdetr_r18vd_640x640", # Or you may use "YOUR_OWN_MODEL.onnx" ) # Prepare some input data input_data = np.random.randn(1, 3, 384, 512).astype(np.float32) # Perform inference outputs = onnx_seq(input_data) # Print the model outputs print(outputs) # Export a new ONNX model that chains up all three models together! onnx_seq.export("chained_model.onnx") ```
## Call For Contributors If kornia is useful to you and you would like to help, contributions of many kinds are welcome: code, bug reports, benchmarks, documentation, questions, answers, and examples. The maintainers have limited time, so we cannot promise that every proposal or pull request will be reviewed or merged. ### Strengthen the Core (Priority) Kornia's differentiated value is its geometry core: warping and sampling, homographies, cameras, epipolar geometry, rotations and Lie groups, and geometry-consistent augmentation. The highest-impact contributions make that core more trustworthy — see the [Roadmap](ROADMAP.md) for the full picture. Great entry points: - **Benchmark results from your hardware**: run the benchmark suite with `--contribute` and send the JSON — CUDA numbers from diverse GPUs are especially useful. - **Convention pinning tests and conformance vectors** for core geometry operations. - **Corrective error messages**: upgrade bare shape assertions into errors that state what was wrong, what was expected, and which convention applies. - **Classical vision in the core domain**: camera intrinsic calibration, fiducial markers (ArUco/ChArUco), classical tracking, dense stereo, and Hough transforms. An early design discussion can be useful for work of this size. See the [Roadmap's contributor areas](ROADMAP.md#areas-seeking-contributors) for more project context. ### AI Models The model zoo is currently **frozen for expansion** while maintainer bandwidth concentrates on the core. Shipped models (LoFTR, LightGlue, DISK, DeDoDe, SAM, and friends) stay available and maintained, and model work approved before the freeze (Efficient LoFTR, SANDesc) will be completed under its existing scope. New integrations — including VLM/VLA models — require a named maintainer sponsor who accepts ongoing ownership of the integration; a contributor implementation alone cannot reopen the surface. See the [Roadmap](ROADMAP.md#guiding-themes) for the reasoning and the reopen condition. ### Documentation And Tutorial Optimization Kornia's foundation lies in its extensive collection of classic computer vision operators, providing robust tools for image processing, feature extraction, and geometric transformations. We continuously seek for contributors to help us improve our documentation and present nice tutorials to our users. ## Cite If you are using kornia in your research-related documents, it is recommended that you cite the paper. See more in [CITATION](./CITATION.md). ```bibtex @inproceedings{eriba2019kornia, author = {E. Riba, D. Mishkin, D. Ponsa, E. Rublee and G. Bradski}, title = {Kornia: an Open Source Differentiable Computer Vision Library for PyTorch}, booktitle = {Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision}, year = {2020}, url = {https://arxiv.org/pdf/1910.02190.pdf} } ``` ## Contributing See [CONTRIBUTING.md](./CONTRIBUTING.md) for our social contract, development setup, and technical guidelines. Participation is subject to the [Code of Conduct](./CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md). ## Community - **Discord:** talk with people who use and develop kornia. [Join the server](https://discord.gg/HfnywwpBnD) - **GitHub Issues:** report bugs and propose concrete changes. [Open an issue](https://github.com/kornia/kornia/issues/new/choose) - **GitHub Discussions:** ask questions and discuss implementations, research, and ideas. [Join a discussion](https://github.com/kornia/kornia/discussions) Made with [contrib.rocks](https://contrib.rocks). ## License Kornia is released under the Apache 2.0 license. ## [0.9.0] - 2026-10-23

### Added

- `kornia.metrics.kitti_d1_error`, the outlier ratio reported by the KITTI 2015 stereo benchmark.
  A pixel counts as an outlier only when its absolute disparity error exceeds `abs_threshold`
  **and** its relative error exceeds `rel_threshold`, both strictly, with the ground truth as the
  relative denominator. That conjunction is what separates it from `mean_bad_pixel_error`, which
  applies the absolute criterion alone and so penalises large disparities for errors that are small
  next to their magnitude. A batch is pooled over every valid pixel, as the devkit accumulates it,
  rather than averaged per image. Closes #3758. ([#3931](https://github.com/kornia/kornia/pull/3931))
- `PadTo` takes `crop_if_exceeds`. The default `True` keeps the existing behavior: an input larger than `size` on an axis is cropped to `size` there. With `crop_if_exceeds=False` that axis passes through unchanged, so the output is at least `size` on each axis and boxes and keypoints stay inside the image. Closes #3518. ([#3964](https://github.com/kornia/kornia/pull/3964))
- Added opt-in `kornia.contrib.augmentation_audit` reports with executed geometric provenance,
  native parameter snapshots, out-of-frame diagnostics and actual keypoint/box round-trip
  measurements, including explicit unsupported transforms and JSON export. ([#4465](https://github.com/kornia/kornia/pull/4465))
- Relevant camera and image-coordinate API docstrings now link directly to the camera and general conventions guides. ([#4501](https://github.com/kornia/kornia/pull/4501))
- Document per-class coordinate, sampling, crop, resize, padding, and non-rigid warp conventions for 2D geometric augmentations, with executable tests for current behavior and known limitations. Clarify sampler migration after module and container moves. ([#4538](https://github.com/kornia/kornia/pull/4538))
- Document per-class value-range, parameter-meaning, filter, noise, weather, illumination and normalization conventions for the 2D intensity augmentations, with executable tests for current behavior and issue-linked pins for the known limitations. Rewrite the stale sampler-migration citations in the 2D augmentation bases. ([#4566](https://github.com/kornia/kornia/pull/4566))
- Document the conventions of mix and 3D augmentations and automatic augmentation policies, with executable tests for their sampling, coordinate, label, and output contracts. ([#4634](https://github.com/kornia/kornia/pull/4634))
- `SIFTFeature` and `SIFTFeatureScaleSpace` now accept `descriptor_backend="pyramid"` for fast extraction at their sparse detections. `SIFTDescriptorFromPyramid` describes supplied LAFs and can share an extraction pyramid between orientation assignment and description.

  The scale-space preset has a dedicated backend that reuses the detector Gaussian pyramid and retained octave/layer assignments, computing gradients once per used level. It preserves sparse detections and integrates rotated SIFT histograms directly from gradient fields.

  The optimized scale-space path also specializes DoG detection: sparse refinement, exact octave coordinates, and top-K response ranking without contrast or edge rejection. The default patch backend remains available.

  CPU Gaussian filtering avoids convolution work buffers; sparse neighbourhood gathers, two-bin angular voting, and device-specific descriptor chunks reduce extraction time without reducing integration support or the requested feature budget. Compiled and eager pyramid backends share checkpoint keys and support full-module serialization.

  CPU inference builds Gaussian volumes directly in their final storage and reuses sampling coordinates; gradient atlases also avoid a full transpose copy. Spatial ties are rejected before bounded sparse gathers. Empty detections and descriptors retain zero gradients, and half-precision masks preserve their suppression semantics.

  CUDA uses packed sparse refinement and separable descriptor histogram pooling to reduce kernel launches and extraction time while retaining bounded descriptor chunks. CPU and MPS keep their existing refinement paths.

  Shared `conv_quad_interp3d` and `iterative_quad_interp3d` now group finite differences and Cramer determinants on CUDA float32/float64, also accelerating the default patch-based `SIFTFeatureScaleSpace` pipeline. CPU, MPS and reduced-precision inputs retain their scalar paths. ([#4638](https://github.com/kornia/kornia/pull/4638))
- `depth_from_disparity` accepts a per-batch-element `(B,)` `baseline` and `focal`, so a batch of stereo pairs from
  rigs with different baselines or focal lengths no longer has to be split and processed one sample at a time.
  Element `b` pairs with `disparity[b]`, which needs a disparity of rank 3 or more with a leading size of `B`; a
  mismatched size still raises `ShapeError`. The shared forms, a Python number, a scalar tensor or a `(1,)` tensor,
  behave exactly as before, and the two may be mixed. ([#4648](https://github.com/kornia/kornia/pull/4648))
- Added `kornia.contrib.connected_components_union_find`, an exact, pure PyTorch 8-connected component labeling alternative using 2x2 block union-find. It converges without a user-selected iteration budget and returns integer labels for boolean, integer and floating-point masks, including half precision. ([#4666](https://github.com/kornia/kornia/pull/4666))
- Document the conventions of `RandomTransplantation` and `RandomTransplantation3D` — mask-driven donor selection, the `(i - 1) mod B` donor rule, label sampling and `excluded_labels`, the replay contract, and the data-key and dtype rules — with executable tests, and export both names from `kornia.augmentation.__all__`. ([#4695](https://github.com/kornia/kornia/pull/4695))

- `RANSAC` gains `local_optimization` (`"lm"` or `"dlt"`), `refine_iters` for the final Levenberg-Marquardt refinement, the `"fundamental_8pt"` model type, and an `offset` argument to `RANSAC.sample` that continues the PROSAC schedule across batches of different sizes. The new pipeline normalizes the correspondences once per call, solves minimal samples through a batched LU null space and scores them with one matrix product per batch; on PhotoTourism fundamental matrices and HEB homographies it is more accurate than the previous defaults and several times faster on CUDA. `sample_is_valid_for_homography` no longer copies index tensors to the device on every call. The minimal solvers share their LU null space with the public estimators: `find_fundamental(method="7POINT")`, the eight-correspondence unweighted case of `find_fundamental`, and the four-correspondence `find_homography_dlt(solver="lu")` replace `eigh`, QR or SVD with one batched LU factorization, which is several times faster on CPU and now runs in float16 and bfloat16; the seven-point cubic is expanded without inverting the null-space basis. `sampson_epipolar_distance` and `oneway_transfer_error` (and so `symmetric_transfer_error`) score several matrices on one set of correspondences with one or two matrix products, faster on CPU and CUDA for RANSAC-sized batches, and `find_fundamental`'s eight-point solver removes the smallest singular value in closed form instead of with an SVD for batches of 128 or more on CPU and 512 or more on other devices, about twice as fast for 2048 samples. ([#5031](https://github.com/kornia/kornia/pull/5031))

- `RANSAC` gains opt-in `degensac=True` (off by default), DEGENSAC's dominant-plane recovery for seven-point fundamental matrices (Chum, Werner and Matas, CVPR 2005), following Chum's implementation in pydegensac: record-setting seven-point models are tested for five or more correspondences related by one homography, and a degenerate one hands that homography to a plane-and-parallax search over the correspondences off the plane. The new `kornia.geometry.homography.sampson_homography_distance` returns the Sampson distance of correspondences to homographies, the first-order geometric error over both images (Hartley and Zisserman, section 4.2.6): unlike `oneway_transfer_error`, it accounts for noise in both images and does not depend on the scale of `H`, and an exact correspondence scores 0. - `RANSAC(compile=True)` runs the whole `local_optimization="lm"` estimation (homography, fundamental and essential
  matrices) as one `torch.compile` graph on CPU and CUDA with torch 2.14 or later. The graph is traced once per configuration and does not
  depend on the number of correspondences, the threshold, the confidence or the sample budget; it is saved next to
  inductor's cache, so a later process loads it instead of compiling. Seeded compiled calls are reproducible but use
  their own random stream without changing the global CPU or CUDA generators. Ordinary and inference-mode calls
  share the compiled artifact. Eager results are unchanged.

  Compiled calls normalize autocast, distinguish thread/default-dtype/default-device settings in the artifact cache,
  and draw their samples from a counter-based hash of the seed, so concurrent seeded calls preserve the global RNG. Large explicit CPU batches
  split to bound scoring memory while retaining the sample budget. Zero-weight singular correspondences no longer
  prevent LM refinement; artifact writes are atomic. ([#5117](https://github.com/kornia/kornia/pull/5117))

### Bug fixes

- The `kornia.metrics` disparity reductions accumulate in `float32` for `float16` and `bfloat16`
  inputs, so `mean_absolute_disparity_error`, `root_mean_squared_disparity_error` and
  `mean_bad_pixel_error` no longer return `inf` on an image-sized map. A `float16` sum saturates at
  65504, and a `bfloat16` sum lost roughly 0.5% over 100k terms. `root_mean_squared_disparity_error`
  additionally squared in the input dtype, so a 300 px error saturated before any reduction ran;
  it now squares in the accumulator dtype. A mixed-dtype pair now returns the promoted dtype from
  every metric in the module rather than the dtype of `input`, matching what
  `mean_absolute_disparity_error` already did. ([#3931](https://github.com/kornia/kornia/pull/3931))
- `warp_perspective`, `warp_affine`, `homography_warp`, `HomographyWarper` and `warp_image_tps` now
  build their sampling grid and homography normalization under the same `align_corners` convention
  they pass to `grid_sample`. Previously the grid was always corner-aligned, so with
  `align_corners=False` an identity homography did not reproduce its input (max deviation `11.25`
  on a 4x4 `arange` image) and a whole-pixel translation resampled at fractional offsets;
  `warp_image_tps` was affected on its default path. `create_meshgrid`, `normal_transform_pixel`,
  `normalize_homography` and `denormalize_homography` gain an `align_corners` parameter (last,
  default `True`, so existing calls are unchanged). `crop_by_transform_mat` drops the #3650
  correction matrix and the 1-pixel `warp_affine` fallback that worked around the mismatch, so
  1-pixel outputs are exact under both settings. `normal_transform_pixel` also writes the
  `align_corners=False` offset as a single division, so eager and graph capture agree bit for bit at
  every size rather than differing by one `float32` step at 5 of the first 4999.
  Fixes #3904, #3928, #3929, #4411. ([#3945](https://github.com/kornia/kornia/pull/3945))
- Align Kimi-VL positional embeddings, rotary embeddings, and projector ordering with Moonshot. ([#3968](https://github.com/kornia/kornia/pull/3968))
- `build_laplacian_pyramid()` now pads mixed image sizes when needed to keep adjacent pyramid levels aligned, while
  preserving the output shapes of sizes that already worked. ([#3971](https://github.com/kornia/kornia/pull/3971))
- `normal_transform_pixel` and `normal_transform_pixel3d` now raise `ValueError` for an integer
  `dtype` instead of returning a rank-deficient matrix. The scale `2 / (size - 1)` truncated to `0`,
  so `normal_transform_pixel(4, 5, dtype=torch.int64)` returned `[[0, 0, -1], [0, 0, -1], [0, 0, 1]]`
  and mapped every pixel to `(-1, -1)`, with no error or warning. Floating point dtypes, including the
  `float8` formats, and complex dtypes are unaffected. ([#3974](https://github.com/kornia/kornia/pull/3974))
- Homography normalization now builds matrices with float64-native constants for float64 inputs, preserving full precision (#3958).
  `normal_transform_pixel` and `normal_transform_pixel3d` also keep float64 constants exact under TorchScript, where they were previously rounded through float32. ([#3979](https://github.com/kornia/kornia/pull/3979))
- `rotation_matrix_to_quaternion` no longer adds `eps` inside the square root of the dominant component, which inflated every `float64` result: the identity used to return `[1.0000000012499999, 0, 0, 0]` and now returns exactly `[1, 0, 0, 0]`, and the unit-norm error of random rotations drops from about `2.5e-9` to about `7e-16`. `eps` is now only a floor on the radicands of the discarded branches; the selected branch's radicand is at least `1` for any real 3x3 matrix, so it never reaches the floor. `ARKitQTVecs_to_ColmapQTVecs` inherits the fix. `float32`, `float16` and `bfloat16` outputs are unchanged. ([#3981](https://github.com/kornia/kornia/pull/3981))
- `RANSAC`'s local-optimization step now keeps the polished model that `verify()` scores best, instead of always
  taking the first candidate the polisher returns, so the returned model agrees with the returned inliers.
  Every built-in polisher returns a single candidate, so results are unchanged for them; the fix matters for custom
  `polisher_solver`s that return several candidates. ([#3991](https://github.com/kornia/kornia/pull/3991))
- Slicing or masking list-backed `Boxes` now preserves each batch element's padding metadata, so `to_tensor()`
  returns the original number of boxes per element. ([#4194](https://github.com/kornia/kornia/pull/4194))
- `kornia.feature.loftr`'s `CoarseMatching` no longer crashes in training mode. Its gt-padding
  branch called `zip()` with four separate 2-element lists instead of two 4-element lists, so
  every resulting tuple failed to unpack (`ValueError: too many values to unpack`) on every call;
  no existing test exercised this path. Restructured the `zip()` to pair each real tensor with its
  ground-truth counterpart. Once reachable, a second bug surfaced: the padding tensor `mconf_gt`
  was built without `dtype=`, defaulting to float32 regardless of `mconf`'s own dtype (which can be
  float16/bfloat16 under autocast) and silently promoting the concatenated result. Fixed by building
  `mconf_gt` in `mconf.dtype`. ([#4359](https://github.com/kornia/kornia/pull/4359))
- `kornia.enhance.image_histogram2d` no longer collapses distinct bins together on a `float16` or `bfloat16` image. The auto-built bin centers were created at the image dtype, which cannot represent the bin indices exactly: `bfloat16` lost 63 of 256 centers at the default `n_bins`, and `float16` lost 511 of 2048, so those bins came back numerically identical. The centers are now built at `float32` for half-precision images (a `float64` image keeps `float64`), and a floating-point image still gets its own dtype back. Integer images and explicitly passed `centers` behave exactly as before. ([#4360](https://github.com/kornia/kornia/pull/4360))
- `kornia.geometry.subpix.render_gaussian2d` no longer distorts the rendered Gaussian's peak location on large grids for `float16` and `bfloat16` inputs. The pixel-coordinate linspace was built at the input dtype, so distinct coordinates collapsed together once `width`/`height` exceeded what the dtype represents exactly: about 2048 for `float16` and about 256 for `bfloat16`.
