Cloud | Documentation | Roadmap | Discord

📕 Table of Contents - 💡 [What is RAGFlow?](#-what-is-ragflow) - 🎮 [Get Started](#-get-started) - 🔥 [Latest Updates](#-latest-updates) - 🌟 [Key Features](#-key-features) - 🔎 [System Architecture](#-system-architecture) - 🏠 [Local Deployment](#-local-deployment) - 📚 [Documentation](#-documentation) - 📜 [Roadmap](#-roadmap) - 🏄 [Community](#-community) - 🙌 [Contributing](#-contributing)
## 💡 What is RAGFlow? [RAGFlow](https://ragflow.io/) is a leading open-source Retrieval-Augmented Generation ([RAG](https://ragflow.io/basics/what-is-rag)) engine that fuses cutting-edge RAG with Agent capabilities to create a superior context layer for LLMs. It offers a streamlined RAG workflow adaptable to enterprises of any scale. Powered by a converged [context engine](https://ragflow.io/basics/what-is-agent-context-engine) and pre-built agent templates, RAGFlow enables developers to transform complex data into high-fidelity, production-ready AI systems with exceptional efficiency and precision. ## 🎮 Get Started Try our cloud service at [https://cloud.ragflow.io](https://cloud.ragflow.io). For local deployment, see [Local Deployment](#-local-deployment).
## 🔥 Latest Updates - 2026-09-29 RAGFlow 1.0.0-rc1 released. - 2026-09-10 Added website content ingestion through sitemaps. - 2026-08-19 Introduced Knowledge Compilation to generate Wikis, Graphs, Trees, PageIndex, Mind Maps, Timelines, and Skills at the document and dataset levels. - 2026-08-19 Introduced Agentic RAG with Low, Medium, High, and Ultra thinking modes. - 2026-07-02 Added Google BigQuery data source ingestion and incremental synchronization. See the [full release notes](https://ragflow.io/docs/dev/release_notes) for more updates. ## 🌟 Key Features ### 🍭 **"Quality in, quality out"** - Deep document understanding-based knowledge extraction from unstructured data with complicated formats. - Finds "needle in a data haystack" of literally unlimited tokens. ### 🍱 **Template-based chunking** - Intelligent and explainable. - Plenty of template options to choose from. ### 🧩 **Knowledge Compilation** - Compile content at the document and dataset levels into structured knowledge artifacts. - Use compilation templates to generate Wikis, Graphs, Trees, PageIndex, Mind Maps, Timelines, and Skills for different knowledge organization and reuse needs. - Configure compilation models and processing rules, and view, update, and regenerate knowledge artifacts. ### 🧠 **Agentic Retrieval** - Perform multi-step retrieval for complex questions: the model analyzes the question and, when needed, breaks it down, retrieves knowledge, and verifies evidence. - Gather more complete context through multiple rounds of retrieval and reasoning to help generate well-grounded answers. - Choose Low, Medium, High, or Ultra thinking modes to control retrieval and reasoning depth according to question complexity. ### 🌱 **Grounded citations with reduced hallucinations** - Visualization of text chunking to allow human intervention. - Quick view of the key references and traceable citations to support grounded answers. ### 🍔 **Compatibility with heterogeneous data sources** - Supports Word documents, PowerPoint presentations, Excel spreadsheets, TXT files, images, PDFs, scanned copies, structured data, web pages, and more. ### 🛀 **Automated and effortless RAG workflow** - Streamlined RAG orchestration catered to both personal and large businesses. - Configurable LLMs as well as embedding models. - Multiple recall paired with fused re-ranking. - Intuitive APIs for seamless integration with business. ## 🔎 System Architecture
## 🏠 Local Deployment Local deployment supports both Docker deployment and launching from source. Docker is suitable for quick evaluation, integration testing, and production deployment, while launching from source is intended for RAGFlow development and debugging. Docker deployment does not require a Go compiler. Launching from source requires the Go version specified in `go.mod`; frontend development additionally requires Node.js and npm. ### 🐳 Docker Deployment #### 📝 Docker Deployment Prerequisites - Recommended starting configuration: 4 CPU cores, 16 GB RAM, and 50 GB of available disk space. Actual requirements depend on the document engine, data volume, parsing tasks, and concurrency. Local models and other optional components may require additional resources. - Docker ≥ 24.0.0, Docker Compose ≥ v2.26.1. > [!TIP] > If you have not installed Docker on your local machine (Windows, macOS, or Linux), see [Install Docker Engine](https://docs.docker.com/engine/install/). #### 🚀 Start up the server 1. If using Elasticsearch, set `vm.max_map_count` on the Docker host to at least 262144. This step is usually unnecessary with Infinity: > To check the value of `vm.max_map_count`: > > ```bash > sysctl vm.max_map_count > ``` > > If you use Elasticsearch and the value is below 262144, reset it: > > ```bash > # In this case, we set it to 262144: > sudo sysctl -w vm.max_map_count=262144 > ``` > > This change will be reset after a system reboot. To ensure your change remains permanent, add or update the `vm.max_map_count` value in **/etc/sysctl.conf** accordingly: > > ```bash > vm.max_map_count=262144 > ``` 2. Clone the repository: ```bash git clone https://github.com/infiniflow/ragflow.git ``` 3. Check out the release tag and start the server with Docker Compose: Enter the Docker deployment directory. ```bash cd ragflow/docker ``` Check out the `v1.0.0-rc3` release tag. ```bash git checkout v1.0.0-rc3 ``` Start the RAGFlow services and their dependencies. ```bash docker compose -f docker-compose.yml up -d ``` With the default MySQL configuration, the image entrypoint runs database migrations before starting Admin, Syncer, Ingestor, API, and other services. > In the RAGFlow open-source 1.0 release, DeepDoc uses CPU inference for layout analysis, OCR, and table recognition. 4. Check the server status after startup: Use `docker ps` to check the dependency services. After the dependencies show `healthy` and the RAGFlow container remains running, use the HTTP endpoint to determine whether RAGFlow is ready. The RAGFlow container itself does not define a Compose healthcheck. ```bash curl -f http://localhost/api/v1/system/healthz ``` After receiving an HTTP 200 response, open the Web UI. If you changed `SVR_WEB_HTTP_PORT`, replace the port in the health-check URL accordingly. If startup fails, inspect the container logs: ```bash docker logs --tail 50 ragflow-cpu ``` 5. In your web browser, enter the IP address of your server and log in to RAGFlow. > With the default settings, you only need to enter `http://IP_OF_YOUR_MACHINE` (**without** port number), because the default HTTP serving port `80` can be omitted when using the default configuration. 6. After signing in, add an LLM, embedding, and reranker on the model provider page, including the model name, service address, and API key. > For details, see [llm_api_key_setup](https://ragflow.io/docs/dev/llm_api_key_setup). _The show is on!_ See the [Quickstart guide](./docs/quickstart.mdx) for details. #### ⚙️ Docker Configuration and Adjustment Docker deployment uses `docker/.env` and `docker/docker-compose.yml`. Configure the image, ports, passwords, document engine, and model image source as described in the [Docker configuration guide](./docker/README.md). For platform support (note that macOS is not currently supported), see the [Go Docker image build and platform support guide](./docs/develop/build_docker_image.mdx). To build the Docker image from source, see the [Go Docker image build and platform support guide](./docs/develop/build_docker_image.mdx). For document-engine changes, configuration updates, restarting services, and retaining or removing existing data, follow the Docker configuration guide. ### 🔨 Launch from Source #### 📝 Source Build Prerequisites 1. Clone the repository and install the Go version specified in `go.mod` (currently Go 1.27), Clang 20, LLD 20, CMake ≥ 4.0, and PCRE2 development files. Go services depend on CGO and native static libraries; [build.sh](./build.sh) sets the required build parameters. ```bash git clone https://github.com/infiniflow/ragflow.git cd ragflow ``` 2. Run the dependency download script once to prepare everything the local Go server needs to build, run, parse documents and count tokens (`download_dev_deps.py` fetches the native static libraries and the runtime resources — cl100k vocabulary, DeepDoc `.ort` weights, embedding tokenizer assets): ```bash uv run tools/scripts/download_dev_deps.py ``` This is the local-dev one-stop: after one run the environment is ready, and already-present files are skipped so re-running never re-downloads. The image-facing counterpart `deps/download_deps.py` fetches the same runtime resources and skips the native `.a` files — run it only when building the dependency image or in CI, not for local development. `download_dev_deps.py` pulls and unpacks pdfium, pdf_oxide, office_oxide, and onnxruntime under `~/ragflow-native-libs`, and writes the cl100k vocabulary, DeepDoc models, and embedding tokenizer assets under `deps/`. It is a Python script; `uv run` installs its declared dependencies (`requests` and `huggingface-hub`) automatically. Skip this step if you have prepared the same resources by other means. When started from the repository root, Go services automatically find `internal/rag/res/deepdoc`; to start from another directory, set `DEEPDOC_MODEL_DIR` to its absolute path. 3. Build the services: ```bash ./build.sh --all ``` 4. Start the local dependency services and make sure the hosts and ports in **conf/service_conf.yaml** point to addresses accessible from the host. If using Elasticsearch, first set `vm.max_map_count` on the Docker host to at least `262144`. ```bash sudo sysctl -w vm.max_map_count=262144 docker compose --env-file docker/.env -f docker/docker-compose-base.yml up -d --wait es01 mysql minio nats kvrocks ``` 5. Migrate the database: ```bash ./bin/ragflow_server --migrate ``` 6. Start the four services in four separate terminals: Terminal 1: start Admin on port `9381`. ```bash ./bin/ragflow_server --admin ``` ```bash ./bin/ragflow_server --ingestor ``` Terminal 3: start Syncer. ```bash ./bin/ragflow_server --syncer ``` Terminal 4: start API on port `9380`. ```bash ./bin/ragflow_server --api ``` The startup modes work as follows: - `--migrate`: Runs database migrations and exits when complete. - `--admin`: Starts the Admin service for management and initialization operations. - `--ingestor`: Starts the Ingestor service for data ingestion and parsing tasks. - `--syncer`: Starts the Syncer service for external data source synchronization tasks. - `--api`: Starts the API service for the Web UI and SDKs. 7. Only when developing the frontend, install Node.js and npm, then start the React frontend: ```bash cd web npm install ``` After the services start, confirm that the API is ready: ```bash curl -f http://127.0.0.1:9380/api/v1/system/healthz ``` An HTTP 200 response indicates that the API is responding. See [Launch Service from Source](./docs/develop/launch_ragflow_from_source.md#5-verify-the-startup) for complete frontend and DeepDoc verification steps. See [Launch Service from Source](./docs/develop/launch_ragflow_from_source.md) for details. ## 📚 Documentation - [Quickstart](https://ragflow.io/docs/dev/) - [Configuration](https://ragflow.io/docs/dev/configurations) - [Release notes](https://ragflow.io/docs/dev/release_notes) - [User guides](https://ragflow.io/docs/category/user-guides) - [Developer guides](https://ragflow.io/docs/category/developer-guides) - [References](https://ragflow.io/docs/dev/category/references) - [FAQs](https://ragflow.io/docs/dev/faq) ## 📜 Roadmap See the [RAGFlow Roadmap 2026](https://github.com/infiniflow/ragflow/issues/12241). ## 🏄 Community - [Discord](https://discord.gg/NjYzJD3GM3) - [X](https://x.com/infiniflowai) - [GitHub Discussions](https://github.com/orgs/infiniflow/discussions) ## 🙌 Contributing RAGFlow flourishes via open-source collaboration. In this spirit, we embrace diverse contributions from the community. If you would like to be a part, review our [Contribution Guidelines](https://ragflow.io/docs/dev/contributing) first.

  [Submitted on 30 Oct 2026] 
      Title: Context as Infrastructure: Knowledge Compilation for Retrieval in Agentic Systems with Harnesses 
      Authors:  Zhichang Yu ,  Baining Cao ,  Sbaaoui Idriss ,  Qi Wang ,  Gangqiang Xu ,  Ling Qin ,  Xiaoling Jin ,  An Liu ,  Shaohao Cai ,  Xiaoyang Bao ,  Shengle Chen ,  Changchang Ding ,  Pengfei Zhu ,  Jingxiang Xu ,  Yifeng Mao ,  Lu Liu ,  Hai Jin ,  Yingfeng Zhang               View a PDF of the paper titled Context as Infrastructure: Knowledge Compilation for Retrieval in Agentic Systems with Harnesses, by Zhichang Yu and 17 other authors 
     View PDF 
     HTML (experimental) 



     
             Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation is becoming agentic. A search harness writes queries, reads results, reformulates, and decides when to stop. This largely solves accuracy: a harness with only BM25/grep and MiniMax M3 answers 85% of BrowseComp-Plus and 91% on multi-hop FRAMES in our runs, without compiled or vector indexes. It exposes a context problem: an undisciplined loop repeats queries, rereads documents, and fills the window with unused passages. The missing layer is knowledge compilation: a configurable ingestion pipeline where LLMs enrich documents with context no chunk contains alone--navigation hierarchies with claim-evidence leaves, entity graphs, timelines, mind maps, ontologies, wikis, and memory. Compilation is not a better retriever: under a competent harness, structural artifacts gave no detectable accuracy gain on FRAMES, and a PageIndex-style outline degraded at scale. It is a supply layer. A navigation tree whose leaves are claim-evidence pairs--the mechanism we measure--cuts query tokens by 91% when evidence suffices and adds 1.9% when it does not, a 38% average reduction; this implies a 2% break-even sufficiency rate and a measured rate near 43%. A decision gate cuts latency from 140 s to 30 s, though substitution's token saving is bought with retrieval rounds and carries its own latency cost. Other artifacts--ontology, graph, wiki, timeline, mind map, memory--pay off in deployment (governance, integration, onboarding, temporal orientation, continuity) where accuracy benchmarks cannot see them. We describe RAGFlow's pipeline and harness (open source at  this https URL ), which turns the loop into five disciplined stations and keeps the context entering the model the smallest sufficient set; together they form an agent-native database: a store that hands the agent compiled, governed context instead of a ranked list of passages.

# Nuxt

Nuxt is a free and open-source framework with an intuitive and extendable way to create type-safe, performant and production-grade full-stack web applications and websites with Vue.js. It provides a number of features that make it easy to build fast, SEO-friendly, and scalable web applications, including: - Server-side rendering, static site generation, hybrid rendering and edge-side rendering - Automatic routing with code-splitting and pre-fetching - Data fetching and state management - Search engine optimization and defining meta tags - Auto imports of components, composables and utils - TypeScript with zero configuration - Go full-stack with our server/ directory - Extensible with [300+ modules](https://nuxt.com/modules) - Deployment to a variety of [hosting platforms](https://nuxt.com/deploy) - ...[and much more](https://nuxt.com) 🚀 ## 🚀 Getting Started Use the following command to create a new starter project. This will create a starter project with all the necessary files and dependencies: ```bash npm create nuxt@latest ``` > [!TIP] > Discover also [nuxt.new](https://nuxt.new): Open a Nuxt starter on CodeSandbox, StackBlitz or locally to get up and running in a few seconds. ## 💻 Vue Development Simple, intuitive and powerful, Nuxt lets you write Vue components in a way that makes sense. Every repetitive task is automated, so you can focus on writing your full-stack Vue application with confidence. Example of an `app.vue`: ```vue ``` ## 📖 Documentation We highly recommend you take a look at the [Nuxt documentation](https://nuxt.com/docs) to level up. It’s a great resource for learning more about the framework. It covers everything from getting started to advanced topics. ## 🧩 Modules Discover our [list of modules](https://nuxt.com/modules) to supercharge your Nuxt project, created by the Nuxt team and community. ## ❤️ Contribute We invite you to contribute and help improve Nuxt 💚 Here are a few ways you can get involved: - **Reporting Bugs:** If you come across any bugs or issues, please check out the [reporting bugs guide](https://nuxt.com/docs/4.x/community/reporting-bugs) to learn how to submit a bug report. - **Suggestions:** Have ideas to enhance Nuxt? We'd love to hear them! Check out the [contribution guide](https://nuxt.com/docs/4.x/community/contribution) to share your suggestions. - **Questions:** If you have questions or need assistance, the [getting help guide](https://nuxt.com/docs/4.x/community/getting-help) provides resources to help you out. ## 🏠 Local Development Follow the docs to [Set Up Your Local Development Environment](https://nuxt.com/docs/4.x/community/framework-contribution#setup) to contribute to the framework and documentation. ## 🛟 Professional Support - Technical audit & consulting: [Nuxt Experts](https://nuxt.com/enterprise/support) - Custom development & more: [Nuxt Agencies Partners](https://nuxt.com/enterprise/agencies) ## 🔗 Follow Us

      

## ⚖️ License [MIT](https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/blob/main/LICENSE)

 rTaste: Do Research Agents Have Taste?
 Evaluating Early Stage Research Judgment 
 
 
 Art Kanke
   
  Affiliation:  University of Minnesota
 
  Email:    kanke011@umn.edu  
     

  Abstract 
    
 Do research agents have taste, the judgment of which experiments are worth running before their outcomes are known? We give six frontier models seven recent NLP papers. Each model, working as a research agent alone or as a team, proposes minimum viable experiments (MVEs), forecasts whether each will pass a threshold it sets and ranks them. A separate executor then attempts every MVE, including those ranked last, and three model auditors judge the results. Of 415 MVEs, 194 are judged sound, valuable and new, but fewer than half of these (73) are also judged beyond the seed paper and non obvious. The agents’ first choices match the auditors’ most valued experiment more often than a random pick, but are not shown to improve on choosing the experiment written first. Their forecasts beat a base rate but are not measurably more accurate than those of a fresh instance of the same model given only the paper and registrations. Teams cost more without a clear overall improvement in proposal quality. The agents produce many worthwhile experiments, but the evidence that their rankings improve the choice of which to run remains limited. The evaluation harness and a dataset of all 415 MVEs, with their forecasts and audited outcomes, are available at  https://github.com/ArtKanke/rTaste . 
  
 
 
 
 
 
     
 
 
 
 
  1  Introduction 

 
 Large language model agents can now carry out much of the empirical research workflow, from literature search and implementation to running experiments and writing reports  ( Lu et al., 2024 ;  Schmidgall et al., 2025 ) . Frontier AI labs report that agents write much of their code and support a rapidly growing number of experiments  ( Favaro & Clark, 2026 ;  OpenAI, 2026 ) . A risk assessment of agents inside four frontier labs, however, found no evidence that any of them relied on agents to set research agendas or make budget decisions  ( METR, 2026 ) . The step that has not been delegated is close to what researchers call taste, the judgment of which questions and experiments are worth pursuing before their outcomes are known  ( Hamming, 1986 ) . In practice this judgment is often exercised through small experiments. A researcher tests a direction cheaply and lets the result decide whether a larger study is needed. Such an experiment is useful only if its outcome is not obvious in advance and the researcher’s expectation about it is accurate enough to act on. An agent that proposes experiments with predictable outcomes or that is confidently wrong about what its experiments will show spends a limited budget poorly even if it runs every experiment correctly. 
 
 
 Existing evaluations address parts of this question. Execution benchmarks specify a task and measure how well an agent completes it  ( Chan et al., 2025 ;  Starace et al., 2025 ) . Studies of research ideas often judge proposals before execution, although those judgments can change when the ideas are carried out  ( Si et al., 2026a ) . Other work tests whether models can predict outcomes or choose among experiments on a given problem  ( Wen et al., 2025 ;  Foster et al., 2026 ;  Zhang et al., 2026a ) . We examine these judgments for experiments that agents propose from a recent paper and compare their expectations with the outcomes of every proposal. 
 
 
 We ask what experiments agents propose from a new paper, how accurately they predict the outcomes, and how well they choose among their proposals. We give each model a recent NLP paper, the  seed paper , with its code. Working as a research agent, once as a single researcher and once as a research team, the model proposes five  minimum viable experiments  (MVEs), inexpensive tests meant to indicate whether a direction deserves further investment. Before any experiment runs, the agent forecasts whether each MVE will meet its registered threshold and ranks the five (Figure   1  ). A separate executor then attempts every MVE, including those the agent ranked last. Three language models audit the results. We also compare the agent with a fresh instance of the same model that receives only the seed paper and registrations and makes the same forecasts and ranking. 
 
   
  Figure 1:  The study design. 
 
 
 Across seven seed papers and 415 MVEs, 194 are judged sound, valuable and new. On average the four larger models propose about three such MVEs in five, and the two smaller models, GPT-6 Luna and Muse Spark 1.3, about one. Two models, GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol, propose most of the MVEs judged beyond the seed paper and non obvious. A research team does not, on average, propose measurably better MVEs than a single researcher of the same model. The agents judge their own proposals less well. Their forecasts are more accurate than a base rate, but their own reading and search did not measurably improve them over those of the same model judge. The agent’s first choice is the auditors’ most valued MVE more often than a random pick would be. We find no evidence that it is better than the MVE the agent wrote first or than the same model judge’s first choice. We release the evaluation harness and the dataset of all 415 MVEs at  github.com/ArtKanke/rTaste . 
 
 
 
  2  Related Work 

 
 Research agents and benchmarks. 

 
 Research agent systems now span the workflow from ideation to written reports  ( Yamada et al., 2025 ;  Miyai et al., 2026 ) , some organized around a persistent tree of hypotheses and isolated executors  ( Jin et al., 2026 ) . RE-Bench, AIRS-Bench, and DeepRSI give agents a task with a fixed metric and score the result  ( Wijk et al., 2025 ;  Lupidi et al., 2026 ;  Rajaghatta et al., 2026 ) . TasteVal, concurrent with our work, measures how efficiently a model’s own experiments reach an expert’s score on a fixed task  ( Jaffe & Sherburn, 2026 ) . EXP-Bench asks agents to reproduce experiments from published papers  ( Kon et al., 2026 ) . Other benchmarks give agents research problems drawn from recent or unpublished work  ( Garikaparthi et al., 2026 ;  Kim et al., 2026 ) . In each, the problem is given to the agent, whereas our agents choose what to test from a seed paper. Studies of such agents report frequent failures to complete experiments, reported results that do not match the underlying code  ( Chen et al., 2025 ;  Zhang et al., 2026b ) , and weak judgment about when evidence is sufficient  ( Kirgis et al., 2026 ) . 
 
 
 
 Evaluating research ideas. 

 
 A second group of work evaluates research ideas directly. Blind comparisons with expert researchers found that large language model ideas were rated more novel than human ideas  ( Si et al., 2025 ) , and studies of expert preferences found that automated judges reproduce those preferences only partially  ( Chen et al., 2026 )  or little better than chance  ( Baig et al., 2026 ) . Judgments of this kind are made without outcomes. When ideas from the earlier study were executed by researchers, the advantage of the model generated ideas disappeared  ( Si et al., 2026a ) . Language models asked to judge the soundness of proposals are also strongly biased toward approval  ( Ho et al., 2026 ) . Agent generated ideas tend to stay close to their source literature  ( Tang & Yang, 2026 ) . Other studies judge research foresight against the later literature, asking which directions will be pursued or will gain attention  ( Li et al., 2026 ;  Tian et al., 2026 ;  Ye et al., 2026 ) . Another study compares a model’s proposed next step in a project with the step its authors actually took  ( Gong et al., 2026 ) . 
 
 
 
 Predicting experimental outcomes. 

 
 The work closest to ours predicts experimental outcomes before execution. Models can predict which of two published ideas performs better on a benchmark  ( Mule et al., 2026 ) , which of two candidate programs will score higher  ( Zheng et al., 2026 ) , or the numeric result of an experiment from its description  ( Park et al., 2025 ) . Recent work also asks models which training recipe will reach the lowest loss  ( Ren et al., 2026b )  and how much a change to a training or inference recipe will improve a benchmark score  ( Wang et al., 2026 ) . Some register expected outcomes before pilot experiments and run only the best supported hypotheses in full  ( Ren et al., 2026a ) , so their expectations about the other hypotheses are never checked at full scale. Others run every candidate, to train a model that scores hypotheses  ( Vasu et al., 2025 )  or to learn from large batches of executed ideas  ( Si et al., 2026b ) . Where calibration has been measured for agents, on coding tasks with clear success criteria, agents are overconfident about their own success  ( Kaddour et al., 2026 ;  Barkan et al., 2025 ) . 
 
 
 
 Research teams. 

 
 Several research systems divide the work among specialized agents that generate, critique, and rank hypotheses  ( Gottweis et al., 2026 ;  Schmidgall et al., 2026 ) , and a lead agent coordinating parallel subagents has improved performance on research style information tasks at a substantially higher token cost  ( Hadfield et al., 2025 ) . Studies suggest that such gains depend on the task and on how coordination is organized  ( Kim et al., 2025 )  and that when total computation is held equal a single agent often matches or exceeds multi agent designs  ( Tran & Kiela, 2026 ) . 
 
 
 
 
  3  Experimental Setup 

 
  3.1  Seed papers 

 
 We use seven NLP papers (arXiv cs.CL) with released code, taken from the daily papers list on Hugging Face  1    1 
               1 
              
              
              
             https://huggingface.co/papers     and first made public between 3 August and 24 September 2026. We chose papers this recent so that little follow up work exists for an agent to find and repeat. The selection also excludes work that requires large GPU training runs or models with more than 8B parameters. The full list can be found in Appendix   A  . Agents receive the paper’s full text, an image of every page, and read access to its code repository. We did not provide a summary, a suggested research gap or direction, or a hypothesis. 
 
 
 
  3.2  Agents and harnesses 

 
 We evaluate six models at maximum reasoning effort: GPT-6 Astra, Claude Fable 5.1, Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6 Luna, and Muse Spark 1.3.  2    2 
               2 
              
              
              
            A reply cut off at the output limit is requested once more at medium effort. This happened for the lead of the Claude Opus 5.5 team on six of the seven seed papers, so 30 of the 415 registrations were written at medium effort.    Evaluation was conducted between 6 and 8 October 2026. Each model works under two harnesses, so each seed paper has twelve  conditions . We refer to GPT-6 Luna and Muse Spark 1.3 as the two smaller models and to the other four as the larger models. The judges (Section   3.3  ) also run at maximum effort, and the executors, novelty judges, auditors, and reviewers at high effort. 
 
 
 A  single researcher  (SR) works in one continuous context from reading the seed paper to committing its forecasts. A  research team  (RT) divides the same work among separate instances of the same model. Two proposers each read the seed paper, search the literature, and draft experiments independently. A critic examines the pooled drafts once for scientific validity and for feasibility. A lead then keeps, revises, or merges the drafts into five experiments, commits them, and makes the team’s forecasts. The critic and the lead have no tools, so the lead has not itself searched the literature or read the code. The comparison asks whether two drafts and one round of critique help a model propose better MVEs than one continuous context. Under both harnesses, agents have the same limits and search the literature with the same arXiv tool. A comparison between models is therefore not also a comparison between their providers’ web tools. 
 
 
 
  3.3  Protocol 

 
 The agent makes two commitments before any experiment runs (Figure   1  ). First, it proposes five minimum viable experiments. Each MVE is specified in a short registration with a hypothesis, its closest prior work, and one  registered event : a stated statistic passes a threshold set in advance. Second, the agent gives each MVE a probability that its registered event will occur and ranks the five from most to least worth pursuing. We call the MVE it ranks highest its  first choice . The proposing agent knows that all proposed MVEs will run, so its ranking states a priority rather than deciding what runs. 
 
 
 We also ask each of the six models, as a  judge  in a new context, for the same forecasts and ranking. They see the seed paper and the five registrations. We do not provide the code, the agent’s reasoning or forecasts, or which model proposed the MVEs, and they cannot search. We call the judge from the agent’s own model its  same model judge . We run the MVEs of a seed paper only after all twelve conditions have committed. 
 
 
 After the experiments are committed and before execution, two  novelty judges , Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol, use the same literature search tool to label each MVE as equivalent to existing work, a close variant, or distinct. An MVE labeled equivalent or a close variant still runs. To see whether an MVE is an obvious follow up, we also ask each of the six models, given only the seed paper and no search, to list ten follow up experiments it would propose. The two novelty judges check each MVE against these lists, and we count it as an  obvious follow up  if either finds it there. 
 
 
 
  3.4  Execution and evaluation 

 
 Executors. 

 
 One of two executors, Claude Opus 5.5 or GPT-6.1 Sol, implements each MVE in a new context. The same two executors serve all six models, so a smaller model’s proposals are not held back by its own implementation. The executor sees the seed paper, its code, and the one MVE it implements. We did not provide the other four MVEs, the ranking, the forecasts, or the name of the model that proposed the MVE. All MVEs of one model on a seed paper go to the same executor and the executors alternate across seed papers. Because both executors are among the six models, 58 of the 412 delivered MVEs were implemented by a separate instance of the model that proposed them. We run every MVE with the same limits, no matter its rank. The executor works on a separate machine with one A100 GPU for at most 45 minutes, may run open models of up to 8B parameters, and may not call hosted models.  3    3 
                 3 
                
                
                
              On the seventh seed paper, 53 of its 60 MVEs were implemented and rerun on H200 machines with the same limits and prompts.    If it refuses or exceeds its limits, the other executor makes one independent attempt. If both fail, the MVE is not delivered. 
 
 
 
 Evaluation. 

 
 We then delete the results that came with the executor’s submission and rerun its evaluation on a new machine the executor never used. The rerun determines whether the registered event occurred. An MVE is  delivered  when the rerun ends without error and writes a number. The rerun repeats the executor’s own code, so whether that code is right is left to the auditors. 
 
 
 
 Audits. 

 
 Three auditors, Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6.1 Sol, and Grok 4.7, judge every delivered MVE. Grok 4.7 is not one of the six models we study and does not execute. The auditors see the registration, the executor’s notes, the output of the rerun, and the files it left. They do not see the seed paper or who proposed or implemented the MVE. Each auditor judges whether the MVE is faithful to its registration and valid and rates its research value from 0 to 3. We take the majority of the three judgments of faithfulness and validity and the median of the three research values. We call an MVE  sound  when it is faithful and valid,  valuable  when its research value is 2 or 3 and  new  when neither novelty judge found close prior work. The auditors also rank the five MVEs of each condition by research value. The MVE with the best mean rank is the auditors’  most valued MVE , against which we score the agent’s first choice. 
 
 
 
 Reviews. 

 
 After the study, we added a review of every delivered MVE. Three reviewers, the same models as the auditors, read the seed paper’s text, the registration, and what the auditors were shown, but none of the forecasts, rankings, audits, or novelty labels. They answered fixed questions: how the MVE relates to the seed paper, how obvious its idea is, and what the evidence says about the hypothesis.

 We count an MVE as sound, valuable and new when it meets all three (Section   3.4  ). Nearly all MVEs were delivered and most were judged sound, so most of those that fall short repeat prior work or have low research value.  Most MVEs build on the seed paper rather than check it, and few open a new direction. By the reviewers’ answers, 66% of the delivered MVEs build on the paper, 24% check one of its claims, and 5% open a direction that the paper merely suggests (Table   2  ). Building on the paper is often the obvious next step: 44% of all MVEs match an experiment on one of the lists of obvious follow ups. The agents also converge on the same experiments. On one seed paper  ( Nguyen-Tri et al., 2026 ) , a method for faster decoding whose appendix gives a correctness argument, all eight conditions of the four larger models wrote the same check of that argument first. 
 
 
 Two models more often go beyond the paper with an experiment that is not obvious. We call an MVE  non obvious  when at least two reviewers say that few or none of ten researchers would list it and that the paper neither reports nor names it, and  beyond the paper and non obvious  when at least two reviewers each say this and also that it builds on the paper or opens a new direction. This rating comes from the reviewers and differs from the lists of obvious follow ups: a fifth of these MVEs are also on a list. GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol proposed two thirds of them (Table   1  ), and they lead for each reviewer separately. Within seed papers, their share of such MVEs exceeds that of Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Opus 5.5 by 48 percentage points (95% CI 29 to 66) and is higher on all seven seed papers. GPT-6 Luna, a smaller model from the same provider, builds on the paper as often, but the reviewers rate few of its ideas non obvious. MVEs beyond the paper and non obvious are sound, valuable and new at least as often as the others, but their registered events occur less often. Of the 194 sound, valuable and new MVEs, 73 are beyond the paper and non obvious. The reviewers recommend a larger study more often for the MVEs of Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Opus 5.5 than for those of GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol. 
 
 
 
  4.3  Registered events and evidence 

 
 Each registration commits the agent to one registered event before the MVE runs and it is natural to read the event as the success of the experiment. For each sound MVE, we compare whether the event occurred with the reviewers’ reading of the evidence. 
 
 
 Whether the event occurs depends on how the agent defines it. In most of their MVEs, GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol compare a bound of a confidence interval with the threshold, rather than a point estimate (Table   7  ), and the other four models rarely do. The events of GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol occur in 25% of their sound MVEs, compared with 52% for Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Opus 5.5 (Table   1  ). On one seed paper  ( Liang et al., 2026 ) , four conditions tested whether a model’s own prediction errors harm decoding more than random errors of the same size, and all three reviewers read all four results as support for it. Three of the conditions had set the threshold at a difference of 5 percentage points and their events occurred. The fourth had set it at 8 points, and its event did not. 
 
 
 When the registered event does not occur, the evidence is often still informative. The reviewers judged the evidence informative for 50% of the sound MVEs whose event did not occur, mostly as evidence against the hypothesis. In the other direction, they judged the evidence inconclusive for 20% of the sound MVEs whose event occurred.

 Both forecasts are more accurate than a base rate that gives every MVE the event rate of the other six seed papers (Brier score 0.240), and the mean of the six judges’ probabilities is more accurate than the agent (0.179 against 0.192). The agent has seen more than its registrations state, but it is not shown to know more about its events than its registrations tell a reader. The agents are also not uniformly overconfident: GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6 Luna and Muse Spark 1.3 state higher probabilities than the rates at which their events occur, while Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Opus 5.5 state lower ones. 
 
 
 
  4.5  First choices 

 
 The agent’s first choice is the auditors’ most valued MVE in 38% of conditions, where a random pick gives 20%. The MVE that the agent wrote first and the same model judge’s first choice are the most valued about as often, and we find no evidence that the agent’s first choice beats either: its advantage over the MVE written first is 3 percentage points (95% CI    −  -   8 to 15). The first choice is also sound, valuable and new no more often than a random pick. 
 
 
 Agents register their obvious experiments first: the MVE written first is on a list of obvious follow ups in 61% of conditions, against 35% for the fifth. The agents then rank largely in the order in which they wrote them, and their first choice is the MVE they wrote first in 47% of conditions, where 20% would be expected if order did not matter. The event of the first choice occurs in 47% of conditions and that of the last choice in 29%, so the first choice is often an experiment likely to come out as registered. The auditors also rank sound MVEs whose event occurred higher, mostly because these MVEs give clearer evidence. 
 
 
 The judges rank in the same way: they too put the MVE written first on top in 39% of conditions on average. They and the auditors also rank obvious follow ups higher, and an agent’s ranking agrees more with the same model judge and with other judges from the same provider than with judges from other providers. On average, a judge’s first choice is an MVE beyond the paper and non obvious less often than a random pick would be, while the agent’s own first choice is one about as often. 
 
 
 
  4.6  Single researchers and teams 

 
 A team proposes more sound, valuable and new MVEs than a single researcher of the same model, 0.71 more of five on average, but the difference is not statistically significant (95% CI    −  -   0.10 to 1.52; Table   1  ). The difference is largest for the two smaller models, about one more of five, at about the cost of a single researcher. Claude Opus 5.5 working alone does as well as its team. 
 
 
 A team changes little in what is proposed. Its MVEs check the paper, match the lists of obvious follow ups, and are beyond the paper and non obvious about as often as a single researcher’s. They are rated non obvious somewhat more often (Table   1  ), but the 95% CI includes zero. What the critic and the lead change is the design of each experiment: teams more often compare a confidence bound with the threshold and state lower probabilities.

 A condition cost $15.31 on average for a single researcher and $23.93 for a team, counting the agent’s model calls and the implementation and rerun of its five MVEs (Table   1  ). Per $100, single researchers produced 13 sound, valuable and new MVEs and teams 11, and GPT-6.1 Sol produced the most. The cost of proposing differs about a hundredfold between models, from GPT-6 Luna to Claude Fable 5.1, while the cost of implementing and rerunning an MVE differs about twofold, since the same two executors served every model. Without the requirement of novelty, a team of GPT-6 Luna produced as many sound and valuable MVEs per $100 as GPT-6.1 Sol, but about half as many beyond the paper and non obvious, where GPT-6.1 Sol produced the most. 
 
 
 The executors delivered 397 of the 415 MVEs on their first attempt, and the limits were rarely reached: the median implementation took 12 minutes, well within its limits (Appendix   A.3  ). The agents reached their tool call limit in 5% of conditions. The MVEs of Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Opus 5.5 take more than twice as much GPU time to implement as those of GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol (Table   4  ). The auditors judge 18% of the MVEs implemented by the Claude Opus 5.5 executor not sound, compared with 3% of those implemented by the GPT-6.1 Sol executor, while the evidence is informative equally often under both. 
 
 
 
 
  5  Discussion 

 
 We began this study to see how many good small experiments frontier models can propose when a recent paper is their source of inspiration. By a good MVE we mean one that is small and not obvious and that opens a direction worth a larger study. Most of the experiments were sound, but most either tested the seed paper itself or extended it in a way that many researchers would propose, and few opened a new direction. Current agents appear better suited to examining a paper and taking its obvious next steps than to moving beyond it. That is useful in itself, since a new paper’s claims can be checked under controls and stricter measurements for a few dollars each, but it is a different capability from proposing new research, and evaluations of research agents should measure the two separately. 
 
 
 The models differ less in how often their experiments are sound than in what kind of experiment they propose. GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol more often go beyond the paper with an experiment that is not obvious and register stricter tests, which pass less often. Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Opus 5.5 stay closer to the paper and register tests that pass more often. The experiments of the two smaller models more often leave the question open. Choosing a model is therefore also choosing a kind of experiment. Because the price of proposing differs far more between models than the cost of running an MVE, a small model working as a team with a capable executor yields about as many sound and valuable experiments per dollar as the most efficient large model, though fewer beyond the paper. 
 
 
 In our study every experiment ran with the same limits, so the agents’ rankings stated priorities and did not decide what would be implemented. Those rankings followed the order in which the agents wrote their MVEs and favored the ones likely to pass. A natural next study gives an agent a fixed research budget to allocate among its own MVEs and to revise after the first results, and asks whether the budget goes to the MVEs that turn out sound, valuable and non obvious. The same budget given to human researchers would show how their allocations compare and provide a human baseline. This would extend the evaluation from what an agent proposes and expects to how it spends a limited budget, the decision in which researchers exercise their taste. 
 
 
 
  6  Limitations 

 
 All labels in this study come from models, so we lack a human baseline. The auditors judged soundness and value after seeing the outcomes and two of the three are models we also evaluate and use as executors. Every MVE was attempted regardless of its rank, so the ranking did not decide what ran. An agent whose ranking decides what runs may rank with more reasoning. Each registration had to be complete enough for a separate executor, so part of the forecasting result may be built into the design. Each condition ran once, so we have no measure of how much a result would change on a second run. 
 
 
 
  7  Conclusion 

 
 We studied whether research agents can evaluate and predict the outcomes of their own experiments before they are run. Given a recent NLP paper, six frontier models proposed small experiments, forecast whether the result of each would pass a threshold they set and ranked them. A separate executor attempted every proposed experiment. 
 
 
 We find that the agents propose experiments that are often sound, valuable and new. However, their own reading and search did not measurably improve their forecasts or rankings over those of the same model judge, which read only the seed paper and the registrations. The evaluation harness and the dataset are available at  https://github.com/ArtKanke/rTaste .

  A.3  Implementation compute 

 
 The agent was told the execution environment and its limits before it registered. Every attempt at an MVE had the
same limits. An executor worked on one machine with an A100 GPU, 12 CPU cores and 142 GB of
memory, and had no keys for hosted API models. Experiments could run open models of 8B parameters or
fewer. The machine ran for at most 45 minutes from the executor’s first command, the implementation had 90 minutes in all, and the rerun on a new machine had 35 minutes. The executor had 60 model calls. Spending limits and the 90 minutes of an implementation are checked between model calls. On the seventh seed paper,
53 of its 60 MVEs were implemented and rerun on H200 machines with the same limits. If an attempt delivers nothing, the other executor makes one independent
attempt. A failure of a machine is not an attempt and is repeated. 
 
 
 
 
  Appendix B  Labels from models 

 
  B.1  The audits 

 
 Each auditor judges whether the MVE is faithful to its registration, whether its evidence is valid, and its research
value on a scale from 0 to 3 (the prompt is in Appendix   D  ). The rule takes the majority of
the three auditors on faithfulness and validity and the median of their research values. 
 
 
 Planted defects. 

 
 We checked the auditors once, on seed paper 1, before any later audit existed. Claude
Sonnet 5.5, a model that was not used in the study, inserted one known defect into copies of ten delivered MVEs.
Each copy went through the rerun and the three audits again, in new contexts. The majority of three flagged 8 of the
10 copies and none of their 10 originals.

  B.2  Novelty 

 
 Two novelty judges, Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol, each searched arXiv as of the day of the evaluation and labeled each MVE as equivalent to existing work, a close variant, or distinct. Claude Opus 5.5 labeled 387 of the 415 MVEs distinct
and 28 close variants. GPT-6.1 Sol labeled 298 distinct, 115 close variants and 2 equivalent. They agree with kappa
0.27. 
 
 
 
 
  Appendix C  The review 

 
 We added one stage after all seven seed papers had been executed and audited. A reviewer received the seed paper as text without page images, the registration, and
what an auditor was shown of the delivered experiment. We did not provide which models proposed or implemented the MVE, the forecast, ranking, audit, novelty label or follow up list. Table   9   lists the questions.

 We take the answer that at least two of the three reviewers give. For how the hypothesis relates to the paper (Table   2  ), the review prompt counts a test of a property or a side effect of the paper’s method that the paper makes no claim about as building on the paper. We call an MVE non obvious when at least two reviewers say that few or none of ten researchers would list it and that the paper neither reports nor names it; an answer of reported or named counts only when its copied passage is found in the paper. An MVE is beyond the paper and non obvious when at least two reviewers each say that it is non obvious and that it builds on the paper or opens a new direction. The evidence is informative when at least two reviewers read it as for, against, or mixed.

None     of     the     four     answers     is     that  .     Writers     set     bars     differently  :     a     point     value  ,     a     confidence     bound  ,     or     a     number     written     into     the     hypothesis  .     So     a     missed     bar     can     come     with     clear     evidence     and     a     met     bar     with     none  .     Look     at     how     large     the     measured     effect     is     and     how     sure     the     run     is     of     it  ,     and     judge     the     same     way     whichever     kind     of     bar     the     plan     used  . 
 
 
 
  Others     have     checked     whether     the     code     follows     the     plan  .     You     need     not     list     departures  .     Take     the     experiment     as     it     was     run  . 
 
 
 
  what_came_out  .     One     sentence     with     the     numbers     of     the     main     comparison  ,     how     sure     the     run     is     of     them     (  its     interval     if     it     gives     one  ,     otherwise     the     number     of     cases     and     repetitions  ),     and     the     model     and     data  .     Do     not     say     here     whether     the     event     occurred  . 
 
 
 
  prerequisite  .     A     test     can     rest     on     something     that     must     hold     before     its     main     comparison     can     be     read  :     that     an     effect     of     the     paper     appears     at     this     scale  ,     that     a     model     trained     in     the     experiment     learned     what     it     was     trained     for  ,     or     that     a     measurement     or     a     control     behaved     as     it     should  .     It     is     something     other     than     the     hypothesis     itself  .     If     you     named     such     a     thing     in     "  needs  ",     look     at     it     first  ;     then     look     for     any     other  . 
 
  -     "  held  ":     as     far     as     the     run     shows  ,     nothing     of     this     kind     failed  ,     or     there     was     no     such     thing  . 
 
  -     "  failed  ":     one     such     thing     did     not     hold  ,     or     did     not     pass     the     plan  ’  s     own     check     for     it  ,     so     the     main     comparison     cannot     be     read  .     Name     it     in     "  which  ". 
 
  -     "  cannot     tell  ":     the     run     does     not     show     whether     such     a     thing     held  .     Name     it     in     "  which  ". 
 
  With     "  failed  "     or     "  cannot     tell  ",     set     "  named_before  "     to     true     if     "  which  "     is     what     you     named     in     "  needs  ",     otherwise     false  . 
 
  A     fault     that     the     run     itself     shows     did     not     change     the     main     comparison     is     not     a     failure  .     Too     few     cases     or     too     much     noise     is     not     one     either  ;     that     belongs     under     "  evidence  ". 
 
 
 
  evidence  .     What     does     the     run     say     about     the     plan  ’  s     hypothesis  ?     A     number     inside     the     hypothesis     is     the     plan  ’  s     bar  .     Do     not     answer     by     which     side     of     it     the     result     fell  :     a     clear     effect     in     the     claimed     direction  ,     somewhat     smaller     than     that     number  ,     is     evidence     for  .     If     the     hypothesis     claims     that     something     makes     no     difference     or     does     not     hold     up  ,     a     run     that     clearly     shows     this     is     evidence     for  . 
 
  -     "  for  ":     the     run     shows     what     the     hypothesis     claims  ,     and     noise     alone     would     not     explain     it  . 
 
  -     "  against  ":     the     run     could     have     shown     what     the     hypothesis     claims     and     clearly     shows     otherwise  .     The     change     being     tested     was     really     applied     and     the     measurement     was     not     stuck     at     its     floor     or     ceiling  .     For     a     claimed     effect  ,     the     measured     effect     is     near     zero     or     reversed     and     an     effect     large     enough     to     matter     is     ruled     out  . 
 
  -     "  mixed  ":     the     run     is     sure     of     two     things     that     point     opposite     ways  ,     for     example     an     effect     on     one     model     and     its     reverse     on     another  ,     or     a     gain     with     a     measured     loss  . 
 
  -     "  inconclusive  ":     the     run     does     not     tell     either     way  :     a     prerequisite     failed  ,     or     the     uncertainty     leaves     room     both     for     no     effect     and     for     an     effect     large     enough     to     matter  . 
 
  -     "  cannot     judge  ":     the     numbers     needed     are     not     in     what     you     are     shown  ,     or     the     code     shows     they     do     not     measure     what     the     plan     describes  . 
 
  If     "  prerequisite  "     is     "  failed  ",     the     answer     is     "  inconclusive  ".     If     the     hypothesis     has     two     parts     and     one     could     not     be     tested  ,     the     answer     is     "  inconclusive  ",     not     "  mixed  ".     If     the     run     gives     no     interval  ,     judge     from     the     number     of     cases     and     repetitions     and     say     so  . 
 
 
 
  next_step  .     An     experiment     of     this     kind     is     a     cheap     first     test     of     whether     a     question     deserves     a     larger     study  .     The     question     is     the     one     in     your     what_it_asks     sentence  .     Going     only     by     what     this     run     shows  ,     what     should     a     careful     researcher     do     next     about     it  ? 
 
  -     "  larger     study  ":     the     run     justifies     a     study     of     many     times     its     cost     on     the     same     question  .     It     need     not     be     the     study     in     the     plan  ’  s     last     field  ,     and     the     evidence     may     be     for     or     against     the     hypothesis  . 
 
  -     "  one     more     experiment  ":     the     run     answered     its     own     question  ,     and     one     gap     must     be     closed     by     a     further     small     experiment     before     choosing     between     a     larger     study     and     a     stop  .     Name     the     experiment     in     "  what  ". 
 
  -     "  repair  ":     the     run     did     not     answer     its     own     question     and     shows     why  .     The     same     question     must     be     asked     again     with     the     fault     removed  .     Name     the     fault     and     the     fix     in     "  what  ".     Too     few     cases     is     such     a     fault  . 
 
  -     "  stop  ":     the     run     justifies     spending     no     more     on     this     question  ,     because     (  a  )     the     idea     was     credibly     shown     not     to     work  ,     or     (  b  )     something     the     whole     question     depends     on     was     credibly     shown     not     to     hold  ,     or     (  c  )     the     question     is     settled     and     a     larger     study     would     add     nothing     that     matters  .     Give     the     letter     in     "  what  ". 
 
  -     "  no     decision  ":     the     run     did     not     answer     its     own     question     and     does     not     show     what     to     fix  . 
 
  A     justified     stop     is     as     good     an     answer     as     a     justified     larger     study  ,     and     neither     follows     from     the     bar  .     If     "  evidence  "     is     "  inconclusive  "     or     "  cannot     judge  ",     the     answer     is     "  repair  ",     "  no     decision  ",     or     "  stop  "     on     ground     (  b  ). 
 
 
 
  You     have     no     tools  :     everything     you     can     look     at     is     in     this     message  .     Reply     with     one     JSON     object     in     this     form     and     nothing     else  : 
 
 
 
  {"  what_it_asks  ":     "  one     sentence  ", 
 
     "  in_the_paper  ":     {"  reason  ":     "  one     sentence  ",     "  answer  ":     "  reported     |     named     |     neither  ",     "  quote  ":     null  },

page:https://posthog.com/blog/moving-off.text: Why we're moving our warehouse off DuckDB                                            Products   Pricing  Docs   Community   Company    More         Get started – free                                                                                                      Home                           MCP                           Self-driving                           Pricing                           Docs                      Demo                           Talk to a human                           About us                           Changelog                           Company handbook                           Store                           Careers                           Trash                              Home                           MCP                           Self-driving                           Pricing                           Docs                      Demo                           Talk to a human                             About us                           Changelog                           Company handbook                           Store                           Careers                           Trash                                                                    Blog                                                                                                                          Copy page                Why we're moving our warehouse off DuckDB           Benjamin Knofe-Vider       Nov 02, 2026     Data warehouse  ,     Infrastructure  ,     Engineering        Contents    DuckDB is brilliant on one machine    DuckLake is built for compatibility, not scale    1 trillion rows was a challenge    Speaking Postgres is harder than it sounds    We're rebuilding on Trino with HogLake        Five months ago,   we rebuilt our warehouse on DuckDB   instead of ClickHouse. We did it because a shared ClickHouse cluster couldn't handle hours-long modeling queries, and it lacked a cost-based query optimizer. DuckDB gave every customer their own instance, and tools like dbt could connect over Postgres. We're still fans.  But we underestimated how big and complex our customers' workloads would get. We didn't want them to have just a good experience, we wanted the best experience you can get when you pay someone else to run your warehouse. It should work at any scale, at a fair price.  So we spent the last three months re-architecting it, this time without DuckDB.        DuckDB is brilliant on one machine  We love DuckDB. It's probably the best single-node tool for analyzing heaps of data, and that node can be your laptop. It's robust and reliable. It almost always finishes your query, and if it runs out of memory, it spills to disk.  The same features that are great locally gave us problems in the cloud. Customers ran more complex queries than we expected, so we had to add huge instances. Adding disks was an option, but queries would have been too slow and expensive to be viable.  To run a single-node engine safely in the cloud, we have to size the worker before the query arrives. The ergonomics here are wonky. We couldn't find a good way to tell customers what resources their queries would need. Predicting CPU and memory for a specific query was even harder.  Users shouldn't have to worry about this. They should be able to run whatever they need to get their work done. Our job is to handle the rest and make it as predictable as possible.  We hit other bottlenecks too, like fetching lots of data from S3 without async fetching. DuckDB only added that recently.       DuckLake is built for compatibility, not scale  To use DuckDB as a fully-fledged data warehouse, we installed the   DuckLake   extension by default. It is a new lakehouse format from the same creators and follows the same principles as DuckDB: keep things simple and run on almost any setup. That works well up to a point, but at PostHog's scale, we needed something designed for distributed scale from the start.  DuckLake's catalog schema has to stay portable across many SQL databases, which limits engine-specific optimizations. At our scale, a single-table write could take more than three minutes because every commit re-read the statistics for the entire catalog.  We tuned DuckLake with table indexes and similar tweaks. But to keep offering DuckLake, we had to stay 100% compatible with its existing, "official" schema. This left us with fewer optimization options.  Another problem is that over 99% of the catalog's statistics rows belonged to tables that no longer existed. Cleaning them up made writes 30 to 50 times faster, but the rows kept growing back.  We also spent a lot of time on the number of connections DuckLake opens to metadata databases. That hurts on shared Postgres instances, where every connection has a real cost.       1 trillion rows was a challenge  DuckLake at PostHog didn't start small and ramp up. We fully committed and put all of PostHog in a DuckLake to dogfood as the first customer.  When we moved off it, it held about 2 PB: roughly 1 trillion rows and 15.3 million snapshots. It broke in lots of ways that were hard to fix within DuckLake's scope.  We'd rather have contributed to the existing community and helped it grow. But we couldn't land changes as fast as we needed, so we ended up carrying patches in a fork which defeats one of the main benefits of using DuckLake: the community.        Speaking Postgres is harder than it sounds  Offering direct Postgres connections over port 5432 sounds like a great idea. In practice, it was much harder to scale than HTTP.  Missing reconnects and managing TTLs and idle connections at scale is hard, and long-running connections are expensive. There's also very little tooling for load balancing pgwire compared with HTTP. Compare the ergonomics of an AWS NLB with an ALB and you'll see what we mean. HTTP headers also make routing in Kubernetes much more flexible.  There's also an endless list of Postgres clients, and each expects its own niche Postgres behavior. Customers kept asking us to fix their client or library. We spent a lot of time shipping many of those fixes, but coverage never got good enough. We'd rather spend our time building an excellent warehouse than chasing the long tail of Postgres compatibility.       We're rebuilding on Trino with HogLake  We've learned not to hype the tech behind a warehouse so much. What counts is the experience it gives you.  Still, we're happy to share what we're cooking next. We rebuilt everything around our own flavor of   Trino   and created our own open table format, HogLake. And yes, we're testing it at PostHog's petabyte scale first. We made it solid before handing it to design partners.  If your current warehouse is slow or expensive,   let's talk  , especially if you have a lot of data to query. We're always looking for design partners.     PostHog is your product's context layer. With a full suite of developer tools –   AI observability ,  product analytics ,   session replay ,  feature flags ,   experiments ,  error tracking ,   logs , and more – PostHog ingests and stores all the data agents need to diagnose problems, uncover opportunities, and ship fixes. A  data warehouse  and   CDP  tie it all together, unifying that context into one source agents can read across. You can steer it all from  Slack ,  the web app , the desktop ( PostHog Desktop ), or your own editor via  the MCP .   I suspect you and the person you are responding to are actually in agreement, making that an additional "point", rather than "counter-point". The crucial choice is not (just) the one made in a pivot: choosing  any  DB (or any similarly foundational stratum of your system) is  always  a crucial decision. Ultimately, you have two choices: put off making an informed, optimal choice, or make an informed, optimal choice now - or if not  now , then as soon as you have enough data/experience to make the optimal choice for your needs. I think you might be attributing the bulk of potential cost to the act of migrating away from an initial choice. But the cost of migrating away from something is proportional to the extent to which it is intertwined/coupled with your system, which in turn is largely a function of the scale at which you are operating. The problem, at least as I have seen it, is that organizations often pick something with minimal (if any) thought put into that initial choice, wait until scale reaches a point that switching away is matter of life and death, and then have to desperately fight against inertia. I  think  that's what the parent of your post is getting at.      reply                             hinkley    11 hours ago       |  root  |  parent  |  prev  |  next   [–]

The problem with internal service teams, of which this seems to be one, is that dealing with noisy neighbors is always a bigger problem than anyone is willing to tackle because it involves confrontation. Team X gets punished every time Team Y introduces a new feature that leans on the shared resource harder. It’s a multi tenant system without the fairness guarantees that we usually build into proper multi tenant systems. Sometimes the easiest way to solve this is sharding. You end up deploying the same service many times and routing different classes of requests to different machines so if Team Y keeps trying to wreck the Commons they slow themselves down faster than they slow everyone else down. Those sped up consequences create a feedback loop that almost works instead of an amorphous one with consequences so far removed from actions as to become academic.
