Figure   2   groups the demise probes of Claude-Opus-4.7 and three other models by the number of search queries issued (see Appendix   H   for the remaining models). Among probes with at least two searches, Claude-Opus-4.7 answers 79% correctly at low effort and 78% at high effort, close to the median of 82% across the other shared configurations in Table   2  . However, it issues no search on 68% of demise probes at low effort and 23% at high effort, while no other model exceeds 8% at high effort. Its larger gap reflects how rarely it searches, not how well it uses what it finds. 
 
  
  Figure 2:  Across models, we observe comparable performance on indirect probes for demises using the shared harness, when grouped by the number of search queries issued. Top, accuracy per group (with at least 9 probes) and its overall accuracy (dashed). Bottom, the share of probes in each group. 
 
 
  Shared vs native harness.  Our analysis of search trajectories relies on the shared harness, so models should perform comparably in both harnesses. At high effort they do, with indirect accuracy higher in the shared harness for 9 of the 12 model-category pairs and at most 12.0 points lower for the rest. At low effort, the shared harness trails on demises for Claude-Opus-4.7, GPT-5.4 and Gemini-3.1-Pro by up to 32.0 points, possibly because with reduced or no reasoning these models use a generic search tool less effectively than their provider’s own. We therefore consider the shared harness a reasonable setting in which to study search behavior. 
 
 
  Comparing models.  To compare models on equal footing, we evaluate five models under the shared harness on a common set of probes retained by all of them (Table   3  ). We include these five models to retain a sufficient number of probes in the intersection for a reliable comparison. At low effort, the three open-weights models are more accurate than the two closed ones on both categories. Search behavior accounts for much of this difference. GPT-5.4 and Gemini-3.1-Pro issue no search on 58.5% and 56.5% of demise probes, compared with at most 30.0% for the open-weights models. When Gemini-3.1-Pro does search, it answers 80.5% of probes correctly, in line with the open-weights models. On tenures, the closed models rarely skip search but search less, issuing a median of 3 queries against 7 to 11 for the open-weights models. At high effort, GPT-5.4 is the most accurate model on demises and performs comparably to the open-weights models on tenures. It issues a median of 16 queries on demise probes, more than any other model, and searches on 97.5% of them. The spread across models is also larger on demises, at 52.5 points at low effort and 18.5 points at high effort, than on tenures, at 12.8 and 7.5 points. This is likely because models search more readily on tenures, skipping search less often than on demises in all configurations. 
 
 
 
  6  Error Analysis 

 
 To understand the gap between direct and indirect accuracy, we further categorize failures on indirect probes. We perform this analysis under the shared harness as it logs every query, every search result and the context the model has before answering. We hypothesize that a model can fail at three stages: it never looks for the update, it looks for it but retrieval fails, or retrieves it and still gives an outdated recommendation. We convert these stages into four mutually exclusive failure modes. We assign each failure to the first one it satisfies, in the order below. 
 
  
  Figure 3:  Composition of indirect-probe failure modes under the shared harness for (a) demises and (b) tenures. Numbers above bars give the total number of failures.
 
 
 
 (1)  Reasoning error.  The model’s context contains evidence of the update, yet its answer still makes the invalid recommendation. Prior work finds that models can favor parametric memory over conflicting context (Appendix   A  ).
(2)  Ineffective but explicit search.  The context contains no conclusive evidence of the update, but at least one query directly asks whether     f  old   f_{\text{old}}    still holds, such as whether the person is alive or who currently holds the position. Such failures often reflect poorly phrased queries rather than limitations of the search tool.
(3)  Indirect search.  No query asks about the update explicitly, but at least one could reveal it indirectly, such as a search for the person’s recent public appearances or actions in the role. Because our events are recent, such searches often return activity from before the update, which can suggest that     f  old   f_{\text{old}}    still holds.
(4)  No/unrelated search.  No query could reveal the update, either because the model does not search or because its searches concern other parts of the request. 
 
 
 We assign failure categories to trajectories with Gemini-3.7-Flash at low reasoning effort (prompt is in the supplementary material). We verified the assigned mode for a stratified sample of 160 demise and 165 tenure failures, with an agreement of 98.1% and 81.2% respectively (Appendix   I  ). Most tenure disagreements involve searches whose relevance depends on background knowledge of the position, such as a search for the current members of a Senate committee, which would omit a senator who has left office. These mainly move failures between indirect and unrelated search, so our tenure conclusions rest on the two modes together. Appendix   J   shows representative failures. 
 
 
  Not searching explicitly drives the gap, especially on demises.  On demises, failures with no/unrelated search make up at least 75% of failures in 13 of the 15 configurations (Figure   3  a). On tenures, failures are spread more evenly across the four modes (Figure   3  b). Even so, indirect and no/unrelated search together account for at least 23% of failures in every configuration and for a median of 50% of failures. In 14 of the 15 configurations, failures with no/unrelated search account for all of the additional failures on demises compared with tenures. Since direct accuracy is similar on both categories, this explains the larger gap on demises. 
 
 
  Higher reasoning helps mainly by getting models to search for the update.  We compare the share of probes in each failure mode at low and high effort for the seven models evaluated at both effort levels under the shared harness. On demises, moving from low to high effort reduces failures with no/unrelated search by 28.9 points on average, nearly matching the average gain in indirect accuracy of 28.1 points. On tenures, the reduction is 9.1 points and the gain is 9.4 points. No other failure mode changes by more than 5.0 points for any model. Higher effort therefore improves accuracy almost entirely by getting models to search for the update on probes where they previously did not. The gain is larger on demises because failures with no/unrelated search are far more common there at low effort, which leaves more room to improve. Kimi-K2.6 is the exception and does not improve on demises because it already has few failures with no/unrelated search at low effort. 
 
 
 
  7  Discussion 

 
 Test-time compute versus performance. 

 
 Our work shows that agents struggle to keep up with a changing world because they rely on outdated assumptions. This happens when nothing in the wording of a request signals which underlying facts need to be checked. An obvious remedy is to instruct the agent to verify everything its answer depends on, for example by adding “Before finalizing your answer, verify the facts it relies on” to the prompt. This follows the common practice of spending test-time compute to improve performance  ( Snell et al., 2024 ) . we speculate that it would help, since higher reasoning effort improves indirect accuracy by getting models to search for the update (§  6  ). However, exhaustive verification scales poorly. The facts that matter are rarely stated in the answer itself. A response that recommends a speaker never explicitly states that the person is alive. The agent must therefore first enumerate what it has implicitly assumed, and then check each assumption for every candidate it considers. Every candidate that fails a check introduces a replacement that must be verified in turn. 
 
 
 One way to reduce this cost is to verify selectively.
Rather than verifying every assumption, an agent can prioritize those that are likely to have changed since its knowledge cutoff. Models already appear to follow this signal, as they check whether a person still holds a position more often than whether the person is alive. However, our results on demises show that how often a fact changes is not a sufficient criterion. A person’s demise is a rare event, yet it invalidates every recommendation that involves them. A good verification strategy should therefore weigh both how likely an assumption is to be outdated and how much the answer depends on it. A promising direction is to train agents to decide what to verify, with the objective of balancing accuracy against test-time cost. 
 
 
 
 Continual Learning. 

 
 Even selective verification has a limit, since an agent can only check the assumptions it thinks of. In our benchmark we consider updates and their direct consequences, but real-world updates often have far reaching consequences.
Consider a user who asks where to go on a safari next month. A drought around a popular wildlife reserve may drive the animals elsewhere. The reserve stays open but sightings may now be far poorer than at alternatives the agent never considers. An agent that verifies its assumptions would likely confirm that the reserve is open and recommend it, even though better options exist. Reasoning forward from a drought to sparse wildlife is easy, but reasoning backward from a safari to the many conditions that could spoil it is much harder. When the update that matters is several steps removed from the answer, verifying the answer’s own assumptions is therefore not enough. Addressing such cases requires acquiring recent knowledge (in this case, knowing about the drought). 
 
 
 This motivates a complementary approach, which is to keep the agent’s parametric memory up to date.
Parametric memory is the source of the assumptions an agent starts from. An agent that has learned of a person’s demise during training would not recommend them, and would not need to verify whether they are still alive.
Interestingly, an update does not have to be recalled exactly to be useful, since search can supply the details. The agent only needs to recognize which of its assumptions are worth checking. For example, a model trained on reports of an upcoming election or of a person’s failing health may be more inclined to check whether the officeholder has changed or whether the person is still alive, just as a model that knows of a drought can reason forward to poor sightings. Continual learning could therefore help not only by updating facts but also by indicating which facts may have changed. Additionally, updating the weights moves cost from test to training time, where it is paid once and amortized over all users and requests. 
 
 
 In practice, we expect the two approaches to be combined. No training schedule can keep a model fully current, leaving a gap between the most recent update and the date of a request. Changes that fall in this gap can only be caught through verification. Continual learning both shortens this gap, leaving fewer assumptions that could be outdated, and helps direct the remaining checks towards those most likely to have changed. 
 
 
 
 
  8  Conclusion 

 
 We introduce  BlindToChange  to track a new axis of agentic search capabilities: do AI agents proactively discover recent real-world changes that affect their responses? By pairing each indirect probe with a direct probe of the same change, we separate an agent’s ability to find a change when asked from its ability to discover the change unprompted and account for its consequences. We show that frontier agents almost always find a change when asked directly, yet often miss it when the request does not inquire about it. Our error analysis traces many of these failures to agents never explicitly checking whether the relevant fact has changed, and shows that higher reasoning effort helps mainly by prompting such checks. Our findings highlight that benchmarks which state what needs to be found overestimate how well agents keep up with a changing world. 
 
 
 AI use statement 

 
 In this work, we used generative AI tools to generate the direct and indirect probes that make up our benchmark (§  3.2  ), to judge model responses, and to support qualitative analysis by labeling failure modes in our error analysis (§  6  ). We validated both the judge and the failure-mode labels against human annotations (Appendices   C   and   I  ). We also used AI coding assistants to help implement parts of our pipeline. We have not used generative AI tools to propose or refine hypotheses, design or provide feedback on our methodology or experiments, clean or reformat the dataset, interpret results, or develop our conceptual framework. Formulating mathematical claims, providing ingredients for or writing proofs, and translation are not applicable to this work. Additionally, we used generative AI tools to edit the paper for readability. We have reviewed all AI-assisted work. We take responsibility for the final content of this work, including text, claims or artifacts produced with the aid of generative AI.

  Appendix A  Extended Related Work 

 
 Agentic Search Systems and Benchmarks. 

 
 Traditional Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems supplement a model’s parametric memory with a non-parametric retrieval corpus that is queried once using the input question  ( Lewis et al., 2020 ) . A line of work later made the retrieval decision part of generation itself. FLARE anticipates the upcoming sentence and, when that anticipation is low confidence, uses it to form a retrieval query  ( Jiang et al., 2023 ) . Self-RAG replaces this heuristic with learned reflection tokens, so the model decides at each step whether to retrieve and whether the retrieved evidence supports what it wrote  ( Asai et al., 2024 ) . A parallel line of work gives the model a set of actions, now commonly called tool calls, rather than a single retrieve operation. WebGPT lets a model search, click, scroll, and quote inside a live browser  ( Nakano et al., 2021 ) , and ReAct interleaves reasoning with acting, so the model can revise its plan from what it observes  ( Yao et al., 2023 ) . The agentic search systems we evaluate, often called agentic RAG, combine the two lineages  ( Li et al., 2025 ) . The model chooses when to invoke a search or browse tool, what query or URL to invoke it with, and when it has gathered enough evidence to answer. 
 
 
 Benchmarks for these systems have followed. GAIA poses general assistant tasks that require tool use, browsing, and multimodal reasoning  ( Mialon et al., 2024 ) . BrowseComp narrows the setting to web research, with short-answer questions whose evidence is deliberately entangled and hard to locate  ( Wei et al., 2025 ) . Because the live web changes between runs, BrowseComp-Plus rebuilds the same style of evaluation over a fixed human-verified corpus, which separates retrieval quality from reasoning over what was retrieved  ( Chen et al., 2026 ) . Other benchmarks shift the evaluation object from the final answer to the search process itself. DeepSearchQA scores comprehensiveness and reasoned stopping on exhaustive-list web tasks  ( Gupta et al., 2026 ) , InfoDeepSeek scores the accuracy, utility, and compactness of the information an agent gathers from the live web  ( Xi et al., 2025b ) , and Mind2Web 2 judges long-horizon trajectories for both answer correctness and source attribution  ( Gou et al., 2025 ) . Two recent benchmarks ask how much of this performance is search rather than recall. LiveBrowseComp builds questions from low-salience facts published in the preceding ninety days, and shows that they largely defeat agents that score well on BrowseComp  ( Fan et al., 2026 ) . LiveNewsBench generates its questions automatically from clusters of news articles about a single recent event and refreshes them quarterly, so both the questions and answers change  ( Zhang et al., 2026b ) . 
 
 
 
 Temporal Freshness Benchmarks. 

 
 Facts differ in how long they stay true. MuLan separates Wikidata relations into mutable and immutable classes and finds that closed-book models are both less accurate and markedly less confident on the mutable ones  ( Fierro et al., 2024 ) . EverGreenQA labels questions rather than facts, and finds that this label predicts retrieval behavior  ( Pletenev et al., 2025 ) . RecencyQA also classifies how often an answer changes, from within an hour to never, and notes that this rate can itself depend on context  ( Piryani et al., 2026 ) . 
 
 
 Benchmarks have taken up how well models handle questions whose answers change. RealTimeQA draws its questions from weekly news quizzes and releases a new set every week  ( Kasai et al., 2023 ) . FreshQA instead fixes a set of 600 questions written by annotators to read like search queries, grouped by how quickly their answers turn over, and its maintainers re-verify the answers every week  ( Vu et al., 2024 ) . Keeping either benchmark current is manual work, and its answers can fall out of date between updates. Later benchmarks instead construct questions from a source that records its own changes, so that answers can be refreshed automatically. PAT-Questions builds questions from templates over time-dependent Wikidata relations, and refreshes every answer by re-running the SPARQL query that produced it  ( Meem et al., 2024 ) . EvolvingQA, GrowOVER, EvoWiki, and DynaQuest instead compare successive Wikipedia snapshots and generate questions from the passages or infobox fields that differ between versions  ( Kim et al., 2024 ;  Ko et al., 2024 ;  Tang et al., 2025 ;  Lin et al., 2025 ) . DailyQA follows the same recipe on a daily cycle, using revision logs to keep the answer key in step  ( Cheng & Dou, 2025 ) . 
 
 
 
 Unstated Constraints and Agent-Initiated Information Seeking. 

 
   Kaur et al. (2026)   represent the factors that determine task success as dimensions and separate the ones a user has stated from the ones they have not, treating the unstated ones as gaps an assistant should recognize on the user’s behalf. Benchmarks that make such gaps discoverable through tool use find that recognizing them is the hard part. Implicit Intelligence places unstated constraints in environments where they can be found through a tool call, and finds that agents commonly act on the initial state without probing for the information that would reveal the constraint  ( Sirdeshmukh & Wetter, 2026 ) . DeepPlanning evaluates travel and shopping plans against rule-based checkers and reports that implicit environmental constraints such as limited seat availability or mismatched attraction opening hours are harder to detect than the requirements a user states  ( Zhang et al., 2026a ) . MapSatisfyBench recovers the decision factors a user left unspoken from behavior logs, and finds that answers are well grounded in the tool outputs an agent did collect while the tool that would supply the missing factor is rarely called  ( Bai et al., 2026 ) . 
 
 
 The same failure appears when the information need itself is underspecified. InteractComp builds queries whose intended target cannot be identified without more information, and reports that agents answer far fewer of them correctly than when the missing context is supplied, and that accuracy on them has not improved over a period in which BrowseComp scores rose sevenfold  ( Deng et al., 2026 ) . DiscoBench separates noticing that a request is ambiguous from acting well once it is noticed, and finds that searching harder in place of resolving the ambiguity can do worse than guessing  ( Tao et al., 2026 ) . 
 
 
 
 Knowledge Conflict and Downstream Behavior. 

 
 A body of work studies what a model does when contextual evidence contradicts its parametric memory.   Longpre et al. (2021)   substitute the answer entity in gold passages, and find that models prefer the memorized answer over the one supplied in the context.   Du et al. (2024)   find that the more familiar a model is with an entity, the less its answer is affected by contextual evidence about it.   Kortukov et al. (2024)   replace synthetic conflicts with real corrective documents and find that updates fail less often than earlier work reported, but that a wrong parametric answer appearing in the context makes failure likelier. Conflicts also arise among the retrieved passages themselves. WikiContradict studies disagreements between Wikipedia passages, where both are equally credible, and finds that models rarely convey that the evidence is inconsistent  ( Hou et al., 2024 ) . 
 
 
 Knowledge editing writes the update into the weights, and MQuAKE and RippleEdits find that editing methods recall the edited fact but leave its consequences unchanged  ( Zhong et al., 2023 ;  Cohen et al., 2024 ) . KUP separates direct probes that ask for the updated fact from indirect probes whose answer changes once the update holds, and finds that models memorize the update and still fail the indirect version  ( Li & Goyal, 2025 ) . TRACK supplies the updates in context instead, and finds that providing the correct fact can leave a model worse off than providing nothing, with the degradation growing as more conflicts enter a single reasoning chain  ( Feng et al., 2026 ) . IMPRINTBENCH compares both update families on the same corpus and scores them on six capabilities, including implicit relevance, where a query invokes an update through its timing or topic rather than naming it, and finds that no method succeeds across all six  ( Kalra et al., 2026 ) . 
 
 
 A separate line of work asks what changes when the fact is temporal rather than counterfactual. HoH builds retrieval corpora in which outdated and current documents about the same fact coexist, and shows that the outdated ones degrade answers even when the current ones are retrieved alongside them  ( Ouyang et al., 2025 ) . WikiRecentChanges pairs stable and recently changed Wikidata facts with contextual statements that conflict with the model, and finds that models reason about change for the facts that did change and almost never for the stable ones, yet this reasoning rarely reaches the final answer  ( Wallat et al., 2026 ) . STALE and HorizonBench build interaction histories in which a later event implicitly invalidates an earlier belief without restating it, and both find that systems identify the current state and still act on the old one  ( Chao et al., 2026 ;  Li et al., 2026 ) . 
 
 
 In all of this work the update is already available to the model, either in its context or its weights, so the only research question is whether the response changes. In our setting the update is not provided, so the agent must first suspect that what it recalls may be outdated and then search for the change. Of our failure categories, only reasoning errors correspond to the failure this line of work studies.

  Appendix I  Failure mode validation 

 
 We validate the failure modes of §  6   for both categories, using failures under shared search in the same 15 configurations. A failure with no search query is assigned no/unrelated search by construction, so we sample only failures that issued at least one query. We take every failure in the smaller failure modes and sample the larger ones evenly across configurations, which gives 160 demise and 165 tenure failures. 
 
 
 One author checked each assigned failure mode against the model’s queries and the context it had before its final answer, using the criteria given to the classifier. The author was shown the classifier’s evidence excerpt and query labels. Table   9   compares the assigned failure modes with the verified ones. Worktrunk

[![Docs](https://img.shields.io/badge/docs-worktrunk.dev-blue?style=for-the-badge&logo=gitbook)](https://worktrunk.dev) [![License: MIT OR Apache-2.0](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT%20OR%20Apache--2.0-blue?style=for-the-badge)](https://opensource.org/licenses/MIT) [![CI](https://img.shields.io/github/actions/workflow/status/max-sixty/worktrunk/ci.yaml?event=push&branch=main&style=for-the-badge&logo=github)](https://github.com/max-sixty/worktrunk/actions?query=branch%3Amain+workflow%3Aci) [![Codecov](https://img.shields.io/codecov/c/github/max-sixty/worktrunk?style=for-the-badge&logo=codecov)](https://codecov.io/gh/max-sixty/worktrunk) [![Stars](https://img.shields.io/github/stars/max-sixty/worktrunk?style=for-the-badge&logo=github)](https://github.com/max-sixty/worktrunk/stargazers) [![maintained with tend](https://img.shields.io/badge/maintained_with-tend-bba580?style=for-the-badge&logo=data:image/svg%2bxml;base64,)](https://github.com/max-sixty/tend) > **November 2026**: Worktrunk was [released](https://x.com/max_sixty/status/2006077845391724739?s=20) at the start of the year, and has quickly become the most popular git worktree manager. It's built with love (there's no slop!). Please let me know any frictions at all; I'm intensely focused on continuing to make Worktrunk excellent, and the biggest help is folks posting problems they perceive. Worktrunk is a CLI for git worktree management, designed for running AI agents in parallel. Worktrunk's three core commands make worktrees as easy as branches. Plus, Worktrunk has a bunch of quality-of-life features to simplify working with many parallel changes, including hooks to automate local workflows & copy-on-write build caches. A quick demo: ![Worktrunk Demo](https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/max-sixty/worktrunk-assets@main/assets/docs/light/wt-core.gif) > ### 📚 Full documentation at [worktrunk.dev](https://worktrunk.dev) 📚 ## Context: git worktrees AI agents like Claude Code and Codex can handle longer tasks without supervision, such that it's possible to manage 5-10+ in parallel. Git's native worktree feature gives each agent its own working directory, so they don't step on each other's changes. But the git worktree UX is clunky. Even a task as small as starting a new worktree requires typing the branch name three times: `git worktree add -b feat ../repo.feat`, then `cd ../repo.feat`. ## Worktrunk makes git worktrees as easy as branches Worktrees are addressed by branch name; paths are computed from a configurable template. Commands that take a branch also accept the path of the worktree it is checked out in.

Start with the core commands

**Core commands:**
Task Worktrunk Plain git
Switch worktrees wt switch feat cd ../repo.feat
Create + start Claude wt switch -c -x claude feat 
git worktree add -b feat ../repo.feat && \
cd ../repo.feat && \
claude
Clean up wt remove 
cd ../repo && \
git worktree remove ../repo.feat && \
git branch -d feat
List with status wt list git worktree list (paths only)

Expand into the more advanced commands as needed

Workflow automation:

- **[Hooks](https://worktrunk.dev/hook/)** — run commands on create, pre-merge, post-merge, etc - **[LLM commit messages](https://worktrunk.dev/llm-commits/)** — generate commit messages from diffs - **[Merge workflow](https://worktrunk.dev/merge/)** — squash, rebase, merge, clean up in one command - **[Interactive picker](https://worktrunk.dev/switch/#interactive-picker)** — browse worktrees with streaming CI status and diff, log, PR and comment previews - **[Share build caches](https://worktrunk.dev/step/#wt-step-copy-ignored)** — ten worktrees get `target/`, `node_modules/`, etc without building or copying them (on APFS, btrfs, and XFS) - **[`wt list --full`](https://worktrunk.dev/list/#full-mode)** — [CI status](https://worktrunk.dev/list/#ci-status) and [AI-generated summaries](https://worktrunk.dev/list/#llm-summaries) per branch - **[PR checkout](https://worktrunk.dev/switch/#pull-requests-and-merge-requests)** — `wt switch pr:123` to jump straight to a PR's branch - **[Dev server per worktree](https://worktrunk.dev/tips-patterns/#dev-server-per-worktree)** — `hash_port` template filter gives each worktree a unique port - **[Aliases](https://worktrunk.dev/extending/#aliases) & [per-branch variables](https://worktrunk.dev/config/#wt-config-state-vars)** — custom `wt ` commands and branch-scoped state for hook templates - ...and **[lots more](#next-steps)** Multiple parallel agents, same simple commands: ![Worktrunk omnibus demo: multiple Claude agents in Zellij tabs with hooks, LLM commits, and merge workflow](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/max-sixty/worktrunk-assets/main/assets/docs/light/wt-zellij-omnibus.gif) ## Install **Homebrew (macOS & Linux):** ```bash brew install worktrunk && wt config shell install ``` Shell integration allows commands to change directories. **Cargo:** ```bash cargo install worktrunk && wt config shell install ```
Windows & other **Windows.** `wt` defaults to Windows Terminal's command, so Winget additionally installs Worktrunk as `git-wt` to avoid the conflict: ```bash winget install max-sixty.worktrunk git-wt config shell install ``` Alternatively, disable Windows Terminal's alias (Settings → Apps → Advanced app settings → App execution aliases → "Terminal"/"Terminal Preview") to use `wt` directly. > Free code signing provided by [SignPath.io](https://signpath.io/), certificate by [SignPath Foundation](https://signpath.org/) — [policy](https://worktrunk.dev/code-signing/). **Arch Linux:** ```bash sudo pacman -S worktrunk && wt config shell install ``` **Conda / Pixi** (community-maintained [feedstock](https://github.com/conda-forge/worktrunk-feedstock)): ```bash conda install -c conda-forge worktrunk && wt config shell install ``` Or with [Pixi](https://pixi.sh): `pixi global install worktrunk && wt config shell install`.
## Quick start Create a worktree for a new feature: ```console $ wt switch --create feature-auth ✓ Created branch feature-auth from main and worktree @ ~/repo.feature-auth ``` This creates a new branch and worktree, then switches to it. Do your work, then check all worktrees with [`wt list`](https://worktrunk.dev/list/): ```console $ wt list Branch Status HEAD± main↕ main…± Remote⇅ Commit Age Message @ feature-auth + ↑ +27 -8 ↑1 +31 4bc72dc 2h Add authenticatio… ^ main ^⇡ ⇡1 0e631ad 1d Initial commit ○ Showing 2 worktrees, 1 with changes, 1 ahead, hidden: Path ``` The `@` marks the current worktree. `+` means staged changes, `↑1` means 1 commit ahead of main, `⇡` means unpushed commits. When done, either: **PR workflow** — commit, push, open a PR, merge via GitHub/GitLab, then clean up: ```bash wt step commit # commit staged changes gh pr create # or glab mr create wt remove # after PR is merged ``` **Local merge** — squash, rebase onto main, fast-forward merge, clean up: ```console $ wt merge main ◎ Generating commit message and committing changes... (2 files, +53, no squashing needed) Add authentication module ✓ Committed changes @ a1b2c3d ◎ Merging 1 commit to main @ a1b2c3d (no rebase needed) * a1b2c3d Add authentication module auth.rs | 51 +++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++ lib.rs | 2 ++ 2 files changed, 53 insertions(+) ✓ Merged to main (1 commit, 2 files, +53) ◎ Removing feature-auth worktree & branch in background (same commit as main, _) ○ Switched to worktree for main @ ~/repo ``` For parallel agents, create multiple worktrees and launch an agent in each: ```bash wt switch -x claude -c feature-a -- 'Add user authentication' wt switch -x claude -c feature-b -- 'Fix the pagination bug' wt switch -x claude -c feature-c -- 'Write tests for the API' ``` The `-x` flag runs a command after switching; arguments after `--` are passed to it. Configure [post-start hooks](https://worktrunk.dev/hook/#hook-types) to automate setup (install deps, start dev servers). ## Next steps - Learn the core commands: [`wt switch`](https://worktrunk.dev/switch/), [`wt list`](https://worktrunk.dev/list/), [`wt merge`](https://worktrunk.dev/merge/), [`wt remove`](https://worktrunk.dev/remove/) - Set up [hooks](https://worktrunk.dev/hook/) for automated setup - Explore [LLM commit messages](https://worktrunk.dev/llm-commits/), [interactive picker](https://worktrunk.dev/switch/#interactive-picker), [Claude Code integration](https://worktrunk.dev/claude-code/), [CI status & PR links](https://worktrunk.dev/list/#ci-status) - Browse [tips & patterns](https://worktrunk.dev/tips-patterns/) for recipes: aliases, dev servers, databases, agent handoffs, and more - [Extending Worktrunk](https://worktrunk.dev/extending/) — customize workflows with hooks & aliases - Watch [@DevOpsToolbox's video on Worktrunk](https://youtu.be/WBQiqr6LevQ?t=345) - Run `wt --help` or `wt --help` for quick CLI reference ## Contributing - ⭐ Star the repo - Tell a friend about Worktrunk - [Open an issue](https://github.com/max-sixty/worktrunk/issues/new?title=&body=%23%23%20Description%0A%0A%3C!--%20Describe%20the%20bug%20or%20feature%20request%20--%3E%0A%0A%23%23%20Context%0A%0A%3C!--%20Any%20relevant%20context%3A%20your%20workflow%2C%20what%20you%20were%20trying%20to%20do%2C%20etc.%20--%3E) — feedback, feature requests, even a small friction or imperfect user message, or [a worktree pain not yet solved](https://github.com/max-sixty/worktrunk/issues/new?title=Worktree%20friction%3A%20&body=%23%23%20The%20friction%0A%0A%3C!--%20What%20worktree-related%20task%20is%20still%20painful%3F%20--%3E%0A%0A%23%23%20Current%20workaround%0A%0A%3C!--%20How%20do%20you%20handle%20this%20today%3F%20--%3E%0A%0A%23%23%20Ideal%20solution%0A%0A%3C!--%20What%20would%20make%20this%20easier%3F%20--%3E) - Share: [X](https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?text=Worktrunk%20%E2%80%94%20CLI%20for%20git%20worktree%20management&url=https%3A%2F%2Fworktrunk.dev) · [Reddit](https://www.reddit.com/submit?url=https%3A%2F%2Fworktrunk.dev&title=Worktrunk%20%E2%80%94%20CLI%20for%20git%20worktree%20management) · [LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/sharing/share-offsite/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fworktrunk.dev) > ### 📚 Full documentation at [worktrunk.dev](https://worktrunk.dev) 📚 ### Star history

             Description 
          

           In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:
ipv4: free inet_opt and ireq_opt after an RCU grace period
tcp_v4_syn_recv_sock() transfers ownership of ireq->ireq_opt to the
child socket (newinet->inet_opt) without copying it.
Another cpu can concurrently process a retransmitted SYN for the same
request socket, and send a SYNACK from tcp_check_req().
tcp_v4_send_synack() and inet_csk_route_req() read ireq->ireq_opt
under rcu_read_lock() only, and ip_build_and_send_pkt() and
ip_options_build() then read opt->optlen twice.
Note that the SYNACK timer itself is not an issue: it holds a
reference on its request socket, and inet_csk_reqsk_queue_drop()
calls timer_delete_sync() before the child can be freed.
Since commit 079096f103fa ("tcp/dccp: install syn_recv requests
into ehash table"), request sockets are processed without holding
the listener lock, so nothing prevents the child socket from being
freed while the SYNACK is still being built. TCP child sockets do
not have SOCK_RCU_FREE, and inet_sock_destruct() frees inet_opt
with a plain kfree(), leading to a use-after-free in
ip_options_build().
A similar issue exists with request socket migration
(net.ipv4.tcp_migrate_req=1, or a BPF_SK_REUSEPORT_SELECT_OR_MIGRATE
program). reqsk_timer_handler() clones the request socket with
inet_reqsk_clone(), so that the old request socket and its clone
share the same ireq_opt, then reqsk_migrate_reset() clears the
pointer in the old one. Another cpu holding a reference on the old
request socket can still be using these options (sending a SYNACK,
or creating a child in tcp_v4_syn_recv_sock()) when the clone is
freed, and tcp_v4_reqsk_destructor() also uses a plain kfree().
Readers already use RCU, and other paths replacing inet_opt
(do_ip_setsockopt(), cipso_v4_sock_setattr()...) already use
kfree_rcu(). Use kfree_rcu() in inet_sock_destruct() and
tcp_v4_reqsk_destructor() as well.
IPv6 is not affected by the first issue, because tcp_v6_syn_recv_sock()
duplicates the options. tcp_v6_reqsk_destructor() has the same
migration issue with ipv6_opt, which is only set by CALIPSO. This
will be addressed in a separate patch.

             Mitigation 
             
cengizcan> IPv4 TCP packet filtering:
 - Requires: nftables and root access through sudo.
 - Assumes: IPv4 options are not needed. For boot persistence,
   /etc/nftables.conf manages the firewall, without UFW or firewalld.
 - Blocks: incoming IPv4 TCP packets that contain IP options.
 - Keeps working: IPv4 TCP connections without IP options. TCP options
   such as timestamps and window scaling are unaffected, as is IPv6.
   Existing firewall rules still apply.
 - Breaks: TCP connections that depend on IPv4 options.
 - Covers: the host, including connections from the host to itself.
   Containers with separate networking need the rule applied separately.
 - Limit: reduces the risk but does not fully prevent exploitation.
 To apply the rule:
  1. Create the rule file:
     printf '%s\n' 'table inet cve_2026_98432 {
       chain input {
         type filter hook input priority -310; policy accept;
         ip protocol tcp ip hdrlength > 5 counter drop
       }
     }' | sudo tee /etc/cve-2026-98432.nft >/dev/null
  2. Check and apply the rule:
     sudo nft -c -f /etc/cve-2026-98432.nft &&
     sudo nft -f /etc/cve-2026-98432.nft
  3. Keep the rule after reboot (run once):
     echo 'include "/etc/cve-2026-98432.nft"' | \
       sudo tee -a /etc/nftables.conf
     sudo nft -c -f /etc/nftables.conf &&
     sudo systemctl enable nftables.service
 To remove the rule and its boot setting:
     sudo sed -i '\|^include "/etc/cve-2026-98432.nft"$|d' \
       /etc/nftables.conf
     sudo nft delete table inet cve_2026_98432

    Self-Hosted  By relay  October 31, 2026  
   Ubuntu LTS kernels still unfixed for critical CVE-2026-98432 
   No patched kernels are available yet for 22.04, 24.04, or 26.04 despite a CVSS 9.8 rating. 
   
     
       
     
     
       
     
     
       
     
     
       
     
     
       
     
     
       
     
     
       
     
     
       
     
   
    Ubuntu has not shipped fixed kernels for  CVE-2026-98432 , a critical vulnerability scored CVSS 9.8, leaving the 22.04, 24.04, and 26.04 LTS releases without a vendor update. 
 Operators running those releases therefore have no official kernel package that closes the hole. The gap matters most for internet-facing and multi-tenant self-hosted systems that rely on Ubuntu’s LTS kernels for isolation and privilege boundaries; until packages appear, those hosts remain exposed to whatever remote or local attack the CVE enables. 
 Ubuntu has not announced an ETA for the fixes. In the interim, affected administrators are left to decide whether to stay on the stock kernel, apply out-of-tree mitigations if any exist, or move workloads onto releases or kernels that already carry the patch.

           One of the biggest releases this year: a reworked MCP server, RAG-ready Markdown in one line, an improved Cloudflare solver, and browser tabs that stay open for automation 🚀  
   Note    Follow us on X for daily tips and tricks   
 
   Warning   This release introduces breaking changes to the MCP server. Check the  breaking changes  section before updating.  
 
 🚀 New Stuff and quality of life changes 
 
  Browser tabs now stay open and get reused across requests  (Check the  docs ):
 
 All browser sessions keep their tabs after a request, and the next request reuses a free tab instead of opening a new one. 
 Every request re-applies its own settings (timeouts, headers, resource blocking) to the tab it gets, so nothing leaks between requests. 
 Tabs that hit an error are closed and replaced, and the new  close_pages()  method closes every open tab. 
 The page you fetched stays loaded, so a  page_setup  function on the next request runs on it before navigating away. That's the building block for chaining automation across requests. 
 
 
  Turn any page into clean, LLM-ready Markdown with  Response.markdown()   (Check the  docs ):
   from   scrapling . fetchers   import   Fetcher 

 markdown   =   Fetcher . get ( "https://example.com" ). markdown ( main_content_only  =  True )  
 
 Scripts, styles, and hidden prompt-injection content are always stripped first, the same as the cleaning the MCP server does. 
 Pass  css_selector  to convert only the elements you need. 
 Available through the new  rag  extra ( pip install "scrapling[rag]" ), which the  ai / shell / all  extras include too. 
 
 
  New  SiteToMarkdownSpider  template to crawl a whole website into a Markdown corpus for RAG pipelines  (Check the  docs ):
   from   scrapling . spiders   import   SiteToMarkdownSpider 

 class   DocsSpider ( SiteToMarkdownSpider ):
     name   =   "docs" 
     start_urls   =  [ "https://example.com/docs/" ]
     allowed_domains   =  { "example.com" }
     output_dir   =   "docs_markdown" 

 result   =   DocsSpider (). start ()
 result . items . to_jsonl ( "docs.jsonl" )  
 
 Yields one item per page with  url / title / markdown , and the optional  output_dir  writes one Markdown file per page. 
  max_pages  caps the crawl, and since it builds on  CrawlSpider , overriding  rules()  gives you full control over which links get followed. 
 
 
  The MCP server is reworked (breaking)  (Check the  breaking changes  and the  docs ):
 
 The 13 tools are now split into two modes: one-shot tools ( fetch ,  bulk_fetch ,  stealthy_fetch ,  bulk_stealthy_fetch ) that always launch their own browser and show their real defaults, and session tools that work through a session opened once. 
 The new  session_fetch  tool fetches through a browser session, while  open_session  now holds the browser-level settings only and returns the session's effective settings for the AI agent. 
 The  get  tool is renamed to  make_request , and it now supports any HTTP method. 
 The new  open_request_session  and  session_make_request  tools give the AI persistent HTTP sessions that keep cookies and the browser fingerprint between requests. 
 This also ends fetches resetting the session's settings, first fixed by  @Yigtwxx  in  #418 . 
 
 
  The MCP server's HTTP transport now requires authentication and binds to localhost by default (breaking)  by  @yamantaka-singh  in  #414  (Fixes  #413 , check the  docs ):
 
 Pass  --auth-token  (or the  SCRAPLING_MCP_AUTH_TOKEN  environment variable) to require a bearer token, or  --no-auth  to serve it unauthenticated on purpose. 
 Pass  --host 0.0.0.0  to accept connections from the network. 
 
 
 
 🐛 Bug Fixes 
 
  Cloudflare Turnstile/Interstitial solving now works regardless of the browser locale, and no longer loops forever on interactive challenges in headless mode . Stealth pages also stop crashing mid-solve, with contributions by  @subediparas5  in  #412 . (Fixes  #411  and  #422 ) 
  Fixed  find / find_all  with  class_  silently missing multi-class elements  by  @yetval  in  #410 ,  and blank  class_  values and unescaped CSS string values  by  @yamantaka-singh  in  #417 . 
  Fixed cached responses in  development_mode  losing the request meta on replay  by  @Yigtwxx  in  #419 . 
  Fixed HTTP requests with  retries  below 1 failing without sending the request  by  @Yigtwxx  in  #420 . 
 
 Docs 
 
  The website sections are restructured : a new "Using with AI" section holds the MCP server, the new  Agent skill  page, and the  Building RAG systems  guide, and the BeautifulSoup migration guide moved next to the Scrapy integration under "Integrations and migrations". 
  Added a  CHANGELOG.md   to the repository with the notes of every release so far. 
 
  🙏 Special thanks to the community for all the continuous testing and feedback  
 
 Big shoutout to our Platinum Sponsors

      Title: Compile as Hypothesis: A Headroom Typology for Prompt Optimization on Real Reasoning Models 
      Authors:  Zhengshuai Yang ,  Changyun Li               View a PDF of the paper titled Compile as Hypothesis: A Headroom Typology for Prompt Optimization on Real Reasoning Models, by Zhengshuai Yang and 1 other authors 
     View PDF 
     HTML (experimental) 



     
             Abstract: Automated prompt compilers search for or rewrite prompts under the implicit assumption that optimization consistently improves downstream task performance. We evaluate this assumption on frontier reasoning models through rigorous paired, same-day measurements. Across four optimizer families (genome search, profile-guided mutation, GEPA, and ESPO) and eight tasks, structured search yields no statistically significant accuracy gains on strong reasoners. However, a discrete structural genome provides essential architectural stability, preventing catastrophic bimodal seed-collapse (where unconstrained search collapses toward the judge floor in 3/5 runs). Through 190-problem evaluations on knowledge-intensive benchmarks, we establish a three-dimensional headroom typology: prompt optimization cannot compensate for intrinsic knowledge deficits or physical token truncation, but successfully resolves protocol and formatting errors. On gpt-6, while free-text reflective search (GEPA) yields a +.14 gain on a task where structured search remains flat, qualitative ablation reveals that ~.035 stems from judge-rubric reconstruction while ~.105 reflects genuine instruction refinement. Our pre-registered AutoAPC-Select deployment gate matches the oracle policy in 5/7 groups and rescues seed-collapse arms with zero regret. Finally, we expose silent backend-mixing in commercial APIs during outage windows and provide automated per-call audit verification tools to ensure empirical evaluation fidelity.

      Title: Satisfied, Not Solving: Wireheading of Bounded Homeostatic Rewards in Reinforcement Learning 
      Authors:  Chase J. Metoyer               View a PDF of the paper titled Satisfied, Not Solving: Wireheading of Bounded Homeostatic Rewards in Reinforcement Learning, by Chase J. Metoyer 
     View PDF 
     HTML (experimental) 



     
             Abstract: Bounded intrinsic rewards are often assumed to be safe from exploitation: if a signal can yield at most a fixed amount, gaming it should not pay. We test this for a homeostatic satiation reward, in which needs build up and relieving them is rewarding, and give the agent a cheap action that resets its needs. In MiniGrid DoorKey-8x8, PPO agents with this action solved 2 of 80 seeds, against 71 of 80 on the same seeds without it; in KeyCorridorS3R1, 0 of 20 against 20 of 20. Their policies stayed near uniform. The reward does not ask for this: a telescoping argument caps any policy's satiation return at the needs' starting drive, and a post-hoc computation shows that, at every growth rate we trained, a solving trajectory beats that cap on all sampled layouts. In DoorKey with advantage normalization on, a satisfaction signal the agent could fill itself was worse than none (11 of 20 solved with task reward alone, 1 of 20 with the tamperable signal), and a per-press cost of 0.1 restored the task in every seed. Farming of positive reward cycles appeared in DoorKey but not persistently in KeyCorridorS3R1. All predictions were pre-registered, and hash-locked from round 3 on; 9 of our 23 hypotheses were not supported, and we report each.

investigating unauthorized access to an internal tool used by our sales and customer-facing teams. This update explains our response and observations on AI-assisted attacks.     
   
    There is no evidence that WorkOS application data was accessed, nor is there evidence that production WorkOS services were accessed or impacted. Our current analysis indicates this incident affected only CRM and customer support data.
   
   On October 30, 2026, we identified unauthorized access to an internal WorkOS application used by our sales team.   The information accessed included business contact details and summaries of customer communications. We are reviewing the affected records to determine the impact for individual organizations.  Our investigation identified the use of an AI-assisted offensive security framework to automate reconnaissance and exploitation attempts.  Data involved  The affected internal application provided access to the following categories of information:    Business contact details:  Names, email addresses, phone numbers, job titles, and company affiliations held in our customer relationship management (CRM) systems.   Business account and relationship information:  Customer account histories and information about sales and customer-relationship information.   Customer communications:  Summaries and excerpts from sales calls, support discussions, and customer Slack conversations.   Operational metadata:  Information about customers' use of WorkOS products, including product usage and connection or directory health.   What we are doing  We disabled external access to the affected application and are conducting a broader review of access controls on internal tools. We have retained an independent digital forensics and incident response firm to help establish the full scope of the activity and evaluate its impact. Our security and engineering teams continue to review the evidence and address the issues identified.  The rise of agentic attacks  Recent reporting from  Wiz ,  Google , and  CrowdStrike  documents growing use of AI agents in real-world intrusions. These systems can choose follow-up actions based on a target's responses and automate multi-step attack sequences.  This increases the speed and scale of attacks that exploit weaknesses such as exposed applications and stolen credentials. It increases the need for timely remediation and monitoring that can connect suspicious activity across systems. The linked reports above provide additional context on this broader trend.  Stay alert to phishing and social engineering  Business contact information and details from previous conversations can help an attacker make fraudulent requests look legitimate. Even when a message references a real colleague or support conversation, verify unexpected requests before sharing sensitive information or taking action.  What happens next  The investigation is ongoing. We will contact affected customers directly and provide further updates as we verify additional information. page:https://openai.com/index/scaling-gi.text: Scaling Git at OpenAI | OpenAI                                             Skip to main content                  Research             Products             Business             Developers             Company             Foundation   (opens in a new window)                         Log in   Try ChatGPT  (opens in a new window)                  Research    Products    Business    Developers    Company    Foundation  (opens in a new window)      Try ChatGPT  (opens in a new window)   Login                                   OpenAI         November 2, 2026  Engineering    Scaling Git at OpenAI    Building agentic-scale scale source control while investing in the Git ecosystem.   By Aaron Friel, Taylor Blau, and Ted Nyman, Members of Technical Staff                  Loading…            Share                Why we needed a new source control system          Why we needed a new source control system    Engineering for Git at scale    Git object storage primer      Existing distributed Git service patterns    Three-phase commit (3PC)    Write-ahead log (WAL)      Architecting Pando    Rethinking constraints    Causal consistency (CC)    Comparing Approaches    Scaling pushes    Line-rate fetch and clone performance    Compaction and time to first byte      Building Pando    Deploying Pando    Contributing back to the Git project    What’s next            Why we needed a new source control system    Engineering for Git at scale    Git object storage primer      Existing distributed Git service patterns    Three-phase commit (3PC)    Write-ahead log (WAL)      Architecting Pando    Rethinking constraints    Causal consistency (CC)    Comparing Approaches    Scaling pushes    Line-rate fetch and clone performance    Compaction and time to first byte      Building Pando    Deploying Pando    Contributing back to the Git project    What’s next        Over the past year, the size and demands on our monorepo have increased at a staggering pace. It was clear that we needed to revamp our source control system to scale to the level of concurrent work that Codex makes possible.      We built Pando, a new backend for Git repositories, without interrupting any engineering work or changing how our team uses Git. Pando now powers all development in OpenAI’s monorepo. Pando is designed to meet two ambitious goals: first, horizontally scalable writes, optimized for concurrent pushes to many branches. And second, maximize read throughput, so clients can download data fast enough to fully saturate their available network bandwidth.      We met these goals while retaining compatibility with the Git protocol and client, enabling both our engineers and agents to seamlessly adopt Pando into their existing workflows. In production, Pando cut median push latency by nearly 5x. It now delivers nearly a petabyte of Git data per day.      Here, we’ll cover our motivations for building a new source-control system, along with why we chose to retain compatibility with Git. We’ll compare our system with common approaches to scaling Git, describing why Pando is uniquely capable of meeting OpenAI’s scalability needs. We also discuss what’s next, and how we’ll continue contributing to Git to support agent-scale work.                  Why we needed a new source control system        Codex has changed the scale and pace of development at OpenAI, enabling engineers to do far more work in parallel. That means more branches and pushes, more merges, and more fetches and clones from development environments, research jobs, and CI.      These demands compound. One engineer now has several changes ready for CI at once, and each push can set several jobs fetching the same commit.      Starting around the end of last year, the systems supporting our monorepo were struggling to keep up. We suffered slow fetches and pushes along with failed merges, with reliability at times falling below 90%. Had we reached a limit of Git itself, or of the way we served our monorepo? Git grew out of a community that exchanged patches to the kernel via email. For more than two decades, developers have adapted their tools around Git as the way they build software has changed. When we started to feel friction in our own monorepo, it mattered to us that we could keep building on that work.      We saw a way to keep that familiar workflow while rebuilding the backend to handle pushes to different branches in parallel and serve the same history to many readers concurrently. Building on Git as the foundation of our source-control workflow meant that improvements to the client could be useful beyond OpenAI. We wanted to contribute those improvements from our     copy of Git  ⁠ (opens in a new window)    to upstream, sharing them with the broader community.        Engineering for Git at scale        Scaling a source control system has two essential dimensions: many writers pushing to different branches, and many readers fetching the same history. Pando optimizes for both.      First, Pando coordinates updates to each branch independently. Updates to unrelated branches can proceed in parallel, and a reader fetching a branch gets the history needed for that revision. The tradeoff is that a reader looking at several branches can see them at different points of time.      Second, Pando reuses packfiles (Git’s format for compressing multiple objects together) across fetches instead of generating an individual packfile for each client. A client may download some objects it already has, but the server can serve the same bytes to many clients with little computation.      These choices let us scale writes across branches and serve reads from caches. To see how they fit together, let’s start with how Git stores and transfers history.        Git object storage primer        Git must be able to keep two parts of a repository in sync:    objects    and    references   .      A Git repository records snapshots of files and the history connecting them as a graph of objects. An object may be either a blob, tree, commit, or tag. Blobs hold the content of an individual file, and trees associate names with blobs or other trees to form a directory structure. Commits point to a root tree and zero or more parent commits, forming the history of your repository.      Objects are identified by a hash of their type and contents. Objects are also immutable: recording a changed file creates a new blob, while unchanged files and directories can reuse existing objects.      Branches and tags are references, or “refs”, that point to commits. Committing on a branch creates a new commit and updates the branch’s ref to point to it.                               Git objects reference each other by their ID, commits to trees, and trees to trees and blobs. The branch refs/heads/main points to commit C2, whose parent is C1. C1 points to root tree T1, where parser.py refers to blob B1. C2 points to root tree T2, where parser.py refers to blob B2. In both root trees, docs/ refers to the same tree, T3. Its README.md entry points to blob B3, and usage.md points to blob B4.              Git stores objects in either a “loose” or “packed” state. Loose objects are stored in individual files identified by their object ID. Packed objects are stored together in a packfile, enabling similar objects to be stored as deltas against one another.                               Git can store blobs as separate files or pack them together, encoding one blob as a delta against another.              In Git, an object is    reachable    from a commit if Git can find it by following links from that commit through its parents, trees, and blobs. During a fetch, the client tells the server which commits it wants and which it already has. The server finds the objects reachable from the wanted commits, excludes those it knows the client already has, and sends the remainder as a packfile in the same format Git uses on disk. A full clone starts without any objects, so it needs all the objects reachable from the history being cloned.      A push transfers objects in the other direction by asking the server to update one or more refs. The client uses the server’s set of advertised refs to avoid sending objects the server already has. The pack being sent can therefore depend on existing objects: receiving the pack alone is not enough to reconstruct the new history.      Replicating a Git repository means keeping both objects and references available across multiple servers. Before a replica can serve a reference’s new value, it must be able to supply the objects reachable from that value. The service also needs to coordinate competing    reference updates   , i.e., pushes that try to move the same branch from the same old tip to different new commits. Systems that impose a single order on all writes to a repository can make pushes to unrelated branches wait on one another.        Existing distributed Git service patterns        While designing Pando, we evaluated conventional approaches for scaling source control using Git: one that coordinates ref updates across repository replicas using three-phase commit (3PC, a protocol for coordinating a commit across multiple nodes), and one that orders updates through a shared write-ahead log (WAL, a record of changes written before they’re applied) in blob storage.        Three-phase commit (3PC)        In the three-phase commit design we modeled, the Git service keeps a complete copy of the repository on several replicas. When any server receives a push, the incoming packfile is copied and sent to all replicas in parallel. To publish the push, a majority of replicas must accept the ref update. The server managing this is the coordinator, and it requires multiple rounds of communication between the coordinator and each other replica.      To accept a reference update, each replica locks its copy of the ref and checks that it still points to the commit the client expects. The coordinator then sends a pre-commit message to the replicas that accept. Once a majority acknowledges the pre-commit message, the coordinator tells them to perform the update. Any up-to-date replica can then advertise the new branch tip from its local copy of the repository.      Keeping complete replicas makes it possible to serve reads locally, and guarantees that clients get a consistent view of all references no matter which replica they pick. As a consequence, references are updated one at a time, and each push requires multiple round trips to coordinate the ref update among replicas.      Waiting for a quorum puts replica disk performance and communication latency on the push path. As write volume grows, the replicas must keep up with incoming packs as well as read traffic.        Write-ahead log (WAL)        In the WAL-based design we modeled, the Git service uses a shared manifest in blob storage to order updates across the repository. When a server receives a push, it uploads the incoming packfile to a blob store and prepares the ref update in its local copy of the repository. To publish the push, it adds an entry to a shared manifest stored in the blob store that records the ref update and points to the packfile. The Git server then updates the manifest using a compare-and-swap operation. This atomically replaces the manifest, or otherwise rejects the change. If another writer has updated it in the meantime, the server reads the intervening entries, checks that its ref update is still valid, and retries using the packfile it already uploaded.      Writers can upload their packfiles in parallel, but even pushes to unrelated branches require updating the same manifest. The round-trip time for a successful compare-and-swap limits how often the repository can publish a new manifest. A low-latency blob store makes this step fast. Batching lets one manifest update several refs at the same time, at the cost of queueing updates and increasing latency.      The blob store can receive packfiles in parallel, but updates to the shared manifest still compete with one another. Increasing the blob store’s capacity alone doesn’t resolve that bottleneck. Each replica still needs to read and index packs from the blob store before it can serve them locally. If incoming writes outpace that work, replicas fall behind and clients wait longer to fetch newly pushed commits.        Architecting Pando        That brings us to Pando. Pando is a new architecture for serving Git repositories with the goal of scaling to many clients pushing simultaneously. Here’s how it works:        Rethinking constraints        Prior to developing Pando, we had a hunch that we could meet our requirements without compromising on Git, but we did need to compromise on some of the things that most Git systems assume to be requirements:         Repository-wide consistency   :       Providing a consistent, point-in-time snapshot of all refs requires coordination across the repository. In a system that orders all ref updates together, pushes to unrelated branches contend on a single coordination point.       Unique packfiles for every client   :       If two clients with different local histories fetch the same branch, the server may need to generate a different pack for each to avoid sending objects they already have. Creating these responses costs CPU and disk I/O, making it difficult to scale to high volumes of readers.        Instead, Pando provides a relaxed consistency model (causal consistency) to scale writes, and reuses packfiles to scale reads.        Causal consistency (CC)        When a client pushes to a branch, Pando stores the incoming packfile as an immutable blob in a blob store. Each time the branch moves, Pando records a    ref version    containing the new tip, the pack that supplied it, and any earlier ref versions the pack depends on in a metadata store. Both the blob store and metadata store are horizontally scalable.      Fetching a commit or reference from Pando requires replaying a set of ref versions (packfiles) to the client, reconstructing the state of the client that created the ref version being fetched. This provides a weaker form of consistency across the entire repository, while providing serializability for updates to individual refs. Clients only conflict when pushing to the same ref simultaneously. A client reading several branches cannot assume those reads describe a single point in time across the repository.                               A push to trunk adds an incremental pack, containing one or more commits. Each push to a side branch includes the topic’s earlier commits again, so a client with the advertised trunk version can fetch the topic in one pack.              This is a form of    causal consistency   . In order to fetch a reference, the reader observes the history of the writer that produced it. During a push, Pando controls what shared history the client and server agree on, ensuring clients produce more easily shared packfiles.      As a consequence, Pando doesn’t provide a point-in-time state of all references during Git operations or an ordering of ref updates within a clone or fetch. Concretely, suppose that branches     foo     and     bar     are both updated during the negotiation of a full clone. During the negotiation, one client may observe     foo     at version 1 and     bar     at version 2, while another client observes     foo     at version 2 and     bar     at version 1. In practice, users and agents are agnostic to the global ordering of ref updates, and instead depend on the order of updates to a single reference.        Comparing Approaches        In this simulation of the three consistency models we configure 1,000 clients to each select a distinct branch and then repeatedly push unique commits, measuring total wall clock duration and push to fetch latency. The latter is an important metric for workloads, as it measures round trip time for users and agents to collaborate or to use other systems which rely on version control. The simulation models hardware ranging from commodity to premium virtual machines and blob storage systems. In this simulation, we’ve relaxed repository-wide consistency for three-phase commit. The modeled three-phase commit system shows significantly greater write latency under load as their disks saturate; meanwhile, write-ahead log systems show significantly greater read latency for the same reason, as servers struggle to keep up with reading from the journal. In both real world testing on our monorepo and in this simulation, Pando supports many thousands of clients able to push concurrently without impacting performance under load.      On handling a push, Pando validates the incoming packfile while streaming it to blob storage, without unpacking it into a local repository. When a client begins a fetch Pando selects the stored packs the reader needs, and the reader downloads them. No server needs to apply packfiles to a local repository or perform costly unpack and packing operations. Because these servers primarily perform negotiation and packfile selection, Pando servers can run on commodity hardware.      This allows Pando to scale to the limits of clients, the network between clients and Pando, and the blob storage service. With enough capacity, clients working on independent branches can each transfer packs as fast as their own connection allows. To serve more clients at that rate, we can add Pando servers and scale the metadata store and blob store alongside them.          Pushing and Fetching a Branch in Pando  Pando stores the writer’s packfile in blob storage and records the ref version in metadata service. On fetch, Pando selects the packs the reader needs, and Express serves them.        Play          Stream the push  Fetch the branch      Packfile bytes   Metadata   Request / acknowledgment   Packfile URIs             An agent edits files and creates a commit locally and runs     git push    , which creates a packfile of those changes to update a branch. Pando receives the pack and streams it to blob storage. After validating the incoming push with a single pass decode, Pando uses a multi-key transaction to record a ref version in our metadata store and atomically update the ref pointer. This enables Pando to provide “read-your-own-write” consistency. This entire write operation requires          O  (  1  )   O(1)         O  (  1  )        metadata reads and writes.      When another client fetches the branch, Pando selects a set of stored packs using the history the client already has. This operation requires          O  (  log  ⁡  Δ  )   O(\log \Delta)         O  (  lo g     Δ  )        metadata reads,          Δ   \Delta         Δ        being the shortest distance in ref versions between what the client has and what the client wants. The server returns packfile URIs, and the client downloads them through a service, Express, that stores packfiles in regional caches.      This design relies on the three central services of Pando’s architecture: pushes, fetches, and compaction.        Scaling pushes        When a client pushes, a conventional Git server is like a poker player showing all of its cards, revealing to the client every branch it has. The client then gathers the commits, trees, and blobs to create a packfile that    excludes    objects it knows the server already has.      Advertising more refs can make the push smaller. It can also make the pack harder to reuse, because another client may be missing objects the writer left out.      Pando takes a different approach. Instead of showing its full hand, it only advertises a select set of branches to the client. This is done for two reasons:        Providing a consistent view of every ref is expensive. With millions of branches, the ref advertisement alone can exceed 100 MiB. Providing this requires each server to either maintain a current mapping, requiring significant coordination overhead, or a database query that scales with the number of refs.      By providing only a subset of the refs to the client, the client will generate a pack that depends only on what the server explicitly allows the client to exclude. Tracking the dependencies allows Pando to reuse the packfile a client generates in one push by serving it as the response to a subsequent fetch.        As a Git server advertises more refs, clients pushing have more sources from which to exclude objects, enabling them to produce smaller packs. However, reusing these packfiles requires the server to be able to prove the clients fetching have each of the dependencies. Otherwise, the packfile may omit objects the client needs.      On the other hand, if a Git server advertises none at all, the client would generate a packfile containing the repository’s full history. That packfile can be used by any other client, but at the significant cost of making fetching any branch effectively a full clone.                               Advertising more refs results in smaller packfiles. Most of the size reduction can come from advertising just one.              By default, when a client pushes a new feature branch, Pando advertises only a designated trunk branch as a base. This keeps the advertisement the same size as the repository gains branches, but comes with tradeoffs. When an engineer either pushes to a single branch many times, or stacks one feature branch on top of another the client has to resend everything outside of the trunk.      This causes successive branch pushes to be larger, containing potentially-redundant objects, and uses additional client bandwidth. In our monorepo, the median packfile produced this way was under 20 KiB, and the 99th percentile was under 3 MiB. For us, this was a sensible trade-off because a reader that already has the advertised trunk history can fetch the branch with that one packfile.      After choosing the set of refs to advertise to the client, Pando accepts the push and updates its metadata store. Pando splits the metadata update into synchronous and asynchronous portions. The synchronous metadata update ensures clients can immediately fetch the newly updated commit. This writes a new ref version and updates the ref pointer mapping to that new version storing that new tip, the dependencies used to negotiate the packfile, and a link to the packfile that was pushed.      At the same time, asynchronous work is recorded in the same transaction, such as scheduling compaction. For very large pushes, only a subset of commits are written synchronously. This allows us to require only a constant number of reads and writes to the metadata store, regardless of the size of the push.      Importantly, Pando servers can accept pushes to unrelated refs independently. The only contended key is the ref pointer, which we guard using an atomic compare-and-swap-like operation. We can scale up write throughput by adding Pando servers, metadata store scaling units, or blob stores.        Line-rate fetch and clone performance        When a client performs a fetch, it provides the server with two sets of commit IDs, known in the protocol as     have    s and     want    s. In a conventional Git server, the server computes the set difference among the objects reachable by the haves and those reachable by the wants, compresses them, and sends the result to the client. While the open-source Git server has a variety of indexes locally to accelerate this operation, these packfiles can be expensive to compute and are generally resistant to caching.      Instead, Pando uses the commit mappings recorded on pushes to look up the client’s     have    s and     want    s, resolving them to a set of ref versions that contain those commits. Each of those ref versions links to a packfile previously received by Pando. The server uses this to solve for what the client needs, selecting the packfiles that cover the set of objects the client needs.          Planning fetches in Pando  Pando compares what a client has with what it wants, then selects the stored packfiles needed—including any missing branch dependencies.        Branch A      Branch B                                                                                   HAVE  4    WANT  31       Already held    Fetch    Missing branch dependency       Fetch 27 trunk packs.  Select a branch to include its trunk dependencies.            Pando maps the Git protocol’s haves and wants to a sequence of ref versions. Wanting a side branch implies wanting up to its dependencies on the trunk.              The Git protocol only allows a single packfile to be sent in the HTTP response on a clone or fetch. However, an under-appreciated feature of the Git protocol,     packfile-uri    , allows a server to return links to download additional packs separately. Pando uses this exclusively, and transmits an empty packfile inline. To support this feature, OpenAI contributed a number of improvements to     packfile-uri     upstream.      OpenAI systems operate in many geographic regions, so we maintain Pando clusters with local caches in each. A pack delivery service, Express, caches our blob store, and a separate service caches the metadata store. These caches enable Pando to serve requests for a commit ID or a special read of a ref entirely from the cached state in that cluster. We use consistent hashing to route requests for a packfile to Express servers, with cache hit rates of over 99%.      This system of caches provides extremely high throughput, capable of saturating the network limit between clients and Pando. Using these packfile URIs and local caches, we’ve validated that using only standard cloud provider virtual machines, we see clone and fetch operations saturate 10 Gbps network links.        Compaction and time to first byte        For most Git servers, repacking and garbage collection are necessary to maintain the performance of a growing repository. Both of these steps reclaim space, but are compute- and I/O-intensive.      In a fast-moving repository like OpenAI’s monorepo, it is infeasible to send an individual packfile URI for every push that has occurred since the last fetch. Each day, a client would need to download tens of thousands of packfiles to catch up their trunk.      Instead, Pando combines packs in the background to reduce this overhead, adopting a design similar to compaction in log-structured merge-trees. Each push produces what Pando refers to as an “L0” packfile, representing the smallest unit of data Pando can transmit. Over time, background workers collect these packfiles into covers spanning a sequence of ref versions, scaling geometrically from L0. Today, our monorepo uses up to L4 packfile covers.      These covers serve a dual purpose. After a cover is sufficiently full, a compaction worker will claim it and produce a single packfile. This improves the compression ratio by reorganizing the objects inside the packfile. But it also improves fetch negotiation performance by acting as skip list over ref versions. By scanning through indexes at each level simultaneously, Pando can select a set of packs to send to a client in logarithmic time. These packfile covers, repacked or not, enable a more efficient solution to fetch planning, reducing both throughput and latency requirements for Pando.           Compaction in Pando  Small packfiles are grouped into larger covers across levels, improving compression and speeding up fetches.
