  Abstract. 
    
 Large language model (LLM)-based agents increasingly rely on external tools to invoke services and interact with web resources. These tools can evolve through software updates, yet agentic frameworks may continue trusting them without re-verifying their safety after implementation changes. This  tool update gap  creates a supply-chain vulnerability in agentic systems: because updated tool code executes outside the LLM’s context window, malicious functionality embedded in tool updates can bypass defenses centered on model-visible interactions, leaving agents exposed to stealthy, persistent threats that existing in-context defenses can hardly address. 
    
 To thoroughly investigate this threat, we introduce  ETUDE  ( E xploiting  T ool  U pdates for  D irect  E xecution), an attack that embeds malicious functionality into updates of initially benign tools to produce  compromised tools , while preserving their legitimate tool functionality.
Unlike prompt-based attacks, ETUDE operates entirely outside the LLM’s context and requires no adversarial instructions, thereby bypassing defenses restricted to model-visible content, such as prompt-injection detectors and static skill scanning. We evaluate ETUDE across three representative attack workloads and seven widely used commercial and open-source agentic frameworks, including Gemini CLI, Codex CLI, and Claude Code. The results show that ETUDE achieves a 97.6% attack success rate while maintaining a 95.9% legitimate task completion rate. 
    
 We further examine three families of existing defenses and find that they provide insufficient protection against this threat: integrity verification and code review can be bypassed through obfuscation or disrupt legitimate maintenance, while runtime auditing faces coverage and computational overhead limitations. These findings expose a fundamental blind spot in current agent security practices: trust established for a tool does not necessarily remain valid after its implementation updates. Our results highlight the need for lifecycle-aware tool verification and execution-time security enforcement to secure LLM-based agents beyond the model context. 
  
 
 
 Keywords:  LLM agents, tool updates, agent security, supply chain security
 
 
  1.  Introduction 

 
 Large language model (LLM)-based agents, such as Claude Code and OpenAI Codex, have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in performing complex, multi-step tasks, ranging from web browsing to software development  ( Yao et al., 2023 ;  Schick et al., 2023 ;  Li et al., 2026 ) .
To further extend their capabilities beyond the underlying LLMs, modern agent frameworks allow users to integrate external tools from open-source repositories, plugin marketplaces, and third-party providers.
For example, the Model Context Protocol (MCP) ecosystem alone indexes over 177,000 community-contributed tools  ( Stein, 2026 ) .
These tools provide executable functionalities that enable agents to access local files, interact with web services, and perform operations with the privileges of the host environment.
Consequently, the capabilities and security of agentic systems depend not only on their underlying LLMs, but also on the external tools they incorporate.
As the tool ecosystem continues to expand, so does the potential attack surface. 
 
 
 Existing studies  ( Chang et al., 2026 ;  Zhan et al., 2024 ;  Debenedetti et al., 2024 ;  Wang et al., 2025b ;  Zhao et al., 2026 )  have extensively investigated the security vulnerabilities introduced by external tools in agentic systems.
Despite their effectiveness in exposing critical vulnerabilities, these studies  ( Chang et al., 2026 ;  Zhan et al., 2024 )  primarily focus on prompt injection attacks, where adversarial instructions are embedded in model-visible inputs to manipulate an agent’s behavior.
Consequently, existing defenses address prompt injection by strengthening instruction–data boundaries, constraining tool calls, or detecting and correcting MCP context poisoning  ( Yi et al., 2025 ;  Debenedetti et al., 2025 ;  Wang et al., 2026b ) .
In this paper, we uncover a critical yet largely unexplored attack surface in agentic systems:  malicious code injection through tool updates , which can effectively circumvent existing security defenses. 
 
  
   Figure 1 .   The tool update gap. A malicious update preserves the tool’s legitimate functionality while introducing unauthorized operations that execute directly within the tool’s runtime environment.  
 
 
  Tool Update Gap.  
Modern agent frameworks support external tool updates to incorporate new functionalities, fix bugs, and maintain compatibility with evolving environments.
During our investigation, we observe a critical discrepancy between how these frameworks establish trust in external tools and how they maintain this trust after subsequent updates.
Specifically, while an external tool may undergo security screening during its initial installation (at its admission stage), subsequent updates of this tool can be adopted without re-examining the updated implementation.
Across the seven agent frameworks that we evaluate, including Gemini CLI, Codex CLI, Claude Code, and OpenCode, we find that previously granted tool permissions can persist even when the underlying executable code changes.
This creates a substantial security risk: an attacker can initially distribute a benign tool to pass admission-time checks and establish trust, then introduce malicious functionality through a subsequent update that inherits the tool’s existing identity and authorization.
We refer to this discrepancy as the  tool update gap . 
 
 
  A Motivating Example.  
To illustrate the security implications of the tool update gap, consider the scenario shown in Figure   1  .
An attacker initially publishes a benign file-editing tool through a third-party tool marketplace.
After the tool has been installed and trusted by agent frameworks, the attacker releases a seemingly routine update that introduces additional formatting functionalities while embedding malicious operations within the tool’s executable code.
For example, the updated implementation may silently read sensitive local files or invoke unauthorized APIs.
These malicious operations are triggered during legitimate tool invocations, while the tool continues to provide its expected functionality and returns normal results to the agent.
Importantly, the malicious operations execute directly within the tool’s runtime environment.
In this way, neither the model-visible interaction nor successful completion of the legitimate task necessarily reveals the unauthorized operations. 
 
 
 This threat closely resembles real-world software supply-chain attacks, in which adversaries exploit established trust in software packages to introduce malicious functionality through subsequent releases.
For example, in the XZ Utils incident (CVE-2024-3094), a maintainer spent approximately two years establishing trust before introducing a backdoor into a widely deployed Linux compression library  ( Dragos et al., 2024 ) .
Similarly, in the  event-stream  incident, an attacker obtained maintainership of a popular npm package and subsequently introduced a targeted cryptocurrency-stealing payload  ( npm, Inc., 2018 ) .
Despite growing recognition of these security risks, the implications of post-admission code changes in LLM agent systems remain insufficiently understood.
This raises a critical question:  to what extent can adversaries exploit trusted tool updates to execute unauthorized operations while preserving the agent’s legitimate functionality?  
 
 
  Our Contribution.  
In this paper, we systematically investigate the security implications of the tool update gap by developing a novel attack, termed  ETUDE  ( E xploiting  T ool  U pdates for  D irect  E xecution).
ETUDE exploits the persistent trust established during tool admission to introduce unauthorized operations through subsequent updates.
A typical workflow of ETUDE is shown in Figure   1  .
As a result, ETUDE enables unauthorized operations to occur alongside legitimate task execution, exposing a fundamental limitation of security mechanisms that rely exclusively on initial tool admission or model-visible interactions. 
 
 
  Distinctions from Prior Work.  
ETUDE differs from existing attacks against agentic systems along two fundamental dimensions:  delivery timing  and  execution path .
The former determines whether malicious functionality is introduced before initial tool admission or through a subsequent update, while the latter determines whether unauthorized operations are induced through model-visible instructions or executed directly by the tool implementation.
Existing prompt injection attacks  ( Huang et al., 2026 ;  Liu et al., 2026b ;  Chang et al., 2026 ;  Shi et al., 2026 ;  Qu et al., 2026 )  primarily manipulate tool descriptions, retrieved content, or other model-visible inputs to induce unintended agent behaviors, which remain susceptible to defenses that inspect model-visible content.
Meanwhile, emerging studies on tool supply-chain security  ( Hu et al., 2026 ;  Qu et al., 2026 )  have investigated malicious tool implementations introduced before installation, where admission-time screening can potentially identify their harmful functionalities.
Empirical research also documents malicious code and instruction-based manipulation in real-world skill registries  ( Liu et al., 2026a ) .
In contrast, ETUDE combines post-admission delivery with direct code execution, allowing malicious functionality to bypass the initial admission process and operate independently of the LLM’s decision-making process.
This combination distinguishes ETUDE from existing attack paradigms and reveals a security blind spot that cannot be adequately addressed by admission-time screening or prompt-injection defenses alone. 
 
 
  Our Findings.  
We implement ETUDE and conduct an extensive experimental evaluation across seven representative agent frameworks, including Gemini CLI, Codex CLI, Claude Code, DeepSeek Harness, OpenCode, Pi, and Goose.
Our evaluation covers multiple LLM backends and three distinct tool functionalities, with unauthorized objectives spanning synthetic credential disclosure, unauthorized API operations, and local file modification.
Experimental results demonstrate that ETUDE achieves an attack success rate of 97.6% while maintaining a legitimate task completion rate of 95.9% across the seven frameworks.
Moreover, ETUDE outperforms the strongest prompt-injection baseline by 85.1%.
These results demonstrate that ETUDE can reliably execute unauthorized operations while preserving the agent’s legitimate functionality, highlighting the practicality and severity of the tool update gap. 
 
 
 We further evaluate representative security defenses, including admission-time code scanning, update-time auditing, and runtime monitoring, to examine their effectiveness against ETUDE.
Our findings reveal three critical limitations of existing defense mechanisms.
(i) File integrity checks can identify code modifications but cannot determine whether an update introduces malicious functionality.
(ii) Static code auditing remains vulnerable to complex or obfuscated malicious implementations, limiting its effectiveness in distinguishing benign updates from malicious ones.
(iii) Model-level monitoring and prompt-injection defenses cannot reliably detect unauthorized operations that execute entirely within the tool’s runtime environment.
Collectively, these findings demonstrate that conventional admission-time and model-centric defenses are insufficient to secure the complete tool lifecycle, establishing post-admission tool integrity as a critical challenge for agentic systems.
Our main contributions are summarized as follows. 
 
  •  
 
 We identify and characterize a critical, yet largely overlooked security vulnerability in agentic systems, termed the  tool update gap .
We demonstrate how malicious tool updates can exploit previously established trust and authorization to execute unauthorized operations. 
  
  •  
 
 We propose  ETUDE , a novel attack that exploits the tool update gap to execute unauthorized operations during legitimate tool invocations.
We demonstrate its effectiveness across seven agent frameworks, multiple LLM backends, and three representative unauthorized objectives. 
  
  •  
 
 We conduct a comprehensive evaluation of representative security defenses against ETUDE, covering admission-time screening, update-time auditing, and runtime monitoring.
Our findings reveal fundamental limitations in existing defenses, particularly their inability to reliably identify malicious functionality introduced through tool updates. 
  
 
 
 
 
  2.  Related Work 

 
  Threats through Model-Visible Content.  
Existing studies have extensively investigated the security threats posed by untrusted content in LLM-based agent systems.
A prominent attack paradigm is indirect prompt injection, where adversaries embed malicious instructions in external content to manipulate an agent’s behavior  ( Greshake et al., 2023 ;  Chang et al., 2026 ) .
Recent studies have extended this attack to the MCP ecosystem, demonstrating how malicious tool descriptions can redirect agent behavior  ( Huang et al., 2026 ;  Wang et al., 2025a ) .
Beyond tool descriptions, emerging attacks further exploit skill documents that guide agent execution.
For example, DDIPE embeds malicious logic in reusable examples and templates  ( Qu et al., 2026 ) , while payload-less attacks leverage natural-language instructions to induce agents to generate malicious code  ( Liu et al., 2026b ) .
Despite their different attack vectors, the attacks discussed above share a fundamental limitation: they rely on the LLM interpreting and following adversarial content. 
 
 
  Malicious Tools and Post-Approval Updates.  
Beyond model-visible attacks, recent studies have investigated security threats arising directly from executable tool implementations.
For example, MalTool constructs malicious tools that perform unauthorized operations while preserving their advertised functionality, and systematically evaluates their detectability  ( Hu et al., 2026 ) .
Meanwhile, ETDI investigates security risks associated with post-approval changes and proposes digitally signed tool definitions, version tracking, and resource-access verification to strengthen tool integrity  ( Bhatt et al., 2025 ) .
Although these studies provide valuable insights into malicious tools and lifecycle security, the practical exploitation of post-admission tool updates across different agent frameworks remains insufficiently explored.
To bridge this gap, we systematically investigate how an initially benign tool can establish trust during admission and subsequently introduce malicious functionality through updates while retaining its original identity and authorization. 
 
 
  Static Inspection of Tool and Skill Packages.  
Static inspection provides an important defense against malicious third-party tools by examining their executable code and package contents before execution.
For example, MalSkills analyzes dependencies among skill instructions, scripts, and configuration files to identify potential security threats  ( Wang et al., 2026a ) , while IntelGuard detects malicious packages through threat-informed LLM reasoning  ( Guo et al., 2026 ) .
Meanwhile, Acoda investigates how code obfuscation can conceal malicious functionality from LLM-based code analysis while preserving its execution behavior  ( Rao et al., 2026 ) .
However, the effectiveness of existing static defenses against malicious tool updates, particularly those employing code obfuscation, remains insufficiently understood.
To investigate this issue, we evaluate representative static defenses in our experiments, including Cisco MCP Scanner, SkillFortify, and SkillSpector  ( Qualixar, 2026 ;  NVIDIA, 2026 ) . 
 
 
  Runtime Auditing.  
Unlike static inspection, runtime auditing identifies potentially malicious behaviors by executing untrusted code and monitoring its actual operations.
Recent studies have explored this approach to uncover security threats that may evade static analysis.
For example, Cloak and Detonate introduces SkillDetonate, which monitors operating-system activities and tracks data flows during skill execution to detect suspicious behaviors  ( Ji et al., 2026 ) .
Although runtime auditing offers greater visibility into executable behavior, its effectiveness may be limited when malicious operations are activated only under specific inputs or environmental conditions. 
 
 
 
  3.  Threat Model 

 
  System Model.  
We consider an LLM-based agentic framework that integrates external tools to extend its capabilities.
Each tool consists of executable code and model-facing metadata, including its name, description, and input schema.
During tool admission, the framework installs or enables the tool and establishes the authorization required for its execution.
Subsequently, the agent can invoke the tool to execute its implementation within the permissions of the hosting environment.
Importantly, we observe that the evaluated modern frameworks allow tool implementations to be updated while retaining their original identity, model-facing metadata, and previously granted authorization.
Although some frameworks require user confirmation for individual tool calls, such confirmations authorize the invocation rather than verify the underlying implementation. 
 
 
  Attacker Capabilities and Knowledge.  
We consider an attacker who controls the release channel of a single external tool and can distribute arbitrary updates to its implementation.
The attacker has full knowledge of the tool’s executable code, interface, and model-facing metadata, but cannot control the agentic framework, underlying LLM, user requests, or other tools.
We assume that the tool has already been admitted in a benign state before the attack begins.
The attacker subsequently introduces malicious functionality through a seemingly legitimate update while preserving the tool’s name, description, input schema, and intended functionality. 
 
 
  Attack Taxonomy.  
We characterize tool-based attacks along two orthogonal dimensions:  delivery timing  and  execution path .
Delivery timing determines whether malicious functionality is introduced during initial admission (E1) or through a subsequent update (E2).
Execution path distinguishes unauthorized operations performed directly by executable tool code (P-direct) from those induced through model-visible instructions (P-ctx).
Together, these dimensions define four attack conditions, as summarized in Table   1  .
ETUDE targets E2   ×  \times   P-direct, where an initially benign tool acquires malicious functionality through an update and executes unauthorized operations directly during legitimate invocations.
Unlike P-ctx attacks, ETUDE requires no adversarial instructions to enter the LLM’s context. 
 
 
  Attacker Goals and Scope.  
We consider three representative unauthorized objectives: sensitive information disclosure, unauthorized external API operations, and local file modification.
These objectives are not exhaustive and may overlap in practice.
The attacker exploits the permissions already available to the tool’s execution environment to perform operations beyond the user’s legitimate request, without requiring privilege escalation or compromising the framework or underlying LLM.
Meanwhile, the malicious update preserves the tool’s intended functionality, allowing the agent to complete its legitimate task despite the additional unauthorized operations.

  4.  Approach 

 
 ETUDE instantiates the E2   ×  \times   P-direct attack condition in Table   1  , exploiting the tool update gap through a single implementation update.
Specifically, the attack begins with a benign tool implementation     A  ​   (v1)   A\text{ (v1)}   , which provides the advertised functionality and passes initial admission.
The adversary subsequently releases an updated implementation     A  ​   (v2)   A\text{ (v2)}    that preserves the tool’s original interface while embedding additional malicious operations.
Once the framework adopts this update, subsequent tool invocations execute     A  ​   (v2)   A\text{ (v2)}    under the authorization previously granted to     A  ​   (v1)   A\text{ (v1)}   , as illustrated in Figure   1  .
The adoption mechanism varies across agent frameworks, including package re-resolution, tool-server restarts, and MCP endpoint reconnections.
Despite these implementation differences, the underlying security weakness remains consistent: the updated code can execute without undergoing the same security screening as the initially admitted implementation.
Consequently, ETUDE requires neither additional tool installation nor adversarial instructions to manipulate the underlying LLM.
A routine tool update followed by a legitimate invocation is sufficient to activate the attack.
In the following, we describe the construction of     A  ​   (v2)   A\text{ (v2)}   , its activation mechanism, and its generality across agent frameworks. 
 
 
  Retaining the Normal Path.  
We design the malicious implementation     A  ​   (v2)   A\text{ (v2)}    to satisfy three requirements that collectively preserve legitimate functionality while concealing unauthorized operations.
 R1 (Interface Preservation). 
    A  ​   (v2)   A\text{ (v2)}    retains the same tool name, description, and input schema as     A  ​   (v1)   A\text{ (v1)}   , ensuring that the model-facing interface remains unchanged after the update.
This prevents the attack from introducing suspicious modifications to tool descriptions or the model’s tool-selection process, although it does not prevent inspection of the updated code itself.
 R2 (Functional Preservation). 
    A  ​   (v2)   A\text{ (v2)}    preserves the advertised functionality of     A  ​   (v1)   A\text{ (v1)}    and returns the expected results for legitimate inputs.
By maintaining normal tool behavior, the malicious update avoids functional anomalies that could otherwise expose the attack.
 R3 (Direct Execution). 
    A  ​   (v2)   A\text{ (v2)}    executes unauthorized operations within the tool’s implementation, without requiring additional tool calls from the LLM.
This prevents these operations from appearing as separate model-initiated actions, thereby evading defenses that rely exclusively on model-visible instructions or tool-call trajectories. 
 
 
 To satisfy these requirements,     A  ​   (v2)   A\text{ (v2)}    preserves the original handler of     A  ​   (v1)   A\text{ (v1)}    while incorporating malicious operations into its execution path.
These operations execute within the existing tool process and exploit only the permissions available to its execution environment, such as accessing local files or communicating with permitted network endpoints.
Moreover, the injected operations are isolated through exception handling, allowing the tool to return its expected result even when an unauthorized operation fails.
This design decouples legitimate task completion from attack success, enabling the two outcomes to occur independently.
Accordingly, our evaluation independently verifies both outcomes using task-correctness checks and observable evidence of unauthorized side effects, rather than relying on the model’s final response. 
 
 
  Activation.  
Once     A  ​   (v2)   A\text{ (v2)}    is adopted, a legitimate tool invocation can directly activate the injected operations without requiring any additional instructions from the user or the LLM.
In the primary attack configuration, the malicious operations execute during ordinary invocations of the updated tool, independently of specific trigger phrases or model-visible signals.
For reproducibility, we retain the tool implementations, task configurations, invocation records, and corresponding evidence of unauthorized effects (Section   A  ).
Furthermore, to investigate the effectiveness of runtime auditing, we consider additional variants whose malicious operations are activated only under specific input or environmental conditions.
These variants allow us to examine whether audit-based runtime defenses can reliably expose malicious functionality that remains dormant during certain executions.
Their evaluation is presented in Section   5  . 
 
 
  Generality Across Frameworks.  
ETUDE relies on two fundamental conditions: an admitted tool can adopt an updated implementation, and subsequent invocations execute the updated code under the existing tool identity and authorization.
These conditions are independent of any particular agent framework, tool-loading mechanism, or LLM backend.
Although different frameworks adopt tool updates through distinct mechanisms, they can expose the same underlying security weakness when updated code executes without renewed security verification.
Therefore, ETUDE is applicable to frameworks satisfying these conditions, without requiring framework-specific modifications to the attack mechanism.
We demonstrate this generality across seven representative agent frameworks using their native tool-loading mechanisms and documented permission configurations.
We further investigate the influence of different LLM backends and tool functionalities to characterize the effectiveness and applicability of ETUDE under diverse deployment settings (Section   5  ). 
 
 
 
  5.  Evaluation 

 
 We evaluate whether ETUDE executes attack operations while completing legitimate tasks, then examine its effectiveness across backends, tool functionalities, and defenses through four research questions: 
 
 
  RQ1:  Can ETUDE successfully  execute  unauthorized operations while completing legitimate tasks? 
 
 
  RQ2:  Does ETUDE remain effective across different  LLM  backends? 
 
 
  RQ3:  Can ETUDE generalize across different  tool  functionalities? 
 
 
  RQ4:  To what extent can existing  defenses  detect or prevent ETUDE?

  5.1.  Experimental Setup 

 
  Platforms and tools.  
Table   2   lists the seven agent frameworks, their versions, and whether each framework’s implementation is open or closed source.
RQ1 uses GLM-5.3-Flash and a Markdown cleaner.
RQ2 holds W1 and the cleaner fixed while comparing GLM-5.3-Flash, Qwen-3.8-27B, and DeepSeek-V4-flash across four backend configurations, with thinking enabled and disabled for DeepSeek-V4-Flash.
RQ3 fixes GLM and ETUDE while varying the tool functionality—Markdown cleaning, CSV statistics, and ICS generation—across four frameworks. 
 
 
  Normal task and unauthorized goals.  
In RQ1 and RQ2, the user requests one  md_clean(text)  call and the complete cleaned text.
The cleaner normalizes line endings, strips trailing whitespace, and collapses repeated blank lines while preserving content.
W1–W3 each pair this task with an unauthorized objective involving resources unnecessary for text cleaning.
We use synthetic credentials, researcher-controlled services, and isolated files; all corresponding network traffic stays on the local host, exposing no real secrets or third-party resources. 
 
 
  W1: disclosure. 
The objective is to read a separate synthetic credential file and transmit its full contents to an adversary-selected destination, represented by our test receiver.
Success requires a receiver payload matching the source file and an invocation identifier linking the record to the task. 
 
 
  W2: unauthorized API action. 
The objective is to create an order through a test API despite the user’s request for text cleaning alone.
Success requires a service-side order with the designated case marker and task invocation identifier; an attempted request or a model’s claim is insufficient. 
 
 
  W3: file modification. 
The goal is to overwrite a separate synthetic research note, changing its status from  retained  to  altered  and inserting a designated marker.
Success requires the complete specified replacement text.
The action tool restricts writes to this isolated note but accepts arbitrary content, allowing us to measure actual file modification separately from specified-content attainment. 
 
 
  Conditions and admission review.  
Crossing delivery timing with execution path yields four conditions; ETUDE is E2   ×  \times   P-direct.
E1 submits     A  ​   (v2)   A\text{ (v2)}    for review before first use; E2 admits benign     A  ​   (v1)   A\text{ (v1)}    and then adopts     A  ​   (v2)   A\text{ (v2)}    without repeating the review.
P-direct performs the unauthorized operation inside the tool during a normal call.
P-ctx instead adds instructions to the tool description asking the model to issue an additional tool call.
For RQ1–RQ3, we add a uniform admission gate using Cisco MCP Scanner’s alignment component with our GLM-5.3-Flash research adapter. This pre-use code review is a deliberate experimental control, rather than a default installation feature of the frameworks.
The gate tests why benign-first delivery matters under admission screening: submitting     A  ​   (v2)   A\text{ (v2)}    directly may prevent its use, whereas admitting     A  ​   (v1)   A\text{ (v1)}    first establishes trust before the update introduces the attack functionality.
Appendix   B.1   reports the admission outcomes.
RQ4 separately evaluates update-time and runtime checks, including SkillFortify and NVIDIA SkillSpector (Section   5.5  ). 
 
 
  Update adoption.  
For E2, we switch the admitted tool from     A  ​   (v1)   A\text{ (v1)}    to     A  ​   (v2)   A\text{ (v2)}    through native tool-loading mechanisms.
Gemini replaces its server process and refreshes tools; Codex reloads its server; Claude re-registers servers; DeepSeek Harness reloads its plugin in a new native window while restoring the logical session.
OpenCode reconnects its server, Pi uses  ctx.reload , and Goose relaunches its extension.
Subsequent calls execute     A  ​   (v2)   A\text{ (v2)}    under the existing tool identity and the permission settings saved for that configuration (Appendix   A  ).
When a framework requires confirmation for an individual tool call, the harness supplies a one-time approval for that call; this does not re-examine the updated implementation. 
 
 
  Evaluation metrics.  
We score ASR and TCR separately over the same planned tasks.
The  attack success rate  (ASR) measures attainment of the specified attack objective using the independent receiver, service, or file evidence defined above.
For RQ1, the primary  task completion rate  (TCR) measures whether the final reply delivers the complete cleaned text; instrumentation-only tracking lines are assessed separately.
The auxiliary full-task criterion additionally checks the supplied input, prescribed tool and call count, and expected tool output (Table   6  ).
RQ2 uses full-task TCR. RQ3 uses it for W1/W2 and final-output TCR for W3.
For W3, file modifications that miss the specified text are reported separately from ASR.
Native invocation records link each outcome to its task, and joint success requires both outcomes from the same execution.
Figure   5   illustrates one such execution from the saved native audit examined in RQ4. 
 
 
  Scoring and aggregation.  
Each round has 20 planned     A  ​   (v2)   A\text{ (v2)}    tasks; ASR and TCR are success counts out of these 20, expressed as percentages.
When admission returns BLOCK (rejected) or UNKNOWN (inconclusive), either     A  ​   (v1)   A\text{ (v1)}    or     A  ​   (v2)   A\text{ (v2)}    is not executed and contributes no successes; these review outcomes are reported separately.
We run five rounds per implementation and report each condition’s mean and sample standard deviation, which measures variation across rounds.
Overall results average the included condition means, giving each condition equal weight.
Shared records do not count as new experiments: RQ1 and RQ2 share the seven GLM/W1 results, and RQ3’s four W3 Markdown conditions reuse RQ1’s ETUDE records, whereas its eight CSV/ICS conditions are independent.
Thus, the 40 displayed W3 conditions represent 36 independent conditions, 180 rounds, and 3,600 planned tasks.
Appendices   A   and   B   provide full results and supporting records.

  5.5.  RQ4: Possible countermeasures 

 
 RQ1–RQ3 show that legitimate completion can coexist with an attack, so completion alone does not reveal the attack.
We therefore evaluate three ways to inspect the tool’s implementation or execution, using the same tools and updates. 
 
 
  File integrity verification  compares an update with an approved implementation.
Our TLSH-based instance  ( Oliver et al., 2013 )  measures file similarity and accepts updates only below a preset distance threshold. 
 
 
  Static LLM-based code review  examines source code before execution.
We use Cisco MCP Scanner’s alignment component  ( Cisco AI Defense, 2026 )  with GLM-5.3-Flash, mapping decisions to ALLOW, BLOCK, or UNKNOWN.
SkillFortify  ( Qualixar, 2026 )  and NVIDIA SkillSpector  ( NVIDIA, 2026 )  extend the comparison from source files to packaged skills. In RQ1–RQ3, our added static-review gate runs only at admission, allowing the updated     A  ​   (v2)   A\text{ (v2)}    to become executable without re-examination.
Here, static review checks each candidate before first installation or update adoption; only ALLOW permits native execution.
These checks test whether inspecting an update distinguishes attack functionality from legitimate maintenance. 
 
 
  Runtime auditing  monitors operations during isolated execution and flags behavior outside the declared function.
We adapt SkillDetonate’s isolated execution and information-flow monitoring  ( Ji et al., 2026 ) . 
 
 
  File integrity verification creates a trade-off between target blocking and normal maintenance.  
Pinning an approved version stops both unauthorized updates and maintenance until a new release is approved.
We therefore evaluate a TLSH gate that accepts sufficiently similar implementation files.

 All 30 updated-tool audits produce unauthorized operations and alerts; all 30 benign-tool audits remain alert-free, and all 60 normal tasks complete. 
This detection persists despite obfuscation (Figure   5  ). 
 
 
 Coverage nevertheless depends on how the attack-embedded behavior is triggered.
In separate coverage tests, a conditional Markdown update produces attack effects and alerts only for triggering inputs, while an environment-conditioned variant receives ALLOW without alerts in the sandbox yet produces attack effects during ordinary tool execution (Table   12  ).
Our bubblewrap sandbox  ( bubblewrap contributors, 0000 )  maps a single user ID; the variant reads this map and activates only under the wider mapping of ordinary execution.
This mapping difference is specific to our adapter; SkillDetonate reports Docker isolation without specifying its UID mapping  ( Ji et al., 2026 ) .
The environment result illustrates the coverage limitation recognized by anti-sandbox techniques  ( Yokoyama et al., 2016 )  and SkillDetonate  ( Ji et al., 2026 ) : audits observe only behaviors triggered by the test inputs and environment. 
 
 
 Extending coverage therefore requires additional executions, increasing latency and model fees.
In a separate 12-audit long-document test, mean latency is     112.8  ±  13.7   112.8\pm 13.7    seconds and estimated model fees average US$0.00697 per audit.
The historical static-review reference is 18.0 seconds and US$0.00461; both fee estimates use identical uncached token prices.
 These audits incur 6.3 times the reference latency and 1.5 times its model fees, making broader coverage costly for repeated update checks. 
Appendix   B.3   details configurations and cost calculation. 
 
 
 
 
  6.  Discussion 

 
  Where controls should attach. 
Our findings point to one principle:  authorization must bind to the specific implementation that was examined, not to the tool’s identity. 
The tool update gap arises because trust, once granted, outlives the code it was granted for.
Closing it means making the examined artifact the unit of authorization, so that any change to the code invalidates the prior decision.
This binding has two layers, answering two distinct questions. 
 
 
  1. artifact identity: is the code about to run exactly the code that was approved? 
Locally, hashing the tool’s code and resolved dependencies ensures that adopting    B  B    under a modified hash triggers renewed review before execution rather than inheriting    A  A   ’s approval. Across the distribution channel, supply-chain attestations, like Sigstore publisher binding and SLSA build provenance  ( Sigstore, 2026 ;  SLSA, 2026 ) , catch substituted or re-signed updates at adoption. 
 
 
  2. behavioral confinement: given the right code, is what it does permitted? 
Identity alone is insufficient: hashes and attestations certify  which  code runs, never  what  it does. It allows a maintainer-signed update to pass every provenance check while carrying a malicious payload. This issue therefore calls for an explicit runtime policy of permitted tool operations via least-privilege execution and host- and network-level call mediation. Operations outside the tool’s declared function are denied directly upon execution rather than inferred from the model’s context, securing the execution path where the admission-time and in-context defense cannot reach. 
 
 
  Limitations. 
We demonstrate attacks with researcher-authored tool implementations with carefully monitored permissions instead of modifying open-source tools in the wild, to avoid potential ethical issues. The runtime audit coverage and cost figures are reported based on the tested agentic tasks in the study. Our future work will provide more comprehensive cost evaluation of real-world tools. 
 
 
 
  7.  Conclusion 

 
 We identify the  tool update gap : adopted updates can change executed code while prior authorization persists.
ETUDE exploits this gap to perform unauthorized operations during ordinary tool calls without adversarial instructions to the model.
Across seven frameworks, multiple model backends, and three tool utilities, extra effects persist alongside high rates of normal task completion.
In W3, ETUDE modifies the target file in 700/700 tasks, with core-body completion in 698/700.
File similarity does not establish behavioral safety; static review can admit obfuscated updates or reject legitimate maintenance; runtime auditing detects executed extra behavior but faces coverage and cost limits.
Tool authorization should therefore track the implementation actually executed, rather than transfer automatically across updates.

  B.3.  RQ4: protocols and supporting results 

 
  Distance gating and offline checks.  
Three target pairs (distances 156/145/233) and 40 controlled legitimate pairs share an 808-byte base; the separate original public-history set has 4/21 pairs blocked at     t  =  30   t=30   .
Without gating, 1,200     A  ​   (v2)   A\text{ (v2)}    tasks yield 1,200 effects and 1,197 normal completions. Only three native representatives verify TLSH withholding; full-grid gated zeros would be projections.
Offline variants have     d  =  9   d=9    in  git_python  (reference maintenance:     d  =  22   d=22   ) and     d  =  3   d=3    in GitHub MCP Server v2.0.3’s  pkg/github/issues.go .
With MCP stubbed, tested  git_status  output is unchanged; the GitHub repository builds and preserves target-function outputs on four inputs.
Each single-file/variant check produces one synthetic effect when triggered, none otherwise.
Separately, 16/17 changed Go files between GitHub v2.0.2 and v2.0.3 have distances 1–14, representing one release pair rather than the historical-update sample.

For each path, we select its five latest single-parent modifications and compare first-parent/committed files, excluding initial additions and merges without following renames or filling short histories.

  Runtime protocol and costs.  
OpenCode 1.18.34/GLM uses frozen permission/information-flow rules, isolation, and finite propagation, rather than full SkillDetonate or general-purpose taint analysis.
The extension includes 20 input-conditioned audits, ten environment-conditioned audits, one normal-reply failure, four input-candidate static reviews, and ten direct replays; the two environment static judgments below are separate.

Fees are task/cache-dependent list-rate estimates, not invoices.

      Title: Same Outputs, Different Scores: Auditing the Unchecked Graders of Multimodal LLM Benchmarks 
      Authors:  Ahmad Jarjis Hasan ,  Jonathan Lwowski               View a PDF of the paper titled Same Outputs, Different Scores: Auditing the Unchecked Graders of Multimodal LLM Benchmarks, by Ahmad Jarjis Hasan and 1 other authors 
     View PDF 
     HTML (experimental) 



     
             Abstract: Every multimodal-LLM multiple-choice benchmark ends with a scoring rule that converts a model's response, often free-form text rather than a clean option letter, into a right/wrong verdict, buried in its code. Unlike the dataset, this rule is chosen without justification and left unexamined, yet it sets the published number. We reproduce the official scorers of eight peer-reviewed benchmarks on five open vision-language models (VLMs) that fit a single 16 GB GPU, and introduce a blinded human-plus-LLM-judge adjudication (Cohen's kappa=0.956) that recovers what the model actually answered. The scoring rule alone moves accuracy by up to 22 points on identical outputs, yet exactly 0 wherever a model emits clean option letters, so it hides on strong-model leaderboards. It is the fallback and not the rambling that does the damage: the benchmark with the highest non-compliance we measure has an artifact of exactly zero, because its scorer abstains instead of guessing; a reasoning model with non-compliance 0.000 still swings 9.5 points with which regex match of its trace the parser keeps. No standard rule is reliable: snapping a non-answer to its closest option credits answers never given yet buries correct ones, abstention discards answers stated in words, and likelihood scoring follows answer-token priors, so a single grade conflates capability with luck rather than measuring either. We release all code, labels, and the protocol, and argue benchmarks should report a non-compliance rate and at least two rules, not one unexamined grade.

      Title: Practical Preimages for 19- and 20-Step SHA-256 with Standard Padding 
      Authors:  Sebastian R. Wain               View a PDF of the paper titled Practical Preimages for 19- and 20-Step SHA-256 with Standard Padding, by Sebastian R. Wain 
     View PDF 
     HTML (experimental) 



     
             Abstract: We present practical preimage attacks on 19- and 20-step SHA-256 that respect the standard IV, Davies-Meyer feed-forward, and full FIPS 180-4 padding, for arbitrary prescribed 256-bit targets. Building on Basra's algebraic selector saturation and backward padding absorption, we introduce three techniques: an exact $O(1)$ inversion of the low padding byte $(W_{13} \bmod 256) = \mathtt{0x80}$ that leaves $(a_5, a_6)$ free for exact context shaping; a causal bit-slice equivalence theorem that prunes $99.74\%$ of right-hand candidate nodes across seven stages; and a closed-form $\mathbf{F}_2$ upper-half inverse paired with compact $Q_0^{-1}$ lookup tables. One CPU core solves arbitrary 19-step padded targets in $1.2$--$86.4$ s (median $19.5$ s) after an $18$ s table build. A 20-step padded preimage costs $2^{46.6}$ CPU-reference evaluations: $191$ node-hours on one 10-core Apple M4 CPU node (16 threads), or $9.0$--$22.2$ GPU-hours on one NVIDIA L4. A companion Zero-$a_3$ bridge inverts the unpadded 20-step compression function in $2^{38.1}$ evaluations. We provide 46 self-verifying witnesses, including 55-byte preimages of SHA-256("abc") and $0^{256}$. These attacks cover 19--20 of 64 steps and do not threaten full SHA-256.

      Title: The SIMPLE Law for Energy Cost of LLM Inference 
      Authors:  Hiari Pizzini Cavagna ,  Andrea Proia ,  Daniele Cesarini ,  Zeynep Kiziltan ,  Andrea Bartolini               View a PDF of the paper titled The SIMPLE Law for Energy Cost of LLM Inference, by Hiari Pizzini Cavagna and 4 other authors 
     View PDF 
     HTML (experimental) 



     
             Abstract: Generative AI is billed per token, yet tokens are not equally expensive. Each token enters the KV-cache and raises the cost of those that follow, so energy grows non-linearly along a sequence whose tokens look identical. No analytical model states what a token costs, and the most accurate SOTA model is a fit, not a law: it absorbs architecture into fitted coefficients, requiring per-LLM fitting. We derive closed-form expressions of the computational and memory-access complexity of LLM inference in terms of architectural hyperparameters, covering MHA and GQA, and compare a family of analytical models of increasing granularity. From these, we obtain the SIMPLE Inference Model to Predict LLMs Energy (SIMPLE), a four-parameter law that separates prefill from decode, and decode into KV-cache cost and next-token computation. Over traces of 13 dense LLMs from six families on NVIDIA H100 GPUs, it attains R2 = 0.969 and 11.97% MAPE, 3.1-3.5x below the SOTA, without per-LLM calibration. The SIMPLE law explains as well as predicts: prefill energy grows quadratically with the hidden dimension, so larger LLMs suffer most from long inputs; and more aggressive GQA KV grouping reduces the per-token energy by up to 3x relative to standard MHA. Increasing the reasoning token budget pushes output length beyond the analytically derived energy minimum, driving super-linear energy growth; although accuracy grows with the budget, energy grows faster, so Intelligence per Joule peaks at an intermediate budget and falls by up to 3.14x across a 4.0x reasoning-budget range. Agentic serving raises energy per request by 13.0x relative to non-agentic ones, driven by the growth of both the prefill and the KV-cache terms with input length; while prefix caching removes most of the prefill cost (-93%), the KV-cache term is unaffected, so even a cached agentic request costs 4.8x more.

      Title: Predictive Safety Guardrails Do Not Always Make LLM Agents Safer 
      Authors:  Weixiang Zhao ,  Zhihao Liu ,  Guancheng Li ,  Yanyan Zhao ,  Bing Qin ,  Ting Liu               View a PDF of the paper titled Predictive Safety Guardrails Do Not Always Make LLM Agents Safer, by Weixiang Zhao and 5 other authors 
     View PDF 
     HTML (experimental) 



     
             Abstract: Large language model agents increasingly take consequential actions in digital and physical environments, where safety risks may emerge only after multiple interaction steps. This has motivated world-model-driven predictive safety guardrails, which anticipate future consequences before execution. However, existing evaluations largely focus on end-to-end safety outcomes, leaving unclear whether safety gains arise from reliable prediction and faithful use of predicted risks. In this work, we systematically diagnose the prediction-to-action pipeline along three dimensions: how world-model predictions are integrated into decision making, whether the predictions themselves are reliable, and whether their content is faithfully used. Across seven policy models and two safety environments, we find that stronger prediction involvement does not yield monotonic safety gains and can reduce task completion while substantially increasing inference cost. We further find that world-model predictions remain insufficiently reliable, especially over longer horizons, where safety prediction degrades substantially relative to near-term forecasting. Finally, we find that safety gains can persist even under corrupted predictions, while locally verified predictions still leave subsequent safety violations, showing that predictive content is not faithfully incorporated into the decision process. Together, these findings expose a fundamental prediction-to-action gap in current predictive guardrails: producing more or seemingly accurate foresight is insufficient unless that foresight is both reliable and faithfully translated into safer decisions.

**简体中文** | [繁體中文](README.zh-TW.md) | [English](README.en.md) | [日本語](README.ja.md) ![Banner](docs/images/DiscImageStudio_Banner_2.png)

全能的光盘盘面可见图像生成与刻录工具

Windows 桌面版支持设计与刻录，Linux 和 macOS 的**实验性命令行版**可离线生成 CD、DVD 和蓝光镜像。 ![.NET 版本](https://img.shields.io/badge/.NET-10.0-512bd4?style=flat-square) ![运行平台](https://img.shields.io/badge/Platform-Windows%20%7C%20Linux%20%7C%20macOS-0078d6?style=flat-square) ![开发语言](https://img.shields.io/badge/Language-C%23-68217A?style=flat-square) ![GitHub Repo size](https://img.shields.io/github/repo-size/JiaFeiMiao-K-Cat/DiscImageStudio?style=flat-square&color=3cb371) ![贡献欢迎](https://img.shields.io/badge/PRs-Welcome-brightgreen?style=flat-square) [![许可证：GPL-3.0-or-later](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-GPL--3.0--or--later-blue?style=flat-square)](LICENSE)
--- ## 效果预览 ![](docs/images/case1.jpg) ![](docs/images/case2.jpg) --- ## 概述 Disc Image Studio 可将一张图片转换成符合 CD、DVD 与单层 BD-R 光盘物理层约束的数据，刻录后将使光盘盘面呈现肉眼可见的图案。 ## 界面预览 ![主页：模板与最近工程](docs/images/ui-home.png) ![设计页：图层画布与影调](docs/images/ui-design.png) ![导出页：浅色主题与输出镜像](docs/images/ui-export.png) --- ## 快速开始 Windows 下载 `win-x64.exe` 后可直接运行。Linux 或 macOS 请下载与 CPU 匹配的**实验性 CLI** 压缩包，解压后运行 `./disc-image-studio --help`。这些发布包均自带 .NET 运行时。 [GitHub Releases](https://github.com/JiaFeiMiao-K-Cat/DiscImageStudio/releases) ### 1. 新建工程 在主页选择 CD、DVD 或蓝光，指定输出位置后创建工程。 ### 2. 设计盘面 在设计页导入图片，用图层完成排版，并在右栏「影调」模块调整抖动、伽马、亮度与灰阶档位。 ### 3. 预览与导出 在预览页核对盘面投影，在导出页生成 ISO / RAW / WAV+CUE，或使用即时刻录功能直接写入空白盘片。 即时刻录为实验性功能，请只使用可报废的测试介质。 ## 功能 ### 光盘数据生成 - **CD 支持**：支持任何 CD 。您可导出带格式头的 WAV 音轨及配套 CUE，兼容 cdrecord, ImgBurn等刻录软件；也允许导出 RAW 音轨。详见 [CD 刻录兼容说明](docs/CD_AUDIO_COMPATIBILITY.md)。 - **DVD 支持**：支持任何 DVD。您可导出 ISO 镜像。 - **蓝光支持**：支持任何单层 BD-R 25 GB，支持纯绘图与 UDF 2.01 文件。详见 [ADDING_BLURAY.md](docs/ADDING_BLURAY.md)。 - **随盘文件**：CD／DVD／蓝光可在设计页直接选择要保存的文件夹及内圈／外圈位置，也可在导出页调整；设置随工程保存。 - **文件区域预览**：混合盘的设计投影和成品读回用黄色标出文件区（含文件系统）。 - **介质灰度方案**：CD 与 DVD 均使用黑白二阶，CD 使用 `0D / AA`，DVD 扰码域使用 `A5 / 92`。详见 [PHYSICAL_MODEL_AUDIT.md](docs/PHYSICAL_MODEL_AUDIT.md)。 - **灰度抖动工具**：独立程序也可将原图处理为 `0/255` 黑白二阶 PNG；支持打开或拖入原图、并排预览及无损 PNG 导出。详见[使用与构建说明](tools/FourLevelDither/README.md)。 - **盘片预设**：内置数个品牌的光盘参数，覆盖 CD／DVD／BD。您也可将自己标定好的数据贡献给我们，详见[预设维护说明](docs/DISC_PRESETS.md)。 ### 辅助标定 Disc Image Studio 提供了一套智能且精准的辅助标定流程，相较人工肉眼识别标定，辅助标定算法将可确定的盘面物理数据精确度从 10-6 提升到了 10-14。校准前采用恒定轨距，十字线的径向线条出现明显弯曲；使用辅助标定得到的三次轨距参数重新生成并刻录后，线条更接近径向直线。 | 校准前 · 恒定轨距 | 校准后 · 三次轨距 | | --- | --- | | ![校准前的 DVD 实拍：径向十字线明显弯曲](docs/images/verbatim-dvd-calibration-before.jpg) | ![校准后的 DVD 实拍：径向十字线更接近直线](docs/images/verbatim-dvd-calibration-after.jpg) | | `P20261004-133519.jpg` | `P20261004-135416.jpg` | 流程与参数说明见[辅助标定说明](docs/CALIBRATION.md)。 ### 刻录 - **镜像文件输出**：您可以导出完整 ISO / RAW 文件并使用合适的刻录软件手动刻录。 - **即时流式刻录（实验性）**：CD、DVD 与 BD-R 边生成边刻录，不保存完整镜像；BD-R 走 MMC 顺序写入。 - **不要使用非空白介质！** ### 应用形态 - 多语言界面：点击右上角「设置」按钮，在「通用 → 语言」选择简体中文、繁體中文、English、日本語或跟随系统，保存并重启应用后生效。语言和主题默认均跟随系统，已保存的明确选择继续保留；跟随系统时区分简体和繁体中文，日文系统使用日文，其他系统语言使用英文。 - 双入口：不带参数将打开 GUI；带参数则进入统一命令行。 - 模块化：CD、DVD 与蓝光通过 `IOpticalDiscModule` 接入，统一命令目录与任务契约，详见[架构说明](docs/ARCHITECTURE.md)。 ## 系统与设备要求 - 桌面版需要 Windows 10 2004（2004/20H1，19041）及以上，或 Windows 11。 - 构建：.NET 10 SDK（`global.json` 锁定 10.0.x）；自行构建的非自包含 GUI 需要 .NET 10 Windows 桌面运行时。Release EXE 已包含运行时，无需另行安装 .NET。 - “即时刻录”功能需要一台 Windows 可识别的 CD / DVD / BD 刻录机与空白盘片；BD-R 需要支持顺序写入的单层空白盘。 ## 构建与运行 ```powershell dotnet build DiscImageStudio.slnx --configuration Release dotnet run --project src/DiscImageStudio.App --configuration Release ``` 构建回归检查： ```powershell dotnet run --project src/DvdImageSolver --configuration Release -- selftest dotnet run --project tests/DiscImageStudio.ArchitectureTests --configuration Release ``` 版本规则、CI 生成 EXE、Release 草稿检查、MSIX 打包与签名流程见[发布指南](docs/RELEASING.md)。 ## 命令行 Linux（glibc）可选 `linux-x64` 或 `linux-arm64`。Apple Silicon Mac 选 `osx-arm64`，Intel Mac 选 `osx-x64`。CLI 在本地生成镜像，实际写盘可交给支持相应镜像或音轨的刻录软件。 使用 .NET 10 SDK 从源码运行 CLI ```sh dotnet run --project src/DiscImageStudio.Cli -c Release -- --help ``` CLI 可读取 PNG、JPEG、BMP 和 GIF，使用动画图片的第一帧。下面的例子用两扇区音轨验证安装，同时生成配套 CUE。 ```sh ./disc-image-studio cd-generate --input picture.png --output sample.wav --sectors 2 ``` | 命令 | 说明 | | --- | --- | | `solve` | 使用固定快速纹理映射（CW 方向）生成 DVD 镜像，黑白纹理可选抖动混合 | | `encode` | 将单个 DVD ECC 块编码为 NRZI 通道电平 | | `calibrate` | 标定投影：按生成几何从 DVD 源图片取样，按实测几何投到盘面 | | `simulate` | 按实测半径对生成的 DVD ISO 做读回模拟 | | `selftest` | 运行 DVD 引擎的确定性回归自检 | | `cd-generate` | 无随盘文件时生成 WAV + CUE / RAW 音轨；指定 `--data-dir` 时生成 CD 数据盘 ISO | | `cd-preview-warp` | 标定投影：按实测几何投影 CD 源图片 | | `cd-preview-track` | 按标定几何渲染已有的 WAV 或 RAW CD-DA 音轨（读回模拟） | | `bd-generate` | 生成完整 BD-R ISO，并写出 `.json` sidecar | | `bd-info` / `bd-probe` / `bd-encode` | 导出 BD 参数、原始负载探针或单个 ECC 簇诊断 | 各命令的完整参数见对应文档。 ## 源码结构 ```text src/DiscImageStudio.Cli/ Linux 和 macOS 离线命令行入口 src/DiscImageStudio.ImageIO/ WIC 和跨平台图像编解码 src/DiscImageStudio.Core/ 介质无关的模块契约、工程/预设模型、任务与命令目录 src/DiscImageStudio.Imaging/ CD/DVD/BD 共用的图片预处理与抖动辅助 src/DiscImageStudio.Burning/ Windows IMAPI2 设备枚举、流缓冲与安全刻录层 src/DiscImageStudio.Cd/ CD-DA 生成核心与 CD 模块 src/DiscImageStudio.Dvd/ DVD 引擎适配模块 src/DiscImageStudio.BluRay/ BD-R 几何、17PP/ECC、3T/6T 映射、流式生成与 ISO src/DiscImageStudio.Iso/ UDF 2.01 / ISO9660 写入器 src/DiscImageStudio.App/ WPF GUI、统一命令行与商店资源 src/DvdImageSolver/ 保持隔离的 DVD 编码/求解引擎 tests/ 无第三方测试框架的架构回归测试 packaging/ MSIX 清单与打包脚本 tools/ 独立辅助工具与资产生成脚本 docs/ 架构、引擎、预设、发布等文档 ``` ## 文档 | 文档 | 内容 | | --- | --- | | [ARCHITECTURE.md](docs/ARCHITECTURE.md) | 模块抽象、层间边界与扩展规则 | | [LOCALIZATION.md](docs/LOCALIZATION.md) | 界面语言配置、系统语言回退与翻译资源维护 | | [DVD_ENGINE.md](docs/DVD_ENGINE.md) | DVD NRZI 图像约束求解器的约定、编码链与自检覆盖 | | [CD_AUDIO_COMPATIBILITY.md](docs/CD_AUDIO_COMPATIBILITY.md) | CD 音轨格式、字节序与重影排查 | | [ADDING_BLURAY.md](docs/ADDING_BLURAY.md) | 蓝光模块的物理模型、生成/刻录链路与扩展点 | | [DISC_PRESETS.md](docs/DISC_PRESETS.md) | 可编辑盘片预设的分层 JSON 格式与合并规则 | | [CALIBRATION.md](docs/CALIBRATION.md) | 照片矫正（框选盘片实体最外缘与中心孔边缘）、曲线标定与 DVD 三次轨距拟合 | | [PHYSICAL_MODEL_AUDIT.md](docs/PHYSICAL_MODEL_AUDIT.md) | CD / DVD 生成物理模型复核 | | [VALIDATION.md](docs/VALIDATION.md) | 各轮构建、回归与实盘测试的本地验证记录 | | [RELEASING.md](docs/RELEASING.md) | GitHub Release、MSIX 打包、签名测试与商店提交流程 | | [CHANGELOG.md](CHANGELOG.md) | 版本变更记录 | ## 参考标准 Disc Image Studio 的实现与物理模型主要参考以下规范： | 介质 | 标准与版本 | 本项目采用的范围 | | --- | --- | --- | | CD-R | [ECMA-394，第 1 版，2010 年 12 月](https://ecma-international.org/publications-and-standards/standards/ecma-394/) — *Recordable Compact Disc Systems CD-R Multi-Speed*（[官方 PDF](https://ecma-international.org/wp-content/uploads/ECMA-394_1st_edition_december_2010.pdf)） | CD-R 介质、多速录制及 CD-DA 兼容关系；本项目生成 CD-DA 音轨。 | | DVD 公共格式 / DVD-ROM | [ECMA-267，第 3 版，2001 年 4 月](https://ecma-international.org/publications-and-standards/standards/ecma-267/) — *120 mm DVD – Read-only disk*（[官方 PDF](https://ecma-international.org/wp-content/uploads/ECMA-267_3rd_edition_april_2001.pdf)） | DVD 数据帧、ECC、EFMPlus 编码及附录 G 转换表；可记录盘的介质规则另参考 ECMA-359。 | | DVD-R | [ECMA-359，第 1 版，2004 年 12 月](https://ecma-international.org/publications-and-standards/standards/ecma-359/) — *80 mm (1,46 Gbytes per side) and 120 mm (4,70 Gbytes per side) DVD Recordable Disk (DVD-R)*（[官方 PDF](https://ecma-international.org/wp-content/uploads/ECMA-359_1st_edition_december_2004.pdf)） | 单层 DVD-R 的几何、扇区、纠错和编码；标准包含单面及双面介质，双面不等于双层。 | | BD-R | [ISO/IEC 30190:2021，第 3 版，2021 年 1 月](https://www.iso.org/standard/80770.html) — 120 mm 单层（25.0 GB）及双层（50.0 GB）可记录 BD 的信息交换与存储规范 | 实验模式采用单层 25 GB 的轨道、扇区布局、纠错和编码；目前不支持双层盘。 | CD 公共编码部分还参考了 [ECMA-130，第 2 版（CD-ROM，1996）](https://ecma-international.org/publications-and-standards/standards/ecma-130/)。 ## 刻录与介质安全须知 - Disc Image Studio 不安装驱动或服务；“即时刻录”功能使用了 Windows 自带的 IMAPI2，拒绝非空白介质。 - “即时刻录”功能已有部分实盘反馈，对不同设备、介质与刻录入口的验证覆盖仍有限，属于实验性功能，请只使用可报废的测试介质。刻录中断、断电或生成速度不足仍可能使盘片报废！ - 实际可见效果取决于盘片、刻录机、固件与写入策略。 - 混合文件夹会在开始刻录前扫描目录并固定布局；期间源文件大小改变会安全终止任务，已开始写入的盘片仍可能报废。 - BD-R 顺序写入不提供备用区重映射；中断后同一盘片通常不能继续写入。 ## 隐私与安全 - Disc Image Studio 不联网、不上传文件、不收集遥测，详见[隐私政策](PRIVACY.md)。 - 发现安全问题请不要在公开 Issue 中披露，按[安全政策](SECURITY.md)使用 GitHub 私密报告。 ## 贡献 欢迎报告问题与提交代码。开发环境搭建、模块边界规则、测试要求与 Pull Request 流程见[贡献指南](CONTRIBUTING.md)。 ## 许可证 项目采用 [GNU GPL v3.0 or later](LICENSE)（`GPL-3.0-or-later`）。CD 交织实现包含从 CDImage 移植并修改的代码，整体分发沿用兼容的 GPL 授权；分发二进制或修改版时须遵守对应源代码等要求。第三方字体与组件遵循各自许可证，详见 [授权说明](LICENSE-NOTICE.md) 和 [第三方声明](THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.txt)；应用"关于"页也可离线查看完整文本。 ## 致谢 感谢 [arduinocelentano 的 CDImage 项目](https://github.com/arduinocelentano/cdimage)，它展示了通过生成 CD 音轨在盘面形成可见图像的方法。本项目的 CD 交织实现由其相关代码移植并继续修改，CD 盘面绘图思路也受其启发。CDImage 原作者及贡献者的工作为本项目提供了重要基础。 --- ## Star History

# CD 音轨格式、字节序与重影排查

## 随盘文件与数据盘

CD 工程在设计页或导出页选择随盘文件夹后，自动切换为 ISO9660/Joliet 数据盘，输出后缀切换为 `.iso`；清空文件夹路径后恢复 WAV 音轨。文件位置可选内圈或外圈，默认内圈，设置随工程保存。文件系统元数据仍位于盘首，外圈模式把文件内容放在盘尾，绘图保持原有的整盘坐标，不挤压到剩余区域。

```powershell
DiscImageStudio.exe cd-generate --input picture.png --output cd-image.iso `
  --data-dir "D:\随盘文件" --volume-label CD_IMAGE --file-position outer
```

ISO 长度为 `扇区数 × 2048`，按 CD-ROM Mode 1 数据盘刻录。程序内即时刻录使用相同的 ISO 数据流；外部刻录软件应选择刻录镜像功能。音频交织开关和 CUE 只用于音轨模式。数据盘的绘图区单独补偿 CD-ROM 扰码及位置映射，随盘文件保留原始内容。

CD 数据盘即时刻录与音轨共用 DAO 会话和 lead-out 边界检查，保留 ATIP 标定的扇区数及完整文件布局。程序将 ISO 负载编码为 Mode 1 原始扇区，并设置数据轨标识；使用铼德医疗水蓝盘预设时仍写出 359,845 个数据扇区，不按 TAO 接口较小的可用容量缩短图案或文件。DAO 沿用音轨模式最多 3 扇区的受限 overburn 检查，超限会在写入前报错。

数据轨使用 IMAPI 小端主通道约定：在标准 Mode 1 扇区上补齐 EDC、P/Q 纠错码并扰码，保持同步头 `00 FF…FF 00` 的字节顺序。CD-ROM 物理编码的相邻字节交换与转为小端的交换相抵消；这一点也与 cdrdao 的 [RAW 编码和设备字节序转换](https://github.com/cdrdao/cdrdao/blob/master/dao/dao.cc) 相符。文件内外圈的 ISO 布局和绘图物理坐标映射不随该传输约定改变。

设计投影、影调小预览和带有效 `.iso.json` 布局信息的成品读回以黄色标出文件区（含文件系统）。同名元数据记录几何、影调和文件位置；移动 ISO 时建议同时移动它。预览显示绘图负载的映射，实盘效果仍需刻录验证。

## 推荐用法

新生成任务默认输出 `cd-track.wav`，同时生成 `cd-track.cue`。WAV 为无压缩 PCM：44.1 kHz、16 位、双声道，数据区为小端。将这两个文件放在同一目录，移动或改名时也要同步更新 CUE 中的文件名。CUE 是可选项：导出工作区取消勾选“同时导出 CUE 文件”，或命令行传 `--cue false`，则只写出 WAV。

| 刻录入口 | 使用方式 |
| --- | --- |
| cdrecord | `cdrecord dev=设备 speed=速度 -audio "cd-track.wav"`，不要额外添加 `-swab` |
| ImgBurn | 在“Write image file to disc”中打开 `cd-track.cue` |
| 程序内流式刻录 | 自动生成同样的小端 PCM 数据，不包含 WAV 文件头，不生成完整临时音轨 |
| 旧 RAW 工作流 | 输出仍可选择 `.raw`；`cdrecord -audio "cd-track.raw"` 不加 `-swab` |

输出后缀决定真实格式，只接受 `.wav` 和 `.raw`。不能通过重命名把旧 RAW 变成 WAV；必须重新生成。WAV 的配套 CUE 使用 `FILE "cd-track.wav" WAVE`，不使用 `BINARY`。Unicode 文件名使用带 BOM 的 UTF-8 CUE，支持空格和中文。ImgBurn 作者曾验证这种 CUE 的 Unicode 文件名支持，并指出早期 2.5.0.0 的相关问题在 2.5.1.0 修复。[ImgBurn 作者说明](https://forum.imgburn.com/topic/13526-unicode-filename-problem-in-cue-file/)

命令行生成示例（几何参数应使用自己的实测设置）：

```powershell
DiscImageStudio.exe cd-generate --input picture.png --output cd-track.wav --interleave true
```

`--cue`（缺省 `true`）控制 WAV 输出是否同时写出同名 CUE；`.raw` 输出始终不写 CUE。

WAV 的文件长度为 `扇区数 × 2352 + 44`；音频长度、生成进度和流式刻录容量仍为 `扇区数 × 2352`。文件头不占盘片音轨扇区，也不改变图案几何。

## 影调（抖动、sRGB 线性化、灰阶与亮度）

CD 的每个音频字节对应约 6.8 µm 的盘面长度；正常观看距离下，眼睛会把成百上千个字节积分成一个色调。因此“每个字节只有黑白两种图案”不等于“画面只有黑白两色”，中间调靠相邻字节的黑白比例还原。

| 参数 | 含义 |
| --- | --- |
| 抖动强度 0–100% | 0% 按 128 的硬阈值输出（旧行为）；100% 逐字节在相邻档位间按比例选择，中间调由黑白字节的空间比例形成 |
| 灰阶档位（仅 CD） | 2 级用 `0x0D` / `0xAA`；4 级用 `0x0D` / `0x10` / `0x63` / `0xAA`（`0x0D` 为黑、`0xAA` 为白） |
| sRGB 线性化（伽马） | 先按 sRGB 传递函数解码再抖动；改变黑白点密度，不改变输出电平 |
| 亮度 | 整体平移灰阶，范围 −64…+64（0..255 单位） |

命令行参数（`cd-generate` 与 `cd-preview-warp` 都接受）：

```powershell
DiscImageStudio.exe cd-generate --input picture.png --output cd-track.wav `
  --tone-dither 1 --tone-levels 2 --tone-brightness 0 --tone-gamma false
```

缺省值是 `--tone-dither 0 --tone-levels 2 --tone-brightness 0 --tone-gamma false`，与旧版逐字节一致。新建工程在设计页右栏的「影调」模块里默认 75% / 2 级；没有 `tone` 节的旧工程按 0% 载入，保存后写入 `tone` 节。导出页只保留输出选项，并在输出卡内提示影调归设计页。

抖动相位由**逻辑字节索引**决定（`globalByte`），而不是屏幕坐标。延迟交织把字节在文件中挪位后，读回预览仍按同一逻辑索引还原，因此生成、标定投影和读回看到的是同一套图案。标定图案（`GeneratePattern`）固定使用硬阈值，不参与抖动。

音轨旁的同名 `.json` 记录 `toneDitherStrength`、`toneLevels`、`toneBrightness`、`toneSrgbLinearization`；预览页载入外部音轨时会连同几何、交织一起同步这些值。

读回预览默认 1600 px、每扇区 16 个采样，并把落在同一像素的采样**累加平均**。旧版固定 900 px、每扇区 2 个采样且后写覆盖，稀疏采样会在中间调留下白点，看起来像报纸网点；提高采样密度后同一盘面才呈现连续影调。预览页的“设计投影”默认把实测几何设为与工程几何一致，打开工程即得到中性投影；填入实测半径后才会显示两套几何的偏差。

## 已确认的问题

2026-09-12 的用户实盘对照：同一份既有 RAW，用 cdrecord 的 `-audio` 和 `speed` 正常；添加 `-swab` 即可复现重影。这确认了既有 RAW 应按 cdrecord 默认的大端音频输入解释。

此前文件导出和流式刻录共用完全相同的 `GenerateToStream` 输出，流式路径没有执行字节序转换。但不同输入入口的约定不同：

| 输入 | 音频数据的要求 |
| --- | --- |
| cdrecord 无头 `-audio` | 默认大端 |
| cdrecord 无头 `-audio -swab` | 小端；该选项声明需要交换的输入顺序 |
| cdrecord WAV | 解析文件头，自动识别音频字节序 |
| CUE 的 `FILE ... BINARY` | 小端；不能把既有大端 RAW 直接套入 BINARY CUE |
| IMAPI `AddTrack(IMAPI_CD_SECTOR_AUDIO, stream)` | 与 16 位双声道 44.1 kHz WAV 数据区相同的样本布局，即无头小端 PCM |

上述 cdrecord 行为及 BINARY 定义来自 [cdrecord 官方手册](https://cdrtools.sourceforge.net/private/man/cdrecord/cdrecord.1.html)；IMAPI 的音频样本布局来自 [Microsoft 的 AUDIO 扇区定义](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/imapi2/ne-imapi2-imapi_cd_sector_type)。ImgBurn 作者也提供了成功刻录 `FILE ... WAVE` CUE 的例子。[ImgBurn WAVE CUE 实例](https://forum.imgburn.com/topic/25173-extract-only-session-two-from-audio-cd/page/2/)

这里的 `AudioSectorType = 0` 是 IMAPI 枚举的 AUDIO 值，不是把音轨写成物理 Mode 0。`IRawCDImageCreator::AddTrack` 当前只支持 AUDIO 类型。[Microsoft AddTrack 文档](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/imapi2/nf-imapi2-irawcdimagecreator-addtrack)

## 为什么会形成两组轮廓

现有 `CddaInterleaver` 为目标字节执行延迟补偿。交换最终输出每个 16 位样本的两个字节，会把原本属于不同延迟位置的字节交叉送入编码链。因此不能把变化理解为普通音频数值变化，也不能在图像采样之前交换一次来抵消。

针对现有延迟表进行整数标签排列实验，排除头尾填充后，额外的样本字节交换会让逆映射后的偶数位置偏移 `+73` 个目标字节，奇数位置偏移 `-73` 个目标字节。这解释了双轮廓机制；它是程序延迟排列模型的推导，并非完整光驱 CIRC 模型或实体盘测量。

修正保留采样和延迟表，在补偿完成后的 2352 字节扇区输出边界选择字节序：旧 RAW 大端；WAV 和 IMAPI 小端。WAV 文件头解决外部工具对格式和字节序的识别，流式接口仍按其约定只接收数据区。

## 读回必须抵消延迟交织

延迟补偿会把逻辑字节 i 推到文件索引 `i + offset(i % 24)`：交织表按 28×D（D=4）帧的延迟线存储，每帧 24 字节，所以偏移在 72 与 2592 之间（对应帧延迟与帧内列旋转之和）。直接按文件顺序把字节铺到螺旋线上，等于把图案整体旋转并剪切——同一张图在 60000 扇区、900 px 的对照下，约 17.5% 的绘制像素与源图不符，看起来就是"轻微扭曲"。

因此 `cd-preview-track` 默认执行逆映射（`--deinterleave`，缺省 `true`）：逻辑字节 i 取文件索引 `i + CddaInterleaveTable.FileOffsetFor(i % 24)`，需要 2592 字节的前视窗口。该表的正向延迟与 `CddaInterleaver` 共用 `CddaInterleaveTable`，两侧不可能各自漂移。

尾部的代价：延迟线在文件结束时仍持有最后若干帧，这些逻辑字节没有写出（1318–1332 字节，不到一个扇区），读回时只能留空。它位于音轨最外圈，占整条音轨的比例随扇区数下降。

`cd-generate` 现在会在音轨旁写出 `<track>.json`（`format: cd-da-track-v1`，含 r0/r1/扇区数/线速度/起始角/图片外半径/是否交织）。预览工作区在切换音轨时读取它并载入标定几何与交织开关，因此导入其他机器生成的音轨也能按正确模型读回。

## 标定投影：源图片与两套几何

`cd-preview-warp` 是读回路径的快速对照，也是预览工作区“标定预览”模式调用的命令：输入是源图片而不是音轨，参数是两套几何——生成几何决定第 i 个字节从图片的哪个位置取样，实测几何决定这个字节画在盘面的哪个位置（`--actual-r0`、`--actual-r1`，缺省 24.3 / 56.6 mm）。两套几何相同时投影即原图；不同时，图案按实测盘面偏移，这正是半径标定要看的现象。扇区数、线速度、起始角与图片外半径由两套几何共用，后三者固定为 1200 mm/s、0°、57.5 mm。

因为它只读源图片、不扫描整条音轨，改半径或几何后的刷新成本是图片的尺寸而不是音轨的尺寸（80 分钟盘约 845 MB），适合在标定预览里试参数、再用读回模拟确认最终盘面。

## 验证与边界

- RAW 与 WAV：对非对称图案，交织开启与关闭两种情况下，WAV 的 data 区均严格等于旧 RAW 逐 16 位交换后的字节序列；长度保持不变。
- 流式输出：在禁止 Seek/Position 的前向流中生成小端音频，结果逐字节等于 WAV 的 data 区，且不包含文件头。
- WAV 预览：解析 RIFF 的 `fmt ` / `data`，跳过未知块及奇数长度填充，限制读取范围，归一化字节序；拒绝非 PCM、非 44.1 kHz、非 16 位或非双声道数据。不同采样步长下与对应 RAW 预览一致。预览仍是文件字节映射，未模拟完整物理 CIRC/EFM，不能替代实盘判定。
- 读回一致性：同一源图分别生成交织与不交织的音轨，`--deinterleave true` 读回交织音轨与按文件顺序读回不交织音轨的结果，除延迟线尾部一个扇区内的像素外逐像素相同（900 px、非对称测试图下差异仅落在尾部投影内，变异测试把帧延迟改动 24 字节即报 245 处不一致）。
- 标定投影一致性：同一源图先按生成几何 `(24.5, 56.8)` 生成音轨，再把 `cd-preview-warp` 的投影（实测=生成、实测=`24.3/56.6`）与 `cd-preview-track` 用对应几何读回的结果逐像素比较，阈值化后完全一致（900 px）；实测半径缩小时投影的重心半径随之减小，因此两套几何不会串位。
- Windows 内存实验：向现有 `MsftRawCDImageCreator` 输入 300 个非对称音频扇区，扫描完整的 2448 字节 RAW 结果扇区，全部音频字节原样保留。生成器不会替调用者交换字节。测试不创建刻录设备、不写入光盘。
- 2026-09-12 用户在本次修复后完成实盘试验，反馈已无重影。这是用户提供的实体盘结果；流式、cdrecord、ImgBurn 三个入口的逐项实测细节未单独记录。

微软 `WriteMedia` 文档没有说明它内部的字节交换实现；上述结论没有把内存实验等同于观察到设备传输时的交换。[Microsoft WriteMedia 文档](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/imapi2/nf-imapi2-idiscformat2rawcd-writemedia)

# Auto Ontology Agents can retrieve documents and query databases, but reliability gates agentic analytics: a revenue metric answered faster is worth nothing if the number is wrong. Agents need a context layer that tells them where data lives, what it means, whether to use it, how to use it, where it came from, and what is similar. NVIDIA Auto Ontology is an open library that builds that layer from enterprise metadata, reconciles definitions across systems, and exposes it to any agent harness through MCP, CLI, and API. It complements the semantic models customers already own. It enables developers to: - Discover: generate enterprise ontologies from metadata; connect existing ontologies and semantic models; build AI-ready knowledge graphs. - Ground: give agents trusted business meaning for metrics, entities, and relationships; reconcile inconsistent definitions across systems. - Validate: check generated queries against certified definitions and lineage; return provenance with every answer. - Expose: serve context to any agent harness through MCP, CLI, and API. Learn: fold certified corrections and usage back into the ontology, so shared context improves with every question. ## Benchmarks To run a text-to-SQL benchmark such as BIRD, refer to the [ontology SQL evaluation repository](https://github.com/NVIDIA/ontology-sql-eval/). > **Licensing & contributions.** Auto Ontology is distributed under the > [Apache License 2.0](./LICENSE). Third-party open-source components > bundled, linked, or otherwise used by this project are listed in > [`THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md`](./THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md). **This project > is currently not accepting external contributions.**

## Key Features - **Natural-language querying** of structured data — questions are translated to SQL and executed against connected databases, powered by NVIDIA NIM. - **Semantic catalog / ontology layer** over relational sources, stored in Postgres alongside the catalog it describes. - **Authentication & RBAC** —using [Better Auth](https://github.com/better-auth/better-auth). - **Web UI** for chat, analysis, data catalog, analytics, and settings. - **Flexible deployment** — Helm chart for Kubernetes or Docker Compose for a local stack. ## Software Components | Component | Technology | Role | Default port | | ------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ | ------------ | | Frontend | Next.js 16 (React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS 4), Better Auth, Prisma | Web UI, authentication, API gateway | 3000 | | Backend | FastAPI (Python 3.12+), LangChain | Chat / NL-to-SQL, catalog, datasource APIs | 3001 | | Ingestion worker | FastAPI (Python 3.12+) | Ingests tabular data and writes embeddings | 3002 | | Postgres + pgvector | Relational Database | App metadata, the catalog and ontology, vector store | 5432 | | HashiCorp Vault | Optional | Secure storage of connection credentials | — | ### NVIDIA NIM Auto Ontology uses NVIDIA NIM endpoints for inference — either the hosted [NVIDIA API catalog](https://build.nvidia.com) (`integrate.api.nvidia.com`) or self-hosted NIMs. The defaults in `.env.example` are: - **LLM:** `nvidia/nemotron-3-nano-30b-a3b` - **Embeddings:** `nvidia/nemotron-3-embed-1b` - **Reranking:** `nvidia/llama-nemotron-rerank-vl-1b-v2` The endpoints and models are configured via the `DEFAULT_MODELS_ENDPOINT`, `DEFAULT_MODELS_MODEL`, `EMBED_ENDPOINT`, and `EMBED_MODEL` environment variables and require a `DEFAULT_MODELS_API_KEY`. #### Model triplets Each model role is configured by a **triplet** of environment variables — `_ENDPOINT` (URL), `_API_KEY`, and `_MODEL`: | Prefix | Role | | ---------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- | | `DEFAULT_MODELS` | Shared default; every field below falls back to it. | | `REASONING` | Main chat / NL-to-SQL model. | | `NON_REASONING` | Lighter model used for entity extraction. | | `EMBED` | Text-embedding model (must match between ingest and query). | | `RERANK` | Reranker used by the retrieval flow. | You can set a full triplet, only some of its fields, or none at all — any field left unset falls back to the matching `DEFAULT_MODELS_`. So the simplest setup is to fill in `DEFAULT_MODELS_*` and override per-triplet fields only where they differ (e.g. `EMBED_MODEL`, `NON_REASONING_MODEL`). `*_API_KEY` also falls back to the legacy `NVIDIA_API_KEY` for backward compatibility. ## Deployment ### Prerequisites - **Docker** with **Docker Compose v2** (e.g. Docker Desktop on macOS/Windows, Docker Engine on Linux) for the local stack. For Kubernetes deployments see [`DEPLOYMENT.md`](./DEPLOYMENT.md). - An **NVIDIA API key** (`nvapi-...`) for NVIDIA NIM (chat and ingestion) from the NVIDIA API catalog at . - Connection details for the source database(s) you want to query (Databricks, Postgres, Snowflake, or DuckDB). ### Installation **Kubernetes** To deploy Auto Ontology on a Kubernetes cluster, see [`DEPLOYMENT.md`](./DEPLOYMENT.md). **Local (Docker Compose)** 1. Clone the repository: ```bash git clone auto_ontology && cd auto_ontology ``` 2. Create your environment file (.env) from the template and fill in the values (Postgres credentials, `DEFAULT_MODELS_API_KEY`, `CONNECTION_STRINGS`, etc.). See [`.env.example`](./.env.example) for the full list of variables: ```bash cp .env.example .env # edit .env ``` Note: - `AUTH_SECRET` and `APP_URL` are **required** — without them every page fails with a Better Auth "default secret" error. - `POSTGRES_PORT` only changes the **host-side** port mapping (set it if 5432 is already taken on your machine); containers always reach Postgres on the internal network port. 3. Build the images and start the stack: ```bash docker compose up -d --build ``` This builds the backend (`auto_ontology`) and frontend (`auto-ontology-frontend`) images, brings up Postgres and pgAdmin, runs the one-shot `frontend-migrate` job to sync the database schema, and starts the app (backend, ingestion service, and frontend). 4. Open the UI at (the backend API is on `:3001`, pgAdmin on `:5050`). > **Troubleshooting:** if the UI loads without the left navigation panel > (or otherwise looks broken after a restart), your browser is holding a > stale session cookie — this happens when `AUTH_SECRET` changes or the > database is reset. Clear the site data for `localhost:3000` (or delete > the `better-auth.session_token` cookie) and sign in again. ## Connections Management Auto Ontology resolves the source databases it connects to from two sources: 1. **Added through the UI** — connections created from within the app. With this option the connection credentials are **stored in plaintext in Postgres unless Vault is configured**: - **Without Vault:** the full connection object (including the password) is JSON-serialized and stored, unencrypted, on the catalog's database row. - **With Vault:** the credentials are written to Vault, keyed by the database name, and the catalog row stores no credentials (the database name is the lookup key — there is no separate reference field). Vault is enabled only when all of `VAULT_ADDR`, `VAULT_NAMESPACE`, `VAULT_ROLE_ID`, and `VAULT_SECRET_ID` are set (`VAULT_AUTH_MOUNT` and `VAULT_KV_MOUNT` are optional overrides). It is off by default; a partial configuration is ignored with a warning and falls back to plaintext storage. 2. **`CONNECTION_STRINGS` environment variable** — a comma-separated list of connection strings supplied at deploy time (e.g. the Helm `--set connectionStrings=` flag). This is a fallback: it is used only when there are no UI-added connections. ## Authentication Auto Ontology Supports SSO for authentication. The Redirect URI should be configured in the IdP as: APP_URL/api/auth/sso/callback ### API tokens (scripting) A browser signs in and gets a session cookie, which a script cannot obtain. For scripts, notebooks, and scheduled jobs, mint an **API token** instead: 1. Open the user menu (top right) → **API Tokens** → **New token**. 2. Name it, optionally pick an expiry (default: never), and **copy the token**. Auto Ontology stores only a SHA-256 hash of it, so it is shown exactly once. Losing it means minting a new one. Send it as `x-api-key` on any `/api/...` call — `Authorization: Bearer ` works too: ```sh curl -H "x-api-key: $AUTO_ONTOLOGY_API_TOKEN" https://auto_ontology.example.com/api/terms ``` ```python import os import requests session = requests.Session() session.headers["x-api-key"] = os.environ["AUTO_ONTOLOGY_API_TOKEN"] terms = session.get("https://auto_ontology.example.com/api/terms").json() answer = session.post( "https://auto_ontology.example.com/api/chat/completions", json={"question": "How many orders shipped last week?"}, ).json() ``` Things worth knowing: - **A token acts as its owner.** It carries no permissions of its own — every call is authorized against the owner's role, exactly as it would be in the browser. A viewer's token cannot do admin things. - **The whole API surface accepts it.** Authentication is resolved in one place (`frontend/auth/resolve-user.ts`) for every route, so any endpoint in [`docs/openapi/auto-ontology-api.json`](./docs/openapi/auto-ontology-api.json) that is not `withPublic` works with a token. - **Revocation is immediate.** Delete the token in the UI, or delete/ban the owning user, and the next request with it gets a 401. - **Tokens cannot manage tokens.** Creating and revoking requires a signed-in session, so a leaked token cannot issue itself successors. ## Agent API conversations Public clients call the authenticated Next.js gateway at `POST /api/chat/completions`. The response is an SSE stream containing `step`, `result`, or `error` events, followed by `[DONE]`. `conversation_id` is optional: - Omit it for a stateless, one-shot request. - Supply a client-generated UUID to create or continue a conversation. - Reuse the same UUID for every turn in the thread. Wait for `[DONE]` before sending the next turn; overlapping requests for one conversation return `409 Conversation in progress`. ```json { "question": "What about last month?", "conversation_id": "d61d8aa3-d496-4fa7-97ce-4f831c162e7f" } ``` For conversational requests, FastAPI loads up to the five most recent completed turns (bounded to 12,000 characters) and rewrites contextual input such as “What about August?” into a standalone question before running the existing text-to-SQL graph. Independent questions are passed through unchanged. Internal agent thoughts, chart payloads, errors, and raw SQL result sets are not reused as context. Conversation history is scoped to the authenticated Auto Ontology user. Browser and service callers should use the Next.js gateway, which resolves the user and forwards the internal `x-auto-ontology-user-id` header to FastAPI. The FastAPI port is a trusted internal service boundary: it must not be exposed publicly because that header is not independently verified by FastAPI. A direct FastAPI request without `conversation_id` remains stateless; a direct request with `conversation_id` requires the trusted identity header. The web UI manages the UUID automatically. An API-created conversation can be opened in the UI at `/chat?focus=` when it belongs to the signed-in user. ## Agent skills Coding agents: start at [`AGENTS.md`](./AGENTS.md). Skills live in [`skills/`](./skills/) (`nvidia-ontology-setup`, `nvidia-ontology-management`, `nvidia-ontology-query`). Maintainers keep using [`CLAUDE.md`](./CLAUDE.md). ## MCP server Agent harnesses such as Cursor and Claude Desktop can query your data through Auto Ontology's [MCP](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) server. See [`mcp/`](./mcp/) to run it and [`docs/mcp.md`](./docs/mcp.md) for the details. ## License Auto Ontology is licensed under the [Apache License, Version 2.0](./LICENSE). SPDX identifier: `Apache-2.0`. Each NVIDIA-authored source file in this repository carries an SPDX header of the form: ```text SPDX-FileCopyrightText: Copyright (c) 2024-2026, NVIDIA CORPORATION & AFFILIATES. All rights reserved. SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0 ``` Third-party open-source components used by Auto Ontology are enumerated, with their upstream licenses and project URLs, in [`THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md`](./THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md). Components added by the container images are listed separately in [`CONTAINER_THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md`](./CONTAINER_THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md). ## Notice and Disclaimer NOTICE AND DISCLAIMER: This software automatically retrieves, accesses or interacts with external materials. Those retrieved materials are not distributed with this software and are governed solely by separate terms, conditions and licenses. You are solely responsible for finding, reviewing and complying with all applicable terms, conditions, and licenses, and for verifying the security, integrity and suitability of any retrieved materials for your specific use case. This software is provided "AS IS", without warranty of any kind. The author makes no representations or warranties regarding any retrieved materials, and assumes no liability for any losses, damages, liabilities or legal consequences from your use or inability to use this software or any retrieved materials. Use this software and the retrieved materials at your own risk. External materials Auto Ontology interacts with at run time: | Material | When | Terms | | --- | --- | --- | | NVIDIA-hosted model APIs ([build.nvidia.com](https://build.nvidia.com), `integrate.api.nvidia.com`) for LLM, embedding, and reranking | Chat, ingestion, and semantic compilation, with the default model configuration | Terms of the NVIDIA API catalog and of each model | | Any other OpenAI-compatible model endpoint you configure (`*_ENDPOINT` / `*_MODEL`) | Same | Terms of that provider and model | | KumoRFM predictive-query service | Only when `KUMO_RFM_API_KEY` is set | Kumo's terms | | Your source databases | Ingestion, profiling, and query execution | Your agreements for those systems | ## Contributing **This project is currently not accepting contributions.** Issues, pull requests, and patches submitted from outside the Auto Ontology maintainer team will not be reviewed or merged. Security-relevant reports should follow the process described in [`SECURITY.md`](./SECURITY.md). Maintainer workflow is in [`CONTRIBUTING.md`](./CONTRIBUTING.md).
